To-morrow is not elastic enough in which to press the neglected duties of to-day. Adversity is the trial of principle. Without it a man can hardly know whether he is honest or not. Character is higher than intellect. A great s-ul will be strong to live as well as strong to think.— Emerson. A local Mrs. Malaprop gushingly says that she "does so love to sit at the piano in the gloaming and impoverish." If we could give, as a charity, to those who employ it well, the time that we waste, how many beggars would be rich. What Is wanting in woman is the intermediate sentiment' between love and bate; she knows nothing of that weapon of the strong man—inoifference. There are some marriages which remind us of the poor fellow who said, "She couldn't get any husband, and I couldn't get any wife, so we got Turried." How TO Br. A CRCESII3.—FoIf a quarter of a century Mrs. Lydia Maria Child and her husband lived without a servant •In their humble and pleasant home in Wayland, 51.11.5. Once, relates- Zion's Ucrald, when ha said to bar, "1 wi.h far your sake, dear,! ras as rich as Crce-ue," she responded, " Inc are Cace lap, for you are king of Lydia." A servant who had been admonished by her mistress babe very careful in " washin' up" the best tea things, was over- heard shortly after wards indulging in the following soliloquy when in the act of wiping the sugar basin:—" If I was to drop this 'ere basin,and 'vas to catch it, I suppose I shouldn't ca.r.cia it; but if I warn to droo it, and wasn't to catch it, I reckon T should inn 01.01 it." 0 You must admit, doctor." said a witty lady to a cele- brated doctor of divinity, with whom she was arguing the question of the " eqaality of the sexes"—" you must ad- mit that woman was created before man." "Well, really, madam," said the astonished divine, "1 muit ask you to prove your case." "That can be easily done, sir," she naively replied. "Wasn't Eve the first maid?" A rase Judge/ whose personal apuearance was as unpre- possessing asits legal knowledge was profound af3l his in- tellect keen, interrupted a female withess—" humbugged you, my good woman. What do you mean by that ?" said he, sternly. "Well, my Lord," replied the woman, "I don't know how to explain it exactly; but if a girl called your Lordship a handsome man, she would be humbugging you." The thought of time is solemn and awful to all minds in proportion to their depth; and, in proportion as the mind is superficial, the thought his appeared little, and has been treated with levity. Brethren, let but a man poetess him- self of that thought—the deep thought of the brevity of time; this thought—that time is short, and that eternity is long,—and he has learned the first great secret of Unworld- liness.—F. JV. Robertlon. "WAIVING arm PRISSTTRE.—A correspondent tells a tale of Mrs. George Tickuor's last summer at Newport, which toth.bee one of the most sympathetic chords of the human heart. In her hall always stood a most impassive and im- preesive liveried footman, bearing a silver salver on which to receive Garde, and showing usually no more emotion than the wooden- hat rack. But one afternoon, when Mrs. Tick- nor was out, and the house was very quiet, an amanuensis, copying notes in an upstairs room, was startled by a series cf howls and yds from below. She kept at her work, think- ing that it the tervants in the kitchen were killing each other it was no hd•ineee of here. Scon up came a maid to wit if she was frightenel- She said she was not. "Oh, ye ain't? Well, I thought I'd tell P, morn, that it's only the footman. When the folks is out an' the house quiet, he can't stand it, an' he has to holler. L's kind o' relievin' to him."

"Wur is Wonsra DOING Is WoaTu DOING WELL."— " There ! " said Harry, throwing down the shoe-brush ; " there ! that'll do. My shoes dol't look very bright, but no matter. Who cares? "—" Whatever is worth doing is worth doing well," said his father, who had heard the boy's careless speech. Harry blushed, while his father continued.: —"My boy, your shoes look wretched. Pick up the brush and make them shine; when you have finished come into the house." As soon as Harry appeared with his well- polished shoes, his father said :—" I have a little story to tall you. I once krew a poor boy whose mother tinght him the proverb which I repeated to you a few minutes ago. This boy went out to service in a gentleman's family, and he took pains to do everything well, no matter bow palm- • p •rtant it seemed. His employer was pleased, and tonk him into his shop. He did his work well there, and when sent on errands he went quichly and was soon beck in his place. 6o be advanoed from step to step until he became a clerk, and then a pricer ia the bueiness He is now a,rich man, and anxious that his son Harry shonld learn to practice the rule wnioh made him prosper." " Why, papa, were you a poor boy °nese ? " asked Harry. "Yes, my son—so poor that f had to go out to service, arid black boots, and wait at table, c.nd do any menial service which was noloired of me. By doing little things well I was soon trusted with more important one,."—Toteng Reaper. Htrsiouns OF EXAMINATIONS.—It is related of a roegle-and-ready examiner in roolchle that on one occasion, hairing failed to elicit satisfactory replies from a student re- gkeing the muscular arrangement, of the arm and leg, he -somewhat brusquely said, " Ab ! perhaps, sir, you could tell me the names el the wineeles I should pot in action were I to kick you ?" "Certainly, sir," replied the candidate; " you would put in motion the flexors and extensors of my arms, for I should use them to knock yon down!" Hietory is Silent, and parhape wisely En, concerning the fare of this particular student. The story is told of a witty Irish stu- dent, Whn, once upon a time, appeared before an examining hoard to ande,go an examiation in medical jurisprudence. The subject of examin Aim WAS poisons, and the examiner had selected that deadly poison prussic acid as the subject of his questions. "Pray, sir," said be to the candidate, "what is a poisonous dose of prussic acid ?" After cogita- ting for a moment, the student replied with promptitude, "Half an ounce, Sir !" Horrified at the extreme ignorance of the candidate, the examiner exclaimed," Half An ounce! Why, sir, yon mast be dreaming! That is an amount which wonld poison a community, sir, not to speak of an in- divielual !" "Well, sir," replied the Hibernian, "I only thought Pa be on the safe side when you asked a poisonous dose !" "But pray, sir," continued the examiner, intent on ascertaining the candidate's real knowledge, "suppose a man dld swellow half an ounce of prussic acid, what treatment would eon piescribe?" "I'd ride home for a stomach. pump," replied the unabashed student. "Are you aware, sir," retorted the examiner, " that prussic acid is a poison wkfich acts with great vapidity ?" Well, yes," replied the student. "Then, sir, suppose you did such itfooliele thing as you have just stated," said the examiner; "you ride home for your stomach-pump; and on returning you find your patient dead. What would you or what could yon do then ?" whiled the examiner in triumph, thinking he had • driven his victim into a corner whence there was no escape. "What would Ido ?" reiterated the student. "Do! Why, Fd heuld a post-mortem l" For once in his life that ex- aminer must have felt that dente ignnrance, united to newer of repartee, was more than a match for him—Chad/I- bers's Journal. CANNING's INTRODUCTION TO GLADSTONR AT Erox.—A few weeks after Byron's eeith, Mr. Canning came down to Eton for the 4th of June, and found time to have nearly an hotit's chat with the son of his principal supporter in the famous Liverpool Election of 1812. Cannine's career exer- cised the greatest fascination over young Gladstone's mind, and an that privileged day when he took the Foreign Secre- tary to see his room and then walked about college listening to ::!s advice and to his remarks about some of the import- ant topice, of the day, the fascination became complete and it vO.l doubtless from a happy recollection of his own precocity that Canning did not speak to his young admirer SIA a boy about childish things, he must have seen the sparkle of hero-won/I,p in Gladstone's eyes, and he laid himself out to produce a deep impression by emitting on all eabjects those generous sentiment, which leave their mark on 'a boy's understanding. His advice, conveyed in the •toae of an elder brother, was all shout school work :—"Give plenty ef time to your verses; every good copy you do will et in your memory some Poetical thought of well-turned m .fortn of speech which you will find useful wben you speak In public," but when ho touched on politics he seoke "almost like one who has need of advice himeelt Befall was he (or seemed to be) of those illusions which official life too often diTele." The universal reign of Parliarnents,he said, was "going to loose the tongues of nations that had been dumb, and set their hearts beating. imagine a Peruvian Parliament, fancy a new Areopagus at Athens!. Greeks in tail coats and beaver hats; Epeminondes, M.P. for Thebes, Alcibiades, M.P. for Athens, Lycnrgns and Draco both sit- ting for Sparta, and being Law Officers of the Crown, Draco of course expecting his speedy promotion to a Lord Chief Justiceship. It all seems so strange and yet its all coming, and what a novel thing it will be for Enelish Ministers to find themselves in communication with nations, veritably with nations, and not with excited or trembling kings speaking throcgh arrogant soldiers or tricky courtiers! . ." MILK Sztruco.-1. To make the finest flavoured and longrt keeping batter, the cream must undergo a ripening process by exposure to the oxygen of the air while it is sweet. This is beet done while it is rising. The ripening Is very tardy when the temperature is low. 2. After cream becomes sour, the more ripening the more it depreciates. The seoner it is then skimmed and churned the better, but it shon,d not be churned while too new. The best time for skimming and churning is just before acidity becomes ap- hareut. 3. Cream makes better butter to rise in cold air than to rise in celd water, but it will rise sooner in cold water, and the milk will keep sweet longer. 4. The deeper milk is set the less airing the cream geti. while rising. 5. The depth of setting should vary with the temperature: the lower it is the deeper milk may be set; the higher, the shallower it should be. Milk should never be set shallow in a low temperature nor deep in a high one. Setting deep in co:d water economises time, labour, and space. 6. While r&lk is standing for cream to rise the parity of the cream, and consequently the fine flavour and keeping of the batter, will be injnred if the surfeee of the cream is exposed freely to air enueli W,Arlila than the cream. 7. When cream is colder than the surrounding air, it take.; up moisture and impurities from the air. When the air is colder than the cream, it takes up moisture and whatever escapes from the cream. In the former case the cream purifies the surround- ing air; in the latter, the air helps' to purify the cream. The eelection of a creamer should hinge on what is more desired —highest quality or greatest convenience and economy in time, space, and labour.—Professor Arnold. TEE CATTLE TRADE OF COLORADO —So rapid has been the growth of this trade, that the cattle of Colorado are now eettimetd to number 1,000,000 head, with a value of $20,000,000 or £4,000,000. The largest owners are the Prairie Cattle Company, in the southern part of the State, who possess 60,000 head, one-half of which are American and fine bred animals, which have cost not less than $3O per head. But three quarters of a million of the cattle of Colorado are the property of men styled "cattle kings," whose ownership ranges respectively from 15,000 to 40,000 head. A Denver journal states that many of the animals owned by the farmers are worth from $lOO to $5OO each; these are the jerseys, the Devone, the shorthorns, the Halsteine, and the white-faced Herefords. Upwards of two millions of money is invested in Colorado in these animals of superior blood. A quarter of a million cattle are grazed In Pueblo, Bent, Huerfano, and Las Anima's counties in the south, while another half million are east of Denver- ' and between Kit Carson ared the borders of Klaus and the Platte River at the north, the remaining quirer of a mil, lion being found in the great parks in the Sin Luis Valley, on the Dolores, over beyond the Continental divide on the Gunnison, the Grand, and the Blue, and with the farmers scattered over the entire State. During the year 1832 the Increase in the cattle through the whole State has been 25

- per cent, greater than in any previous year, and the valua- tion has almost doubled. This was owing to the mild win- ter of 1881, and the abundant grass of last summer. The great rise in the valuation was due to the scarcity of beef in the East and in Europe, and the growing interest of Eoelish and scotch capital in the great grazing business in tae interior of America. No less than £3,000,000 sterling of English and Scotch capital has been paid for cattle in Colorado since the year 1872, and another million has been paid for water privilege', grazing lands, Sz.c. In 1882 there were shipped abroad from Colorado 60,000 head of beef, which netted $2,000,000. The trade has nearly all sprung up since the year 1864, and in six years from that date the number of cattle in the State rose to 750,000 head. But many of these were young buffaloes. since the introduc- tion of railway§ they .have been eupplanted by beautiful Texas, Durham, and Hereford animals, and the animal that was worth $2O only in 1870 is now wank $4O or $5O. "A FAHBI THAT PAYS." Let us place here, where no one can neiskit, a note which we have just received from "Rugby,* which will, no doubt, excite the curiosity and criticism of our readers neighbour, who has made a balance to the good for 41 years, has at last given me per- mission to send to you a copy of his yearly statement for the last year, 1882, which shows a good profit on a stiff. hard-workineclay farm. The size of the farce is about 130 acres. The management on the farm is of the simplest de' scription. Svredes and a few mange' are, with vetches, always grown :on the fallows. Wheat is usually sown after the fallow; then beans; after beans, wheat; or, if the sea. son is like the present, barley or oats. There is no set rule about cropping, for the seasons rule the rotation; beans are sometimes planted after beans, wheat after wheat, dm For instance, this year no wheat has been got in, consequently all the ground will be planted—beans, oats, and barley. As a rule, the barley and oats are never up to the average; but the wheat, beans, vetches, swedes, and clover are usually the beet in the neighbourhood. I find sixty years ago this farm was considered the poorest in the parish, as is shown by the valuation list; now it is the best. Nearly the whole of the live stock are kept in the yards from October till June, as the season is sooner or later. At the present time there is on the farm 32 cow-kind, 8 horses, 22 ewes, 26 lambs, 83 pigs, 3 turkeys, 3 geese, 9 ducks, 140 hens, 9 stocks of bees. The wholel of tle hay, clover, vetches, and straw is con- sumed, and all the barley, rots, oats, and beans, and the wheat, too,' if it goes not fetch over 16s. a bag of 3 bush. But about this there is no fixed rule—the price makes the rule. Generally from 400 to 700 tons of manure are made and put on the land every year. Farmers, seeds, and beans are usually manured 15 tone to tbe acre, but in this there is no fixed rule, as, for instance, when beans are planted after beans, wheat is put after 'wheat, and no muck. No cake or feeding stuff of any kind is need, only what grows on the farm. No chemical or artificial manures are used. All the live stock is bred on the farm with the exception of a bull, ram, and boar pig; conseqnently the book-keeping is sim- ple, as everything that is sold is profit : Statement for 1882. _ _

In addition to these Scotch cattle, Mr. Cochrane also took away 40 Here- fords, three Guernseys. two Jerseys, and one Shorthorn. PH3EONS.—How To TELL COCKS AND U5-Ns.—ln breeding high-class birds it is neceeeary to pair or mate the birds up with very great care and skill, or in all probability the pro- geny wilt be worthless. Whether there is any desire to exhibit the earns or not does not matter, and we should ad- vite even those who keep them only for their own amuse. ' ment, to spend both time and thought in the patting of the birds together. If they are only the very commonest speci- mens, their young ones can be bred better than themselves, if they are properly selected. It is to this fact that we owe the present high-class stocks of birds. But, as with care- less pairing the best specimens m4y.be of no use, it is all the more necees try for those who have good birds to attend to the matter. Often have new beginners given good prices for prize birds, and allowed these to pair together without regard to their pints, with the result that their progeny have been wortbless. It is often difficult to tell the differ- ence between cocks and hens, as, in order to distinguish them, no infallible rule can be given. Both sexes are very much alike, as it has been the object of breeders /or many years to obtain the hens as near like the cooks as possible. As a rule, cocks are more massive and thicker about the head and beak. stouter In the neck and in the conformation of the body. Bat it has often been known that a large and well developed hen will be bigger and surpass an ordinary sized cock. Thus in the reports of shows, as published in the Poaltry journals, we often find an expression like this: —"lf a hen, very good, but If a cock not so good." There are only one or two ways In which a cock may be distin- guished from a hen, but we must warn our readers that these are most liable to fail. First, as a rule, the cock's breast bone is rather less than that of a bee, and the bones near the vent of a hen are wider apart; also the voice of the cock is more powerful, but as these are only comparative terms they cannot be depended upon. The surest test is to Place tiff" birds In a cage together, when, if a pair, the cock . will tegin to "play up io btad 11'14 keherally the ' methcds adopted in lofts when the sex of a bird is regarded as uncertain. Even this plan, however, cannot always be regarded as certain, for two hens or two cocks have been known to play up and actually pair together. With two hens they have been known ta lay eggs, which have been hatched, the father being some stray bird in the loft, not admitted to the inner recesses of this female home. And even with cocks they have been known to hatch eggs given to them, and feed faithfully the squeakers. These are, how- ever, exceptional cases, and the putting of birds into a pen may be regarded generally as a good test.

TEE REMOVAL OF THE EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT LIBERAL CLUB is expected that the Earlestown and District Liberal Club will be removed to the new premises in Fairclough-storeet in a weiek or two. The premises have been altered and beautified in view of the "new departure," Of rather entrance into them, and certainly they give every appearance of satisfaction. Mr. Dickens, of Esrlestown, has been appointed caretaker, and will live on the premises. It has been decided to celebrate the opening by a tea party and demonstration, which will be held in a few weeks. A STonst.—The silent falling of the snow is to me one of the most solemn things in nature. The fall of autumnal leaves does not so much affect me; but the driving storm is grand. It startles me; it awakens me. It is wild and wofel like my own soul. I cannot help thinking of the sea. How the waves nun and toss their arms about, and the wind plays on those great sonorous harps, the shrouds and masts of ships. Winter is here in earnest. How the old churl whistles and threshes the snow! Meet and rain are falling too. Already the trees are bearded with Icicles; and the two broad branches of yonder pine look like the white mous- tache of some old German baron.—Longfelkne.

traced down to the Middle Ages. The wealth of small art objects found by the excavators is surprising, considering the historical non-importance of the town. The number of graves found in a sequence of excavations was nearly four thousand, of various degrees of pretension' most being merely square depressions cut in the tufa rock, and covered with a :tone or earth mounds, a few round tombs or regular chambers. Sometimes there was merely a hole in the tufa to contain the vessel with ashes. Most corpses had bees burnt outside the graves, but there wertr signs in some in- stances that cremation had takes plan within the tOlittle. The rarely-to-be•found tombstones generally were only in- scribed with the name of the deceased, but a few were em- bellished with bas-reliefs. Most tombs, no doubt, had been used by subsequent generations to repair the town. The graves He in all directions, showing that in very ancient times there was no law as to the placing of graves from east to west, as is believed to have been the case with Greek graves. As usual, the tombs contained ancient colas (mostly of Myrina), weapons, bronze mirrors, ornaments, and articles of the toilet, hilt the chief trea.ure was *burl- dance of terra-Cotta statuettes of various siz es, some still showing remains of colour and gilding. Of such one grave contained thirty-five, another forty-five, and tbere were at least several in the other tombs. It is a *carious fact that most of the statuettes and the other objects had been evi- dently purposely broken, but so that they could easily be put together again. This was probably done in order to render the objects valueless for the living, so that the dead might the more surely remain in possession, and most likely the objects were not placed in the graves in the genteelly prevalent ancient belief that life beyond the grave resembled the earthly life, but because the dead had been fond of what they used when alive. The graves were found to belong almost ..exclusively to the_ second century

Tam Mars AND ?nu Bssat.—l have sometimes tried to persuade men that they had a " MOMS " in their eye, and I confess that I have very rarely suc'ceeded. Now and then you may be able to persuade a man who makeeno profession Of religion that he has done some wrong thing, or has said something that is indefensible; but, if I may jadge from any own experience, it is very hard to persuade a man who is really a Christian that he has committed any moral fault. 81n, in general, he be always ready to acknowledge, but he will not admit a specific moral offence. The reason does not seem far to seek. When a man is conscious that his general purpose is to de the will of Gall, when he is honestly en- deavouring to avoid sin, he is very apt to take it for granted that, in the region of common morality, he cannot have failed seriously. He retreats upon his habitual in- tegrity. He is sure that in the main he means right, and this seems to him to be a sufficient proof that in any par- ticular case he cannot have been In the wrong. His motives are so good that he resents the suggestion that any part of his conduct can deserve blame.—R. W. Dale, in "Good Words."

THE BLUE RIBBON MISSION AT EARLESTOWN.—A9 We re- ported in our last issxe a series of meetings was held in the Mission Tent, Legh-street, Earlestown, last week, in connec- tion with the Blue Ribbon and Gospel Temperance move- ment. They were on the whole well attended, and con- siderable interest was taken in the addresses of Mr. nos- bottom, by whom the meetings were principally conducted. On Saturday evening last the chair was occupied by Mr. T. Newman. After the meeting bad been opened with singing and prayer the chairman gave a short address, after vihich Miss S. A. Lackland recited "Close the ale-house door' and Mr. J. Warburton "Arouse ye men of England." The Edge Green Temperance Brass Band was present, and dur- ing the evening gave several capital selections. Miss A. Marsh gave the recitation "Dick's resolution," and Mr. G. Clarke " A temperance speech." "'Temperance men" was nicely sung by Mr. J. Taylor, and Miss Twist recited "The lips that touch liquor shall never touch mine," and Mr. J. Clarke "The Prodigal." Another recitation " Owd Enoc " was given by Mr. Ball, and was followed by the song "Where is my wandering boy to night," by Miss Ros- bottom. Mr. Rosbottom then addressed the meeting, which was afterwards brought to a close with singing and the Benediction.

A very talkative little girl used often to annoy her mother by making remarks about visitors that came to the house. On one occasion a gentleman was expected whose nose had been accidentally flattened nearly to his face. The mother cautioned the child to say nothing about this feature. Imagine her consternation when the little one suddenly exclaimed, "Ma, you told me to say, nothing about Mr. Smith's nose. Why, he hasn't got any." A few years ago the magistrates of a certain burgh, which may be seen on a clear day from the Calton Hill, upon the south side of the Forth, received information of the theft of a cart wheel. Highly incensed at the circutnstAnce, they resolved to spare no pains to di.cover the offender ; and hearing next laming that a recruiting piny which had been quartered in the town was ith,ut to march to another station, they caused the whole of their knapsucks to be searched.

div.head: CAIRO ST. CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.
div.p: CAIRO ST. CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.

About 300 persons attended the annual congregational soiree in connection with Cairo-street Chapel, 'Warrington, held in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday evening. The hall had been tastefully decorated with flowers, evergreens, banners, and flags, and conspicuous amongst the latter was one bearing the date of the commencement of the school- -1788. Tea having been partaken of, the tables were removed, and an entertainment was given under the presidency of the Rev. R. Pilcher, 8.A., who was supported by the Rev. Wm. Binns, of Birkenhead. In opening the proceedings, The rev. CHAIRMIN said it was with sincere pleasure that he met them again at their congregational soiree, and bade them very heartily welcome, Ile waa glad to bid welcome alio to the great many friends from other congre- gaiions. It was a Very pleasant thing to himself personally, and he was sure it was to his people, to think that, whatever might be the reasons, so many of their outside friends should come to them on the occasion of their annual rejoicings. He was glad to think that the prejudices—which could only arise in the main from ignorance of what they were and what they be• hewed—against them had very greatly diminished- if they could not say that they were altogether .absent. That they had diminished was shown by the fact that so many were willing to come and htstp them on other occasions besides the occasion which they met there to celebrate. They had had a very eventful year for their congregational life. They had, as those present knew, opened a very fine all beautifully toned organ, which they were fortunate enough by the help of their friends to pay for on the day of open- ing. (Applause.) They had also built a congregational parlour, which they had not paid for—(laughter)—but which he might say for the benefit of those who were come to them from without, they intended honourably to pay for some time. They intended to fit it up in a superior manner, and use it for social gatherings of a smaller kind, and for other purposes as well, but especially for the meet- ing of the Ladies' Sewing Society. It was a great addition, in his opinion, to the schools ; it was a great addition to the appearance of the building, and he was quite sure that it would be of immense service to them generally. It had entailed a great deal of work, as they might imagine, on the part of a great many, and he bore very willing testimony, and tendered very hearty thanks to those ladies and gentlemen who had worked so well with them during the past year. He had also the -pleasing duty to welcome several new friend, amongst them. It was a very great and sincere pleasure to them to know that there were those in the town who, hold- ing the same religious views as themselves, were bold enough to come amongst thorn and share their reproach. He could only say that he had regarded with very great thankfulness the increased attendance at theii Sunday services. He was exceedingly proud at tide healthy condi- tion of the various institutions connected with their chapel and school. He was more proud still at the kind feeling which he believed existed amongst them, and must acknow- ledge with very heartfelt thanks the immense kindness which had been shown to himself during • the year. It was only that afternoon that he was enjoying a very beautiful and very costly chair which some of his friends had just lately given to him. (Applause.) These things were very encouraging—encouraging to their minis- ter and encouraging to theolselvee, for it showed that the good old cause they had to heart—the cause of free thought, the cause of true religious life—WAS dear to many of them, and was prospering. In the name of his people he bade the visitors welcome' and lie bade them very heartily welcome; and he trusted that it would be given to them to have many gatherings of that description. He knew that they had a great treat in store, and therefore he would not detain them with many more remarks. He had so many opportunities of speaking to them that it would ill become him to do so. He could only repeat that the past year had been one affording to himself very great satisfaction and comfort, and he trusted it had given equal satisfaction and comfort to them. (Ap- plause.)

The Rev. W. BINNS, who was cordially greeted on rising to address the meeting, said he was glad fh see such a goodly assemblage as that. He thought it was the largest assembly that he-lied ever seen when he had come to Warrington, larger he fancied than they would have been able to pack into that little schoolroom of theirs—(laughter)--and how they all managed to crowd into the chapel on Sunday he could not tell. (Laughter.) He was glad to see and hear that they were a very mixed lot that night. (Laughter.) He d d not mean the phrase to be disrespectful at all ; he meant it to be taken simply in its etymological sense. It was perfectly true they were mixed. They were mixed in the sexes, as a matter of course; they were mixed as old and young; perhaps they were mixed as rich and poor, and they were mixed as beautiful and so-so. (Laughter.) They were also mixed, no doubt, in a theological way Mr. Pilcher told him, and he was glad of that too. He (the speaker) had been a very mixed personage himself in his own time—(laughter) —and he was the result of a mixture which had boon in process of brewing now for a pretty good number of years, and he thought that the mixture as it had finally come out was not particularly bad. (Laughter.) He was going to consider this mixedness of them with respect to their theological ideas, and to take it for granted that there really might be present Roman Catholics, Church of England people, Presbyterians, Independents, and Methodists of various kinds. Well, all of them had their creeds and their ideas of what they themselves believed religiously, and he supposed that religious people always wOuld require a creed of some kind or other in which to express their present theological state of mind. For his own part he did not see any harm in men having creeds so long as, while their creeds told what they believed just now, they also kept the windows of the soul open for any fresh sunshine to be poured in upon them in future time. Then a creed did no harm; it was rather a helpful kind of thing. However, these creeds of theirs might easily do harm in two different ways. They might do harm , if they said that the conclusions to which they had reached at the preeent time were final ccnclusions, and that they need not go any further than they had got already ; so that they might really\sum up the whole universe of truth in a few very easily pronounced phrases of their own. Then their creeds did harm, for they put an end to progress an d development, and they made the rivers of thought like the river Jordan, run into the Dead Sea. Creeds might very easily enough do harm in another way. They might do harm it they attempted to make them exclusive or damnatory —if on the strength of them they felt themselves at liberty to proclaim the wrath of God and the files of hell on all ! people who either said less than Unitarians said, or who were brave enough to say a little more than they said. For creeds of that exclusive and damnatory character did more than just put a stop to progress. They encouraged a cruel disposition in the people themselves who held these exclu- sive and damnatory creeds, and often led them to paint God in the likeness of narrow-sou Jed men; and, over and above all that, they made the very inheritance of the life to come itself really worse, he thought, than the unbroken shop in the grave would be. There were creeds, too, which they might say were mere matters of indifference, and these were creeds which had no direct reference to practical life; but there were other creeds—and he took it that these were ' substantially the creeds which they were all aiming to master as far as they could—which were brave and splendid attempts of the spirit of man to interpret the mysteries of God, and these creeds were the creeds that really help on the life of the world, especially if these attempts to interpret the mysteries of God be carried out in a thoroughly honest, generous, brave,and open-minded fashion. But there were no perfect creeds notwithstanding this, and there never were any perfect creeds, and there never will be any perfect creeds. In religious matters there was always a hole present to them, which they could not entirely see, and which they could not therefore adequately interpret, and when they had seen as much as they could there were mysteries still stretching beyond them. In these religious ideas he took it that they were really in much the same position as astronomers were when they looked into the depths of space. The things rhat they saw were ferfectly trustworthy and absolutely real. There was no mistake about the things being there that the astronomers did see, but then they saw there was this also: beyond the reach of the naked eye the telescope revealed to them stars in the dim distanoe, and then, too, beyond the reach even of the strongest telescope, they were always able to catch vague suggestions of worlds crowding upon worlds until they were lost in wonder and adoration before the infinity that stretched out before their gaze, that the throne of God lay shrouded in darkness in excess of light. It was so in all their religious ideas too. They were always making fresh discoveries in same of the reali- ties of divine mind snd providence, and God was always making fresh revelations to them of realities that there were in Himself; and of the discoveries that they made there was no end, and of the revdations that God made there was no end. Ira the interpretation that they made of these revelations and discoveries at any time, they never made any interpretation which was not susceptible of being improved, and capable of being made to grow into a clearer and more adequate picture of the reality that there was before them. He took it that was substantially the view which all of them would occupy with respect to these religious ideas. That was what they meant by their creeds. They might call them the Baptist creed, the Independent creed, the Roman Catholic creed, or Unitarian. They were just the interpretation which for the time beim., they themselves put upon the religious realities whiob they were conscious of within. Whenever be met with a creed which had very few points about it which commanded his own intense personal sympathy, and when it had many points about it also from which he heartily dis- sented, he still could manage when he tried to see that the believers in that creed were seeking the same thing that he himself was seeking, and he could manage be thought also generally to discover that all the creeds that there had been in the world were useful phases of thought and educa- tion through which the common mind of the human race had passed. These various religions of the world, and these various sects which had often quarreled so foolishly and so ' bitterly one with another, had really helped the world itself to grow better,and to go further onward,and they bad helped us to become what we ourselves were to-day. We were indebted to the past, and yet we were lifted above the past, and we built our own new spiritual homes on the foundation of these old and sacred ruins. If there were a tangled mesh of opinion and speculation all round about them, he thought they could manage to get hold of the gold thread of the eternal creed in this multiplicity of creeds. . No creed was ever purely and simply an arbitrary. Freston. There was always a Principle at work in the onton and develop- ment of creeds just as there was in the origin and develop- ment of political constitutions, scientific ideas, and artietic principles; and if any creed at any tune be taught to the I people at large, and if it be largely accepted, they might be

sure that in some way that creed met and fairly satisfied some want of the age, and it seemed to be to the balk of the people the best solution that could be given to the problems that were at that time waiting for solution, otherwise it would not be able to secure acceptance among the people at all. Love to God and love to men were in themselves the essential and fundamental basis of the Christian system and teaching, but then the early Christians could not be content with this practical teaching, and they were compelled to formulate some theologicaCdogmas that were to be in con- trast to the Pagan and other dogmas in existence in the world. If they looked at the way in which some of these dogmas came into existence, and the historical niche into which they fit, they would see the enormous step in advance which humanity at that time took, The popular religion of the time was Polytheism, with their gods many and lords many, but Christianity said "God the Father Almighty," and down at once went all that multiplicity of deities and one God remained, He went on to say that looking behind them they could see the truth struggling to be born in the distant recesses that they had left behind, and they could see them flourishing vigorously now and growing V) a fuller and riper manhood in the ages to corn& He thought they might re-utter these old ideas in this more modern style: "I believe in God the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth," and so he was filled with an indestructible con- fidence that the Almighty Father would ultimately be victorious over every form Q trror and evil, and he could trace the presence of the Maker of heaven and earth in all his works. "I believe in Jesus Christ," and when nature filled his mind with perplexities, and when disaster seemed to overtake the fortunes of humanity and cover the history of the world with gloom, he felt that the heart of Jesus Christ was a finite symbol of' the infinite heart of God, and his perplexi- ties vanished and the disastrous fortunes of humanity were but temporal clouds followed by sunshine. "I believe in the Holy Ghost." God did not speak to one son alone, or through one son alone. He is the life of all our lives, elle soul of all our souls, and His Holy Spirit is the energy by which we live and move and have our. being. "I believe in the Holy Catholic Church," which was made up of Pagans, Jews, and Chris- time, and of all men and women who set their faces God- ward, and strove to establish the kingdom of God, which was the kingdom of righteousness and love. "I believe' in the communion of saints." The members of the Holy Catholic Church were themselves the communion of saints, and they strpve to join them and make sweet music together with them. I believe in the life everlasting." He knew that this material body. of his mouldered away into the dust, and that many material bodies had done that already before this, but they had not made an end of him though they had made an end of themselves. He survived. This body that he should some time throw off was not him. It was because they sought this soul of good- ness in all things seemingly evil, this truth hidden in the midst of so much that was erroneous and destined to pass away, that they now grew, and that there was a bright and promising future opening out. before them. They looked forward to this future and saw those imperfect conceptions, those unworthy conceptions, those gloomy pictures of God, those gloomy pictures of the life to come. Those all Walt their doom from that great law, Which makes past time serve to-Jay; And Reeler life the word will draw From their decay. Life everlasting would flourish when this transitory life perished. (Applause.) Councillor MONKS was then called upon, and he apologised for the absence of Mr. Broadbent and Mr. W. Long, after which he thanked Mr. Binns on behalf of the congregation for the vast amount of underlying truth contained in his address that night. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was a hopeful sign that they had heard what he might call affir- mative truth that night. He pointed out that it was ..a great thing to belong to a church which did not ' seek to f6ttet the human mind and which allowed freedom of thought, and said he hoped while holding strongly to their own views, they would yet have the courage and frankness to acknowledge the good they saw in others, and in those movements in which they could join with them and work hand in hand for the promotion of Christian work it was their duty to do all they could. He was happy to say no far as Cair4-street congregation was concerned they had never ben behind any congregation in Warrington in supporting any movement that had really been for the good of the town. (Applause.) Mr. T. BIRCHALL also delivered a brief aAdres9, and The CHAIRMAN then tendered thanks to Mr. Binns and all who had assisted at the tea and entertainment. The room was then cleared for dancing, which was en- gaged in for a few hours.

STAFFORDSHIRE V. CHESHIRE. —The sixth annual match be- tween these two associations took place at Macclesfield on Saturday afternoon. Stsfordshire won by four goats to three. BAYDOCK TEMPERANCE Y. GOLBORNE (2ND TEAms).—The return match of the above teams was p'ayed at Go!borne on Saturday last. Owing to the unfavourable state of the weather only 30 minutes' play each was indulged in, and at the call of time the Temperance team were victors by one goal to nil. WARRINGTON WANDERERS V. ST. ELPHINS. The return match between these clubs was played on the ground of the former, on Saturday, in the presence of a large number of spec- tators. The first scrimmage took place in the Wanderers' quar- ters, but the home team, not to be denied, rushed the leather down the field and got well into the visit rs' stronghold before the ball was held. Scrimmage again being formed, it ended by going in touch from the throw out. One of tte Wanderers' forwards secured the ball and kicked it dead. The ball was brought Into play and operations agate commenced, when it was evident the home team were determined to reverse a for- mer verdict, although the visitors had pressed into their service two substitutes from the Wart It gton Football Club. One of them made frantic efforts to avert defeat, but they proved of no avail. Play was progressing in the visitors' quarters when half-time was called. On the resumption of hostilities the play commenced with vigour, the home forwards rushing the leather down the field, and compelling the vislurs to resort to saving tactics. Eventually the leather was rusLed over the line, four pia ; ers scouring it. A maul ensued, which resulted in Uns- wor th wresting the ball from his opponents and securing a try. Elelsby kicked a neat goal therefrom. During the preparation to kirk the goal a quarrel took place, and the visitors retired from the field, without stating any reas(n, before the appointed time for the expiration of the game, leaving the Wanderers victors by one goal and five minors to one minor. LANCASHIRE CHALLENGE CUP COMPATITION.—BIackburn Rovers v. Padtham : The holders of the -Lancashire Association Chaltenge Cup visited Padiharn on Saturday to meet the prin- cipal team of that town in the fifth round of the competition. The home team played with the wind and a slope of the ground in their favour in the first half, and six minutes from the start Bury scored the fist goal. Twice subsequently they claimed that Woolfall was over the line when he stopped the leather, but the referee roled against them, and just at half-time the scora was equalised, gay turning the lest her through his charge, instead of outside, when tent in by Strachan. After the change of ensis Brown (two) and Strachan (one) acored, and the goal- keeper put the ball through, making the Rovers the victors by five goals to one.—Blsckburn Park Road v. Eagley : After their training in the English cup competition and the form they showed against the Welsh Druids a week ago, Bagley were considered to have a good chance of winning their Llneashlre cup le (lourthround) against the Blackburn Park Road Club, which WAS contested at Audley Hall. Blackburn, on Saturday. In the first Ulf the Bagley men played with the wind, and had all the best of the game; but in the second, the wind and rain being In their faces, they deteriorated perceptibly, and were outplayed by the Park Road team, who won the tie by sin goals to two.—Bslton Wanderers v. Darwen St. John's: gibe tie in the fifth round of the competition for the Lancashire cap between the above clubs was played at Bolton on Saturday, when the Wanderers won easily by five goals to ODO.

WIDNES WASPS v. WIDNES RECREATION...—These teams met on the groand of the ViraBfS on Saturday. when a oleasant'y contested game was played, ending in a vfctory for the visitors. Jameson, losing the api.), kicked off. Quinn made a god re- turn, to which Grundy repliel,punting into touch in mid-field. On the lie out Quinn and Radcliffe were very prominent in a fine dibble into the Rec, eation half, and Dennett, picking up, passed to t•tiebing, who struggled through his opponents and grounded the loathe". R. Broome ran well unti, cAlared by Grace when he passed to Rewitt, who made further progress, going in touch by half flag. Quinn and Chrimes dribbled well, when Noon kicked into the Wasps' 25 flag, and Groome, mak- ing a splendid run, followed up his kick and complete y over- hauled the Wears' back. He crowned his efforts by gaining a try, no goal resulting. Play again ensued in the Wasps' half, when they made a momentary invasion in the Recteation 25,. Jameson and Williams finely clearing the danger, both sue:tes- ; sively making progress into mid-field. Quinn began to move I in another direction, Stiching bringing him down quickly from a terimmage on the Wasps. Grundy nicely kicked over the line, Woods touching down. °Limes and Ratcliffe taking the leather to centre field. On change of ends, Barber kicked off, Hewitt returning nicely to Btiching, who ran well, and Jameson followed up by a nice dribble which Raiding arrested I from a scrimmage. W. Barber, making a good attempt to I Score, being conared, passed back to Ratcliff who kicked I nicely into the Recieation 25 flag, when Noo ti Hewitt. Jame- eon, and alai-ling, In some good sterling nlay, carried the leather over the lints. After touching down, Grace ran the oval out, and the Wasps getting together carried the leather into the Recreation half. Williams, however, was equal to the emergency. ond kicked back, the leather sailing in mid-field. when Harding again advanced into the Recreation half, they, howevet, warmed up to their work, and re'urned the attack. Quinn stopped the attempt to dribble by Jameson and Fraynor. Harding and Radcliffe moved in another direction. Stiching,. smartly stopping the attempt, returned the leather past the centre flag. Quinn replied to Stiohing. and following up, was caught with the ball in hand. Nothing more was scored at any importance up to the call of time, when the Recreation won by one try. ()Le dead ball, and two touchdowns, to the Wasps' two touchdowns. The Recreation forwards to a man played a fine forware game. In the back play they also did their work well, the way Jameson and Noon took away the ball on the dribble being a treat to witness. William's and Dickson were very pro- minent for the Wasps, and Harding, Quinn, and W. Barber played vary well.

George Miller, a soldier who served in Egypt, was tried at Glasgow Circuit Court, on Wednesday, for the murder of a roman named Drew, in a cell, on December la. Evidence of insanity having been given, the jury returned a verdict that prisoner was insane at the time he committed the act.

GOOD TEMPLARS' MEETING.—The members of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars - held their usual weekly meeting on Monday evening last, in the lodge room, Bridge-street. There was a very large and full attendance of members, and Bro. G. E. Warburton, W.C.T., presided. After formal business the forthcoming united temperance demonstration came up for discussion, and a few arrange- ments in connection therewith were made. Afterwards the lodge programme was proceeded with, the subject being "Facts and scraps." A number of interesting and instruc- tive facts and amusing scraps were read by Brothers John Taylor, John Warburton, E. Newman, George Bailey, Thomas Gorse, George Clarke, and the Chairman, the meeting being a very pleasant and enjoyable one. 1A visitor from one of the Warrington ktiges was also present and briefly addreued the meeting. The proceedings concluded about 9-40.

div.head: EXAMINERI, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 24, 1883
div.p: THE EXAMINERI, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 24, 1883

We understand that the Earl of Stair has accepted the chairmanship of the Life Association of Scotland, vacant by the death of Sir Archibald Hope, Bart. The miners of East Fifeshire, at a meeting at Kit kcaldy, on Tuesday, decided, in consequence of a reduction of wages, to work only seven hours daily. The nomination for Newcastle took place on Wednesday, when Mr. John Morley (Liberal) and Mr. Gainsford Pruce (Conservative) were nominated. The polling is fixed for Saturday. The Manchester and Bury steam tramway was on Wed- nesday inspected by General Hutchinson, of ,the Board of Trade, who is said to have expressed himself pleased with it. The tramway commences near Kersal. At a meeting of the Conciliation and Arbitration Board for the North of England iron trade, held at Darlington, it was unanimously decided that Mr. David Dale, the first pre- sident of the Board, should oe appointed referee to settle local disputes which may arise. The Board having been reorganised and strengthened, steps will shortly be taken to adopt a sliding scale -for regulating wages, as has been done in Staffordshire. BILLS OF SALE AND FAILURES. In the week ending February 17, 1883, there were 234 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 831 over those of the correspond- ing period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 233, an increase of four. The totals for portion of year to February 17, 1883, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 1,685, a decrease of 5,302; the failures gazetted number 1,525, an increase of 34. /Stubbs' Mercantile Gazette.

Eliza Ebbon, for whose supposed murder a laan named Stratton was convicted, has just written to her friends. Ebbon was missing last summer from Elstree, and Stratton was believed to have been last in her company. A dead body was found which the friends of Ebbon identified as hers, and Stratton was tried and sentenced to death. He was afterwards reprieved and sent to Broadmoor Criminal Lunatic Asylum. Ebbon states that she was in Northampton at the time of her supposed murder. On Thursday morning, a shocking tragedy occurred at North Shields Police Station. Two drunken men were placed in a cell on Wednesday night, and one of them murdered his companion. The discovery was made on the prisoners' cell being visited by reserve officers about two o'clock on Thursday morning. The murdered man, whose throat was cut, was Patrick Rourke, fireman, belonging to Roscommon. The other man, Thomas Le.ithead, belongs to North Shields. He was on Thursday morning remanded on a charge of murdering Rourke. A NOTORIOUS BURGLAR.-At Leicester, on Wednesday, William Stenson, a notorious burglar, who was recently captured after a most exciting chase, was committed for trial for stealing £6O worth of skins from a boot manufac- tory. The prisoner had eluded the pole for years, and committed daring burglaries even whilst tliF detectives were watching him, but always managed to get away. On this occasion he would have escaprd but for the courage of an officer who held him, although suffering from severe injuries received in the pursuit. The Albert Medal of the first class (land division) has been presented to Mr. R. Smallman, mining engineer, Nun- eaton; Mr. Stokes, Inspector of mines, Derby; Charles Day and Charles Chetwynd, Collieries, Baddeslev ; and the Albert Medal of the second class upon Mr. Samuel Spruce, mining engineer, Tamworth ; Mr. Marsh, colliery manager, Hallend; Mr. Mottrin, colliery :nanager, Tamworth ; William Morris, William Pickering, and Joseph Chetwynd, Collieries, Bad- desley, for baavery displayed by the recipients on the occa- sion of the fire and explosion on the Ist and 2nd of May last.

THE GRIEVANCES OF THE CALEDONIAN RAILWAY MEN. —The Caledonian Railway Board on Tuesday considered the statements of the heads of departments regarding the demands of the men lately on strike, and the same evening gave their reply to the memorial of the men. It states that mineral engine drivers and firemen willte allowed half an hour before leaving, and half an hour after returning to the shed. The three-shift, or eight hours' cabin arrangement for signals, will be introduced. The hours of mineral brakes- men will be reduced from twelve to ten. The hours of yards- men will be twelve, but relief men will be provided in winter when necessary. The directors state that it is their desire to reduce Sunday duty to the lowest possible limit. ACTION AGAINST A PRESBYTERIAN MINISTER.—At the Whitehaven County Court, on Tuesday, the Rev. Alexan- der King, Presbyterian minister, Whitehaven, was sued for three guineas, the cost of two books on " Picturesque Pales- tine," which an agent for Messrs. Virtue and Co. alleged had been purchased from him. The point in the case was as to whether the book agent had forged two signatures of the rev, gentleman, who denied he had ever signed two documents produced bearing his signature. •Judge Ingham said he did not know that he had ever bad a more painful case to decide, but he felt as convinced as he sat there that Mr. King had signed the documents, and he gave a verdict for the plaintiff. Mr. King persisted that he bad not signed the order. _

_ THE MANCHESTER AND SALFORD BANK LIMITED.—The annual report af the directors of this bank has just been issued for the year 1882, with a copy of which we have been favoured. It states that the directors have pleasure in reporting to the shareholders that the net profits of the busi- ness for 1882, after making allowances for bad and doubtful debts, for rebate of interest upon bills in .hand, and for salaries and charges amounted to £102,630. Sc; plus a balance from last year, after paying income tax, of £2,110 4s Bd, making together £104,749 12s Bd. The directors have declared the usual dividend of ten per cent. per annum

(45,827) with a bonus of 21 per share (£9,478 ris 6d), and have applied £17,000 to the redemption of the Bolton and Rochdale purchase, leaving in profit and loss account to cover income tax £2,444 5s 2d. The paid up capital of the bank is now £760,000, and the reserve fund •£340,000. A branch of the bank has recently been opened at Newton Heath. The branches generally are making satisfactory progress. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE. Business continues

fairly steady in the coal trade. For house fire coals a moderately good demand is maintained, but the commoner sorts for ironmaking and steam purposes move eff only in- differently, requirements for these not having shared in the recent improvement in the demand for domestic consump- tion. In the Manchester districts the pits are kept going pretty near full time, without any material accumulation of stocks, and in other Lancashire districts there is an absence of any pressure of supplies which to some extent no doubt is due to the irregular working of the collieries, which with very few exceptions are stopped entirely on the Saturdays, and in many cases are not raising their ordinary get on other days. Prices generally are maintained, and at the pit month remain about as under :—Best coil, 9s 6d to lOs ; seconds, 7s 6d to 8s; common house fire coal, 6s 6d to 7s; steam and forge coal, 5s 9d to 6a ; burgy, 4s 9d to ss; and ordinary qualities of slack, 3s 6d to 4s per ton. In the shipping trade a fairly good business is being done on the basis of late rates, the average prices for delivery at the high level, Liverpool, or the Garston docks being about 7s 9d to 8s for steam coals and 9s to Os 6d per ton for house tire qualities. ENGLISH PATENTS. The following patents, amongst others published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal, were sealed during the week:—John Young and Edwin Furniss, Mellor, Derby, for improvements in the construction of ring spinning and doubling framPs ; Jatnes McGregor, Manchester,for improvements in ring spinning and doubling machinery; Christopher Catlow, Burnley, for improvements in looms for weaving; Daniel Smith, Henry Smith, and William Smith, Keighley, wool combers, for improvements , in screw gill boxes for preparing wool and other fibrous sub- I stances; Joseph Waddington and Benjamin Longbottom, Barro ar-in-Furness, and James Ashworth, Dalton-in-Furness, for improvements in machinery or apparatus for making bore holes for mining and other like purposes; Charles Roberts, of the Railway Wagon Works, Wakefield, for im- provements in couplings for railway wagons or other vehicles; Charles Henry Lea, Stafford, for improvements in appliances or apparatus for working gates or crossings on railways, partly applicable in other; Gustavus Adolphus John Scott, Bradford, for improvements in the construction of vessels for holding mineral and other oils and liquids.—List sup- plied by Mr. George Davies, C.E., Feb., Inst., P.A., patent solicitor, 4, St. Ann's Square, Manchester. THE LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY COMPANY. —The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company was held o n Wednesday, and was unusually protracted. There was also a larger attendance than usual; and the policy of the Board of Directors in the past was subjected to much criticism An amendment to the customary resolution as to the adop- tion of the report was moved, expressing the opinion that in consequence of the Unsatisfactory character of the report a "change in the policy of the administration is absolutely necessary," and that it was of "the most vital importance that a gentleman possessed of railway experience he invited to join the Board as chairman, and that such position be offered to Sir E. W. Wallin, Bart., M.P." The amendment was only defeated by 116 votes against 84; but if necessary the directors could have utilised proxies for a very large amount. A resolution practicially affirming the desirable- ness of making the chairman of the company managing director, with an adequate salary, found favour with a majority of the shareholders present, and the subject will be considered at a special meeting to be held within the course of a month. The directors who retired by rotation were ail re-elected, an attempt to substitute Mr. Alderman Bennett (who, it was suggested, was wante-1 to " deodorise " the present directorate) for Mr. Joshua Radcliffe proving , unsuccessful.

AN IMPUDENT SWINDLER.—For some time past the London police have been endeavouring to arrest a person who has been going the rounds of the West-end clubs, dining in them as if a member, and cashing cheques made out for an amount larger than that of his bill. On. Wedne- sday, about eight o'clock, a well-dressed man drove up in a cab to the Junior Army and Navy Club, St. James's-street, entered it, and borrowed from the ball porter is to pay the cabman. He then asked for any letter there might be for Mr. Spottiswoode, an officer in the Princess of Wales's Own (Yorkshire) Regiment, and a member of that club. He was given two, upon which he ascended the stairs, and, entering the smoking-room, proceeded to read them. A page boy, knowing that the in- dividual was not Mr. Spottiswoode, spoke to a member of the committee, who at once proceeded towards the smoking. room. The suspected person, possibly having become aware of his danger, met him in the upper ball. The member of • the committee at once accosted him, and, in reply to ques- tions, he said, "Yes, lam Mr. Spottiswoode." The police at Vine-street were sent for, and the prisoner was recognised as the man they were in search of. He was then taken into custody. The only things be had upon him were a latchkey and two pawn tickets for £2. One of the members of the club said he remembered the prisoner—a small, insigni- ficant-looking man, about twenty-eight years of age, as having been in the Army. , BAT'S COMPOUND, for Colds and Coughs. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

REPLY To-,rir- E ADDRESS.—EarI SYDNEY brought up the reply of Her Majesty in answer to the Address voted by their lordships. BILLS IN THE HOUSE OF LoßDS.—Earl GRANVILLE stated that the Bills to be first introduced in the Upper House would be a Bill to amend the Factory Acts, and Bills with regard to Scotch peerages, the protection of young girls, the regulation of fisheries, naval discipline, medical councils, contempt of court, and education in Wales. There will also be an Irish Bill, which will be introduced by Lord Carliiagford. THE WELLINGTON STATUE.—The question of what should be done with the Wellington statue that has been removed from the marble arch at Hyde Park corner was raised by Lord Mount-Temple, who suggested that it should be plackd on the Horse Guards parade, but the Duke of CAMBRDGE objected that there was not room there, and Lord SUDELEY, speaking for the Government, stated that no decision would be arrived at as to the disposal of the un- fortunate statue until it was fairly on terra firma. NATIONAL SCHOOL TEACHERS IN IRELAND.—A discus- sion on the appointin.eut of a sister of mercy as a teacher in a National School in Ireland open to non-Catholic children, occupied the time of their lordships until they rose, shortly before six o'clock,

ROUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. THE IRISH DISCLOSURES.—Sir H. MAXWELL gave notice of his intention to ask whether the P. J. Sheridan mentioned by Carey on Saturday was one of the men who conducted the negotiations which led to the release of certain suspects from Kiltnainham prison, and of whom Mr. Parnell before his release said he hoped to- make use of him to put down conspiracy and agitation.—This was followed by a notice by Lord R. CHURCHILL, that Mr. Gorst would, in consequence of what had recently transpired at Kilmainham, move an amendment on the Address, praying Her Majesty that no further attempt be made to purchase the support of persons in Ireland disaffected to her rule by concessions to lawless agitation.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE then asked the Chief Secretary whether the person described by Carey on Saturday as P. J. Sheridan, of Tubercurry, is the same person as the Sheridan referred to in the memorandum sent to the Prime Minister and other members of the Government by the late Chief Secretary at the time that the release of the suspects was un- der consideration in April last.—The reply of Mr.TREVELYAN was that according to the information he had been able to obtain at the Irish office in London Sheridan was the same man who was referred to. Absolute certainty could not per- haps be acquired, but they believed it was the same man, ARABS PASHA. Answering a question from Mr. Labouchere, Lord E. FITZMAURICE stated that Arabi Pasha was not a prisoner in Ceylon, but remained there in , accordance with a solemn undertaking in writing that he would remain there till his place of abode was changed by permission of the authorities. LOCAL Orriox.—ln reply to Sir Wilfred Lawson, who asked if the Government would this session carry out the 1 resolution in favour of local option, Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said the G)vernment regarded the subject as part of the 1 question of local government, and they Fould deal with I the licensing question in connection with their measure on local government. DISTRESS IN IRELAND. Replying to Mr. O'Shea, Mr. TREVELYAN stated that there was considerable distress in Clare, but the poor-law machinery could deal with it. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Sir W. BARTELOT, who ad- dressed the House on agricultural distress during the past , seven years, and urged that effect should at ()ace be given to the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the sub- ject of local taxation.—Mr. W. FOWLER thought if the sea- sons were against the farmers the Government ought to take care that the laws were not against them also.—Sir M. LOPES urged that the Government, having given Free ; Trade, ought to give fair taxation, and remove the excep- tional burdens which agriculture had borne under Protec- tion.—Mr. J. HOWARD contended that if a tenants' compensation bill would not suffice to restore prosperity so long as such seasons as we had of late ex- perienced continued, such a measure would lay the founda- tion for future prosperity.—The debate was continued by ' Mr. Harcourt, Mr. Inderwick, Mr. Gregory, Mr. Duckham, Mr. Marurn, Mr. Illingworth, Mr. Biddell, Mr. Arthur Arnold, Mr. S. Hill, Mr. Barclay, Sir W. Hart-Dyke, Mr. Goschen, and Mr. Chaplin.—ln the course of a brief reply, ! Mr. MUNDELLI, alluding to a proposal made during the de- , bate for the exclusion of all live foreign animals, said such ! an undertaking was inadmissable, and no Government dare undertake it, as its effect would be to raise food to famine 1 prices.—After some remarks from Mr. Lowther, the debate was adjourned, on the motion of Mr. GORST.

THE AFFIRMATION B(LL.—The House then went into Committee on the Affirmation Bill.—Sir STAFFORD NORTH- COTE stated that he should not oppose the introduction of the bill, but he should support Sir R. Cross in opposing the second reading.—Leave was given to bring in the bill, which was read a first time, and the second reading was fixed for Monday next.—The House adjourned shortly after one o'clock.

He said one of the principal reasons why he thought the amendment was well brought forward was that it gave the House an opportunity of expressing its view of that class of politicians who from want of knowledge of Ireland made unguarded speeches which did a great amount of mischief in that country.—Mr. JESSE COLLINGS defended Mr. Herbert Gladstone from the censures passed upon him in respect of his speech at Leeds.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL for IRE- LAND denied that the administration of the Crimes Act had led to an increase of crime and said the reverse was the fact.—On the motion of Mr. LOWTHER the debate was adjourned. _

SOUTH AF-RICA..—Lord BRABOURNE inquired whether the report was true that the Transvaal Boers had used dynamite against the native tribes, and whether: her Majesty's Government had taken any steps to prevent the persecution of those tribes which had remained loyal during the British administration,—The Earl of DERBY, in reply, said he had looked carefully through the despatches relating to Transvaal affairs, but could not find any reference in them to the statement referred to; nor had he seen any evidence that persecution had been directed against those who re- mained faithful to the British authority,
