THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.—There were nearly fifty ques- tions to dispose of in the House of Commons. One of more than ordinary interest referred to the views of the Govern- ment respecting the Channel Tunnel.—The PRESIDENT of the BOARD of TRADE stated that in accordance with a pro- mise made last session he should move a joint committee of both Houses to consider the whole matter—five to be nomi- nated by the Commons and five by the Lords. He suggested that the Bills before the House should be postponed until the committee make their report. MISCELLANEOUS.—In reply to Mr. O'Brien, it was stated by the CHIEF SECRETARY that the witnesses examined by Mr. Curran at Dublin Castle were not subjected to threats or improper inducements during the inquiry, and no intoxi- cating liquor was proffered to them.—The Marquis of HAR TINGTON intimated that provision would be made in the Army Estimates for the training of the Irish Militia, and added that it would depend upon the state of the country whether they would be called out.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE informed Mr. Gourley that the answers from the European Powers in regard to the neutralisation of the Suez Canal were, so far as they had been received, of a favourable character. The Sultan, he remarked, bad no direct pecuniary interest in the Canal. DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS: MR. FORSTER'S DEFENCE: SUSPENSION OF MR. O'KELLY. -- The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. JAMES LOWTHER, who de- nied the inference drawn by the Home Secretary that Mr. Gorst's amendment approved of the official career of Mr. Forster. Another misapprehension was that the Opposition was desirous of heaping encomiums upon the administra- tion of Lord Spencer. It was only in reference to the Crimes Act that they thought it their duty to support the Government in the direction in which their policy now tended. —Mr. FORSTER urged that the amendment would if carried have the effect of destroying the Government at a very critical time. No one could doubt that it was intended to weaken the Government, and no argument had been shown as to the necessity of bringing it forward. Adverting to the differences which forced him to separate from his colleagues, the right hon. gentleman said they were confined to one point, and he received a loyal support in all he did. The assurances he gave to his colleagues were not satis- factory to him, first, because they were conditional mainly upon the Arrears Bill, and, secondly, because he did not want assistance from Mr. Sheridan or from any other organiser of the Land League. He felt that these assurances would do more harm than good, and would give the impres- sion in Ireland thal they could not govern without the assistance of the hon. member for Cork. He admitted that the mention of Mr. Sheridan's name shocked him. The supposition that Sheridan had been made use of by the Government was absolutely untrue. The main reason why he could not consent to the release of the suspects was because the Government had not obtained fresh powers. The Protection Act had enabled him to put down the "boycotters" and break up the Land League. Murders were stopped and checked in many dis- tricts, but he wanted fresh power to deal with secret so- cieties. As to the course to be taken with regard to the amendment, he recommended that the best thing to do with it would be to withdraw it. Tuning to the Irish members in the House, the right hon, gentleman asked Mr. Parnell if he had read and approved of the articles in United Ireland, to which the hon. member tor Cork replied that he had read them and did approve of them. Mr. Forster asked if the hon. member was aware that murder, arson, robbery, insults to the dead, and attacks up- on women, were habitually described in that paper ? It had been shown that outrages followed the meetings and actions of the Land League, and the hon. member for Cork had, he would not say directly planned or perpetrated outrages, but he connived at them.—At this point Mr. O'KELLY shouted excitedly, "It's a lie ; it's a lie."—He had already been twice warned, and the SPEAKER now named him.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON thereupon moved his suspension, and the motion was carried by 305 to 20.—Mr. FORSTER, resuming, said what he was about to remark when interrupted was that whether Mr. Parnell con- nived at the outrages or not he was determined to remain in ignorance of them. He felt bound to say that until the hon. member had expressed regret and repentance, he could not hold conference with or have confidence in him. There were now two grounds for hope. One was that the Govern- ment had now the power to uphold the law and would use it, and the other was that the hon. member for Cork and his fellow-chiefs in this so-called agitation had been found out, the wickedness of the agitation bad been unveiled.— The debate was continued by Mr. Yorke, Mr. T. P. O'Conror, and others.—Lord HARTINGTON said it was understood that Mr. Parnell was to move the adjournment of the debate, and if he wanted to reply to the grave charges against him he should have time to do so, but it now appeared Mr. Parnell was not going to speak.—Mr. PARNELL said he would move the adjournment of the debate.—The Marquis Of HARTINGTON said it would then be too late. He thought the observations of Mr. Forster would have produced a reply. The public would draw their conclusion from the conduct of Mr. Parnell, whose silence admitted that there was a prima facie case against the Laud League. The leaders of that League ought to place at the disposal of the House and of the public all the material that would enable them to form a judgment on the subject. As to the legislative intentions of the Government in regard to Ireland he held that this was not a time for discussing them, but the Govern- ment had no intention of proposing large changes that would give rise to great difference of opinion or occupy much time. As to Mr. H. Gladstone's speech, he had not read a full report. If the Times summary of it was correct , there was much in it he did not agree with, but no Govern- I meet was held responsible for the expressions of all its members. The Government maintained that it was their remedial legislation that had saved the landlord class from the destruction that public hostility would have brought , upon them if a reform had not averred it. It would have I been more dignified on the part of the Opposition to give notice of such an amendment as the present, than to follow at the heels of a section of their party. He pointed out the waste which was going on of the short time at the dis- posal of the House before Easter, and expressed his belief that if the amendment were carried it would be interpreted in Ireland as meaning that the Govern- ment should rely on coercion measures only, while the Government believed in the good effects of their remedial legislation. He then proceeded to review the course of events in Ireland under the Coercion Act, which partly succeeded and partly failed. In speaking of the re- lease of the suspects, he asked what proof there was that the Government ever accepted Mr. Parnell's offer to use Sheridan to put down outrages. He (the noble Marquis) had no knowledge of such a thing. On the contrary, the warrant against Sheridan remained in force till the Act expired. He went on to say that the Cabinet bad agreed to the Crimes Bill before Mr. Forster resigned. (Mr. Forster : "No, no.") He reminded Mr. Forster that he was often absent in Ireland at the time, but be himself had a most perfect recollection of the bill being sanctioned by the Cabinet before Mr. Forster's resignation.—Mr. PARNELL moved the adjournment of the debate. Sir S. NORTHCOTE presumed the Government would not oppose the adjourn- ment. He thought the noble lord had unfairly commented on the delay of the Opposition in challenging the conduct of of the Government, as it was only postponed from consider- ations of public prudence. The Opposition would now accept the challenge in the fullest sense, and he would state the way he proposed to do so to-morrow. Sir W. HARCOURT, amid several interruptions, asked whether Irish affairs were not as grave now as they were nine months ago.—The debate was then adjourned, and the House adj urned at 1-10 a.m.

The inquiry was resumed on Monday. On Carey enter- ing the court the prisoners commenced to hiss and jeer at him, and one attempted to strike him. In cross-examina- tion by Mr. Walsh, whoappearedon behalf of Kelly, he said the object of the Fenian Brotherhood was to procure the separation of England and Ireland. He denied indignantly that he had derived any pecuniary advantage from his posi- tion as treasurer. He had personal differences with mem- bers of the Invincible Society, but that was not the cause of his resignation. None of the men in the park on the day of the assassination knew Lord Frederick Cavendish. None of the prisoners had any feeling of personal animosity against Earl Cowper, Mr. Forster, or Mr. Burke, but they were bound by the oath of the Society of Invincible,, and the penalty of the violation of that oath was death. None of them had any idea that Lord F. Cavendish was to be in the park that day. Asked when he and his party first resolved to murder Mr. Burke, Carey said "It was when we read in an article in the Freeman's Journal of the 2nd May that the officials of the Castle should be removed." The order for the murder came, he added, on the following day, May, from "Number One." Joseph Neill, a labourer, stated that he was returning from work at twenty minutes to seven o'clock on the evening of ' the Gth of May, and saw the prisoner Fitzharris standing ita Phcenix Park beside a cab. George Goddin, park ranger, who had previously identified Brady, now identified Thomas Caffrey, since arrested, as another occupant of the car driven out of the park at a rapid pace on the evening of the assassinations. Mr. Murphy applied that all the pri- soners should be committed for trial on the charge of murder and conspiracy, with the exception of Whelan and Joseph Smith. Whelan would be charged with treason- felony, but bail would be accepted in his case. As to Smith, his case would be set aside in the meantime. The prisoners I were then formally remanded till Tuesday. The magistrates' investigation of the conspiracy was brought to a close on Tuesday. About three hours were oc- cupied with the reading of the depositions of the many wit- nesses, and at the close of this part of the procedure 21 men were committed for trial charged with having engaged in a conspiracy to murder, and with having in pursuance of such I conspiracy assassinated Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. I Burke. They Made no reply to the formal charge. Several of them are said to have made merry over it. The remain- ing prisoner, Patrick Whelan, was committed for trial on the charge of treason-felony, and was allowed bail. DESCRIPTION OF "No. 1." A Dublin correspondent of the Daily Telegraph says : The followipg particulars respecting the individual who styled himself "No. 1," and who organised the Assassination Committee and supplied it with money and weapons to carry out the murders, which were planned and executed in Dublin during the last 18 months, have been obtained from the most reliable aources and will throw a flo of light on the chief investigator an e d originator of the Assassination Committee in Dublin, whose name never transpired and whose movements, as related by Carey in his evidence, were enshrouded in such mystery, As will be seen by the evidence, this individual never allowe3 his name to transpire. He always signed himself "No. 1," and was designated by the members of the organisation " General." He is an Irish-American, but resided in France and Germany occasionally. During the last year and a half he has been in the habit of visiting Dublin at frequent intervals, and stopping long and short periods. While in the metropolis he used invariably to stop at one of the prin- cipal hotels in the city or at a well-known marine hotel situated a short distance outside Dublin and near to Black- rock, where Carey in his evidence deposed to having had an interview with him last summer. This individual had ap- parently unlimited money at his disposal, and an inquiry addressed by a large business establishment in Dublin with which he had some financial transactions to a large banking firm in Paris, given by him as a reference was replied to in the following manner :—" The gentleman in question has seemingly unlimited means, derived from large drafts in his favour from America." "General " is a man of about fifty years of age, sft. 101 in. in height, well preserved, full face, cleanly shaved, except a long fair moustache, which is inclined to be reddish, military bearing, and walks slightly lame on the right leg from the effect of a wound be received during the Franco- Prussian war, in which he served in the capacity of a minor officer in the Franc-Tireurs, and he has also seen some service in the American War. During last summer he was in the habit of visiting Dublin frequently, and it is now found that the periods at which he, is known to have been in the city coincides with the dates Carp, states he had interviews with him. His last appearance in Dublin was about two months ago, and since then all trace has been lost of him. The police, since Carey has furnished them with the information, are diligently endeavouring to get on his track, but have succeeded in doing little more up to the present than getting the dates of his visits as furnished by the registers of the two hotels referred to, but they are confident of obtaining enough information to trace his whereabouts on the Continent or in America where they believe him to be.

MR. FORSTER'S ESCAPES. - Some facts are furnished in connection with the narrow escapes of Mr. Forster during the murderous exploits of the "Invincibles " in Dublin. On the occasion when, accot d- ing to Carey's evidence, some of the assassins looked into the carriage at the railway station and saw only Mrs. and Miss Forster, it happened that by the anetest chance, and

almost at tbe last moment, the right honourable gentleman had accepted an invitation to dine with the Yacht Club atiL Kingstown, instead of dinium at the Kildare Club and meet-k- -ing his wife, as he was in the habit of doing. He did not accept the invitation to dine at Kingstown for the purpose pf avoiding any apprehended clinger, nor was he at other times aware of the risk to which it now appears he was 80 !requently exposed. Careful precautions were; of course, adopted to protect Mr. Forster in his movements, but the 'right hon. gentleman never realised until reading the die. closures made in tbe course of Saturday's evidence that he had so narrowly escaped death. Mr. Forster remembers par. lectly well the first occision upon which, • according to the evidence, the signal failed. He was thin driving out with his daughter, but nothing occurred in the course of the drive to suggest that the assassins were ;ying in wait for hint.

1 THE STATE OF IRELAND. THE CONSPIRACY TO MURDER OFFICIALS. MORE STARTLING REVELATIONS. The astounding revelations made at Kilmainharn, on Saturday, by James Carey, the town councillor, one of the guiding spirits of the conspiracy, will send a thrill of horror throughout the kingdom. Although it had been announced the previous Thursday that the court would no longer be open to spectators, that decision was departed from, and as many persons were admitted on Saturday as could be conveniently accommodated. Carey's disclosures explained the constitution and working of the assassination conspiracy, and it is believed that for some days the nature of his evidence had been in the hands of the Crown. During the five hours he was under examination the greatest excitement prevailed in the dock. The inquiry was proceeded with before Dr. Keys and Mr. Woodlock, and the prisoners in the dock were James Mullett, Joseph Brady, Henry Rolls, Thomas Martin, Timothy Kelly, Peter Carey, Edward M'Caffrey, Edward O'Brien, Joseph Hanlon, Laurence Hanlon, Peter Doyle, Wm. Moroney, Daniel Delaney, Joseph Mullett, Daniel Curley, George Smith, Michael Fagan, Patrick Delaney, James Fitzharris, Thomas Doyle, Thomas Caffrey, and Joseph Smith. They were charged with conspiracy to murder, and, in pursuance of the conspiracy, with mur- dering Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke, and at- tempting to murder Mr. Field. On the wit- ness James Carey (originally charged with the murder) being placed in the box, he at once proceeded to explain the formation of the Irish Republican Brotherhooo, an organ- Nation which was to "make history" and to "remove all the tyrants in the country." It bore the name of "Irish Invincibles." It was composed of picked men belonging to the Fenian Brotherhood, and was not intended to number more than 250 members throughout the kingdom, 50 of whom were to constitute the Dublin branch. The witness and James Mullett, Edward WCaffrev, and Daniel Curley were appointed to select members in Dublin and to organise the society by a man named Walsh, and afterwards by Cap- tain APCaffrey, and still more recently by an individual only known to the witness as "No. 1." The witness related the circumstances of the plot against Mr. Forster, which they endeavoured to carry out on March 3rd and several subsequent occasions. Each attempt was frustrated, however, by the presence of police at the spot or by the non-appearance of the Chief Secretary himself. Mr. Forster, Earl Cowper, and Mr. Burke were the first three named for "removal," and in the case of Mr. Burke the assassins met on several occasions before the 6th of May, but failed to accomplish their purpose till that day. Carey corroborated Michael Kavanagh's evidence regarding the occupants of the car, and said that he himself went in a cab driven by Fitzharris. He was accompanied by Joe Smith, the man 111-rested on Friday, and Joe Hanlon. The witness said he waved a white handkerchief as a signal as he and Smith were being driven to where the main body of the men were gathered. They were Joseph Brady, Timothy Kelly, Daniel Curley, Joseph Hanlon, Edward O'Brien, Thomas Caffrey, and Patrick Delaney. After telling them that Mr. Burke was coming the witness left them, having previously sent Smith away, and pro- ceeded towards Island Bridge. He looked round as he went and saw Brady strike Mr. Burke with his left hand. He saw Daniel Curley the same evening in Dublin, and be told him that Brady attacked Burke and afterwards stabbed Lord Frederick Cavendish. The witness also saw Brady himself the same night, and he detailed the circumstances of. the murders, saying he stabbed Mr. Burke on the Leff shoulder. Lord Frederick Cavendish then struck Brady with his umbrella. Brady then struck Lord Frederick on the arm, followed him into the roadway, and there, as he said, "finished him." He afterwards saw Kelly at Burke's body. Brady wiped his knife on the grass and threw it on the car. Another knife and it were afterwards broken in pieces and destroyed. , Startling disclosures as to the operations of P. J. Sheridan,' who moved about disguised as Father Murphy a priest, ; In Irish circles in the Metropolis rumours are afloat as to were also given by the witness, and these -disclosures the probable suppression by the Government of the National included the selection of Mr. Clifford Lloyd for assassina- Land and Labour Ldague Organisation, which succeeded to tion. Mrs. Byrne was conveyed across deace of the witness, upon the case being adjourned, Mr. , the Channel on Tuesday morning, and in the course of the Murphy, the counsel for the Crown, warned the counsel for day she was taken to Kilmainbam Gaol to be seen by James the defence that he might have another surprise in store for Carey. The result was that she was set at liberty, Carey them. As the prisoners passed from the court to the cells failing to identify her. the crowd cheered and waved their hats. On Sunday a crowd collected in front of the house until lately occupied by Carey, and the police were stationed around it for Imo- tection.

His father was a bailiff on the property of the %\ hen a young man Sheridan married Mary Anne M`Dermott, daughter of a hotel keeper in TubbercurrY• county Sligo. They went to England, and lived for some time near London, where they became acqu tinted with the leaders of the Fenian movenr.nt in this country. Their stay in England, however, was a brief one, and on returning to Ireland Sheridan was appointed master of the Swinford Workhouse, but, in consequence of an official inquiry into the management of that institution, he held the office only one year. He next became proprietor of his father-in-law's hotel, and acted as commercial traveller until the Land League agitation began, when he took to the platbrm, and was remarkable for the violence of his language. He was appointed Land League organiser for the province of Con- naught. Mr. Sheridan afterwards went to Paris, and left that city for America, where he is or was until recently on the staff of the lush World in New York, Mrs Sheridan is still in Tubber, urry. LADY FREDERICK CAVENDISH ON THE KIL- MAINHAM DISCLOSURES. The following letter was written on eaturday by Lady Frederick Cavendish to a local clergyman, who asked per- mission to dedicate to her a sermon on the late Chief Sec- retary :—" The Dublin disclosures do indeed enforce the awful lesson contained in the last verse of the third chapter of Samuel. You will, lam sure, forgive me if I beg of you, before sending the MS. to the printers to look through it first with the special view of seeing if there is any word that could be turned into a desire for vengeance. You will readily understand how I must shrink from any such feel- ings. I would rather, as far as I may, reverently adopt the Lord's Prayer on the Cross—' Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' The law, I know, must take its course, for the sake of the unhappy country itself. I pray that neither the unspeakable greatness of my sorrow, nor the terrible wickedness of those men, may ever blind either myself or any of the English people to the duty of patience, justice, and sympathy in our thoughts, words, and deeds with regard to Ireland and its people at large.—Believe me, dear sir, yours truly, LUCY FREDERICK CAVENDISH. P.S.— I can't say how deeply I feel all the kind sympathy shown me, mast especially by Lord Frederick's _constituents."

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The Runcorn Board of Guardians held their fortnightly meeting at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon when there were present the Revs. Canon Barclay (chairman), J. W. N. Tanner, and John Lockwood; Messrs. J. Ashton, J. Mid- wood, J. Mclntyre, J. Campkin, J. Knowles, T. Norman, J. Darbyshire, C. Rigby, E. A. Wallington, W. Fisher, W, Whittaker, and W. Handley.

A SURCHARGED -ASSISTANT OVERSEER. A communication was read from Mr. John Dolby, district auditor, stating that at the audit he had surcharged Mr. Tipping, assistant overseer for Walton Inferior, in the sum of £33. He had written to Mr. Tipping on the question, who stated that he was unable to pay the amount. He, therefore, rcquested the Guardians to make application to his sureties for the repayment of the money.—lt was decided that application be made to Mr. Ganaon, Halton, and Mr. Brereton, Walton (Mr. Tipping's sureties), for the payment , of the amount surcharged by Mr. Dolby.

COUNTY RATE. The CLERK produced the precept for the County Rate, amounting to £BO4 2s. id, being a decrease of £228 as compared with the corresponding quarter of lasi year. MEDICAL OFFICER FOR THE BUDWORTH DISTRICT. The 'CLERK reported that he had received only one application for the post of medical officer for the Bud- worth district, it being that of Mr. F. Sque Boreharn, of Barrow. Excellent testimonials accompanied the appli- cation.

MASTER'S REPORT. • Mr. JONES reported that there were 194 inmates in the house, against 192 in the corresponding week of last year There were 30 boys and 28 girls at the Workhouse school, and 12 boys and 10 girls rec-iving industrial training. The amount piid for ont-deor relief was £7l 7s 5d., as against 62 153. 6d., in the corresponding week et last year.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUBSDAY.

THE ORDER OF BUSINESS.—The Marquis Of lIARTINGTON informed Mr. Newdegate that the Oaths Bill was only in- formally put down for Monday next, and that there was no intention of asking the House to take the second reading on that day.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN intimated that if there was an opportunity be should take the second reading of the Bankruptcy Bill on Monday.—Sir S. NORTIICOTE appealed to the Government to make the Oaths Bill, when taken, the first order of the day; and Lord HARTINGTON, who thought the request a reasonable one, promised to consider the matter.

THE TRISH PRISONERS. Sir H. MAXWELL put the question of which he had given notice, whether the man Sheridan described by James Carey in his evidence at Kil- mainham was the same as the man Sheridan mentioned in the negotiations that led to the release of the suspects last spring, and of whom Mr. Parnell and Mr. Forster spoke at the time,—Mr. TREVELYAN replied that he had answered the first part of the question, and the other part should be addressed to the hon. member for Cork and the right hon. member for Bradford.—ln reply to a question whether there was any prospect of Sheridan being brought to justice, Sir W. HARCOURT declined to answer such an inquiry, remark- ing that if any hon. gentleman thought that the Government were not desirous and anxious to put the law into force by every possible means against these culprits he ought to take some means of expressing it. THE ADJOURNED DEBATE .ON THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. GORST, who criticised the Irish policy of the Government. He asserted that at the time the Prime Minister granted the Arrears Bill, he was really the dupe of an inner circle in the Cabinet, which had also its" No. 1," and that the mem- ber for Bradford was the first object of both the inner circle in the Cabinet and the " Invincibles." Until the hon. member for Cork gave an explanation or refused to make a disclaimer, he was willing to believe that he did not know Sheridan's true character. The Homo Secretary had accepted Sheridan as a colleague and associate, and the House had a right to a disclaimer from that right hon. gentleman. He asked the Home Secre- tary to assure the Rouse that he would have repudiated all connection with Sheridan had he known the part he was taking in the affairs of Ireland.—Sir W. HARCOURT declared that the Cabinet were always agreed that if the imprisoned men would give an assurance for the future with regard to not breaking the law they ought to be let out of prison. He asserted that there was no communication made to the prisoners at Kilinain- ham except with the full knowledge and under the direction of his right hon. friend the member for Bradford. It was Mr. Forster who gave leave to Captain O'Shea to go to Kil- ' mainham and communicate with the hon. member for Cork, and that leave was given for the purpose of ascertaining whether the assurances which were to be given were in his opinion satisfactory or not. He denied the assertion that the Government had associated itself with Sheridan, and said he believed that that person had never been in Ireland since the warrant was issued for his arrest. —Mr. GIBSON contended that after all that had come out it was impossible to avoid the grave conclusion that the Cabinet had consented to avail themselves of a criminal organisation and of the services of a man described to them as an organiser of outrage.—Sir W. HARCOURT retorted that the Government did not accept Sheridan. and had nothing to do with him.—Mr. GtasoN then urged that the debate could not come to a satisfactory close without a speech from the hon. member for Cork. He asked for some explanations from the representatives of the Land League on the topic of money. Referring to the recent speech of Mr. H. Gladstone, he said it was a gratuitously mischievous speech, and if he had not been relying upon his name he dared not, as a sub- ordinate of the Government, have made it. In making that speech he was interposing obstacles to the good governmeat of Ireland.—When Mr. Gibson sat down there was a pause, and an apparent expectation that either Mr., Parnell or Mr. ' Forster must speak. Neither rising, the Speaker was put- ting the question, when Mr. Wharton interposed, and saved the debate. The discussion was continued in a thin House up till half-past eleven, at which hour Lord Randolph Churchill, rising, had a better audience. The noble lord did not, however, equal expectation of. enlivening the de- bate, and once a pathetic yawn coming from the Conserva- tive benches caused some laughter. Mr. Goschen, amid cheers from both sides of the House, commented severely on the recklessness of Mr. Gorst and Lord H. Churchill in bringing forward a motion of this kind at the present time, when the Government were battling with crime in Ireland, and even before the trial of the Phoenix Park murderers was completed.—On the motion of Sir HERBERT MAXWELL, the debate was, at half-past 12, adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDIsTESDAY.

THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—The debate on the Address was resumed by Sir H. MAXWELL, who expressed surprise that Mr. Parnell had not disclaimed all knowledge of the true character of the man Sheridan, and that M. W. O'Brien (recently elected for Mallow), who nominated James Carey for a seat in the Dublin Town Council, had no regret to express at his connection with a confessed murderer.—Mr. O'BRIEN explained that he never saw Carey till three weeks after the latter's election to the Council, and be only supported him because of his repute as "Nationalist" and as)a working men's candidate who had shown an intelligent interest in municipal affairs. Mr. O'Brien proceeded to make a violent attack on the administration of Irish affairs dur- ing the lat six mouths. Mr. O'DONNELL followed, in another speEck of exceeding bitterness.—Mr. Prom= supported the amendment moved by Mr. Gorst.

div.head: CASEY'S REVELATIONS.
div.p: CASEY'S REVELATIONS.

The hatred of Town Councillor Carey among the lower orders in Dublin increases in intensity, and it may safely be said that nothing at all approaching it has ever been dis- played towards any one person. Mrs. Carey is guarded by police when going to early mass,and her children dare not show themselves out of doors. Were it not for tlae police and marines who guard her residence, there can be no doubt it_would be attacked. In conversation with a person some days before her husband became an approver, Mrs. Carey said, " If any- thing happens to my husband, I can give such evidence as will incriminate the very highest among them." The person understood her to mean those occupying a leading position in the present agrarian movement. If Mrs. Carey's threats have any foundation, it is evident her husband has not yet told all he knows.

EvER- since Parliament met, Her MAJESTY'S PPosition in the House of Commons have ,heen doing their very utmost—which they ave a perfect right to do by every legitimate 11eansto defeat the Government; so far ,F efforts have signally failed, as, we they will continue to fail. • The res- Ponsible leaders of the Conservative party -(3 the occupants of the front Opposition ~euch—shrink from directly challenging the t3licY of the Government in any particular, 7t.e,t they .are not above taking advantage of issues raised by some of their followers, • even by a member of the Radical party, uni do as much as they possibly can to discredit • Government in the eyes of the country. time was when it would have been • usidered beneath the dignity of a leader of e OPposition to avail himself of such means °l. dealing a blow at the party in Power, but e times have changed, and the leaders of 1e ‘JPPosition have changed with them. tz.very little trifling matter is now snapped at Y them for the purpose of making political Vital, even if the advantage to be gained s ould be only temporary. The time also Was when an Address in reply to the Royal •Lessage could be agreed to at the first or ' B.eCOrld sitting after the House met; now it lst.the exception if the Address can be got rid ;It within a week. Of course the leaders of 611 Opposition are not wholly to blame for "Is', still, they are not blameless They can- not, for instance, be expected to control the actions of the Home Rule party; but it is not f°o much to cxpect that they should be able 1° guide to some extent the course of conduct , their own supporters. Even this, however, • e front Opposition bench seems unable to d°, and, instead of leading, we find the „ I•jectipants of that bench compelled, in the interests of peace, to tamely submit to the e°tUtnands of those whose duty it ought to be to Obey. "s'IES WOUNDING C.—!t W.(l-, :',:!y Ss- pure after-thought, and but for the disclosures i ,v, Tr.omas Quinn was lit 01: ul.) on at Kilmainham on Saturday it would never . twfully wounding Ju..11 Ci era, on have been submitted. It was never hinted • •nt Barker stlt.,: ;!-, the in- atworkhouse hospital at on Thursday or Friday, not until Monday to appear.— was it placed upon the notice-paper. Its terms are most offensive, and paradoxical though it may seem it conveys alike a com- pliment and a censure. It gives the Government credit for the improved condition of Ireland, and expresses a hope that the change of policy which has brought that about will be maintained. That change of policy, we may say, was not effected without most strenuous opposition from the Conser- va!ive benches, the Fourth Party more especsally rendering the Home Rulers all the assistance in their power in resisting the passing of th,e Crimes Act, to the administra- tion of which .the success which has been achieved is in. a greatmeasure due. But the , amendment proceeds' •further, and says it ! hopes no more attempts will be made to I purchase the support of persons disaffected 1 to Her MAJESTY'S rule by concession to i lawless agitation. This is the portion of the I amendment which conveys the censure; it i refers of course to the release of Messrs . PARNELL, DILLON, and 0' KELLY . from 1 Kilmainham, the whole of the circumstances I connected with which are now brought under i review. 'I hat was done some months ago, 1 when it was clearly shown by the PREMIER 1 and his colleagues that there was nothing in ! ,b I the "Kilmainham Treaty"- so-called; but notwithstanding this the whole question is , revived, and with a great deal more of party i rancour. Mr. GORST now charges the HomE , SECRETARY with havi-g had criminals or a ! criminal for an associate and colleague, an assertion, however, which carries its own reputation with it. A statement such as this is only characteristic of a person like Mr. GORST, whose irresponsibility protects him; . but it is a pity that it should be made, if tor I no other reason than that it lowers the tone ' ,of debate. The same member would fain trace , the cause of the recent horrible crimes in ! Ireland to the doors of the Land League, and I I more particularly to the leaders of that I organisation; but reading the informer 1 CAREY'S evidence with special reference to : 1 dates it will be found, as pointed out by the I Daily News this week, that Messrs. PARNELL, DILLON, and O'KELLY were actually in prison I —and consequently beyond the influence of the murderers—when the crimes were decided 1 1 upon, if they were not actually committed. i This being so it effectually •disposes of any shadow of complicity on the part of Mr. 1 PARNELL and his closest followers. A debate such as that on Ireland which has taken place this week serves on useful purpose. It relates to the past and has no connection - whatever with the future, it stirs up angry , passions in certain members, and keeps alive a party feeling which, in a matter of so much gravity, ought to be allowed to slumber. It will not secure a single vote to either party, and it is anything but a straightforward means of attacking the Treasury Bench. It is a mode of warfare to which the leaders of the Opposition should give no countenance, they should rather discourage it. It is their duty either to deliberately censure the Ministry or support them, and it is only by doing either the one or the other that they will command any respect in the country.

Sessions, on WIDNES DRUNKARDS.—At Widnes Petty for being Wednesday, Michael Burn was fined 5s and costs gt drunk in Parke's Railway Hotel; and Wm. Wallace t•tg mulcted in a similar penalty for being drunk in the Rt.. O'Bells public-house, Farnworth. The following persona I were each fined for drunkennessi—Jarnes Pye, Geo. Fowett, Patrick Kelly, Budget Mulraney, John Wells, Rose McMul- len, and Catherine Hyne. The fifth annual report of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Accident Insurance Company (Limited) shows that the balance to the credit of profit and loss account amounts to £3,247 63. 9d., from which sum it is proposed to carry £l,OOO to the reserve fund, to write off £69 3s. ld from the furniture account, reducing the item to £l5O, and to pay a final dividend of 61 per cent., making 10 per cent. for the year carrying the balance, £303 3s. Scl., to the profit and loss account for next year. THE SILTATION ARMY AT WIDNES.—The members of the Salvation Army held special services at Widnes on Monday, on the occasion of the installation of a new captain and lieutenant. In the morning a meeting of officers, at which "Major " Taylor was present, was held in Licey-street, schoolroom, and in the afternoon a "holiness council " took place in the Volunteer Hall. A "hand to mouth fight, in the shape of a great tea banquet," as the placards phrased it, then took place and it was largely attended. The usual parade along the streets of the town followed, the day's proceedings concluded with an " indescribable meet- ing" in the Drill Hall. TEETOTALISM AT WIDNES.—The members of the Star of Widnes Lodge 1.0.G.T. received a "fraternal visit" from the Hope of Appleton Lodge on Tuesday evening, when the chair was taken by Bro. 'l'. Reay. An enjoyable enter- tainment was given. Sisters Rylance, Hollins, Holland, Bros. 0. T. Harrison, I. Thompson, and Hollins taking part. Bro. Reay delivered an earnest address.—An entertain- ment in connection with the Widnes Silver Star Brigade was given on Tuesday evening under the presidency of Captain Mason, who delivered an address; Messrs. C. J. Roberts and S. J. Taylor each gave a recitation, and J. Taylor and Capt. Taylor each a reading, and Capt. Davies contributed a song. A TRUMPERY CASE AT Ilcercoteet.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Selina Buchanan, a well-dressed young woman, was summoned on a, charge of assaulting Mary Ana Payne, who resides with her uncle at the Devonshire Arms.—The prosecutrix said on the 10th inst. her aunt sent her to Dustsdale's butcher's shop, in Church-street, to get same change, and whilst on her way there she met the de- fendant, who struck her on the face and then ran away. She also used some bad language. Prosecutris gave her no provocation.—Defendant said about Christmas one of Mrs. "Marsh's boarders" took her into a shop to buy her a pair of gloves. He said "What will you have, my dear,,a pair of gloves or a feather ?" and every time she had passed the house since the two servants had said "What will you have my dear, a pair of gloves or a feather ?" The complainant struck her first.—The Rev.-E. A. P. Campbell said it was a trumpery case—the whole thing was too ridiculous to come into court, and defendant would be fined is. and costs 11s. 6d. A WIDNES PUBLICAN HEAVILY FINED.—At • Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. E. Gibbon and J. C. Gamble, John Barrow, landlord of the Waterloo Vaults, Waterloo-road, was charged with having, on the 12th inst., permitted drunkenness on his licensed premises. Mr. Bremner, of Liverpool, appeared for the defence, and pleaded not guilty. From the evidence of Police Sergeant Clarkson and Police Constable Skinner, it appeared that on the day in question a man named Furlough was seen to leave a public- house, and in consequence of his condition he was warned. Subsequently Furlough was found in the defendant's house, , standing at the bar with a glass of beer before him. The barman- acknowledged that he had served the beer, but added that as Furlough was leaning on the counter he did not see that he was drunk.—Ackroyd Rogers, barman' de- posed that he "did not see any signs of drink upon Fur- lough." He had, in the course of the same evening, refused Ito serve two men who were under the influence of drink,and i he was exercising every caution.—William Fitzpatrick and ! another witness stated that Furlough was to all appearances sober.—Superintendent Barker remarked that the defendant ! had previously been before.the court on a charge of permit- ting drunkenness.—The Bench fined the defend 40s and , Costs.

COLLISION BEfWEEN TWO FLATS.—At Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, an action was brought before Mr. Justice Kay and a special jury, to recover damages for a callisioa be- tween two flats.-31r. Russell, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. French were for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Gully Q.C., and Mr. Big- land for the defendant.—The plaintiffs, Messrs. Clere and Ridgway, are the owners of the flat Alert, and the defend- ant, Mr. Mousley, is the owner of another flat called the ITam o' Shanter. On the 3rd October last the two flats were in the approach to the lock of the Widnes canal, waiting to be admitted when the gates were opened. The Alert was loaded and the Tame o' Shanter was empty, and there seemed to be a custom with the authorities of the canal ta give priority of entrance to loaded flats. When the gates were opened the Alert was signalled by the lockmaster to enter the lock, and the master of the Tam O'Shanter also moved on his vessel, although he was ordered by the lockmaster to keep back. The result was that both vessels were jammed in the lock, and the Alert was seriously damaged. The master of the Tam O'Shanter was summoned by the London and North-Western Railway authorities, who are the lessees of the canal, for disobeying the regulations of the canal by entering the lock without permission, and he was fined £5 and costs, or a month's imprisonment in de- fault. It was shown for the defence that the Tam O'Shanter was a canal boat belonging to West Bromwich, and that the terms upon which she was to be navigated were that she was not to be taken upon tidil waters. In the present ease the master had taken the boat across the Mersey from Run- corn to Widnes, and from this arose a question as to whether the master of the Tam O'Shanter was at the time acting within the scope of his employment. The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff, and the question of damages was reserved.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the School Board, represented by Mr. J. H. Danhy, the clerk, prosecuted the following per- sons for breaches of the Education Act, and the usual fine ' was inflicted in each case :—Michael Roach, John Hayes, Henry Annetts, Adam Green, James Carr, John Hill, Eliza- beth Boyle, John Peacock (two cases), Thos. Kerley, Henry Rimmer, John McLoughlin, Mary Grierson, James Stanton, Robert Hoey (two cases), John Riley, and Peter Sheridan. A FARNWORTH MAN FINED AT ST. HELENS. Joseph Liptrot, of Farnworth, was on Monday charged at the St. Helens Police Court, with having been drunk and disorderly in St. Helens railway - station on Saturday night last. It was stated that the prisoner had acted in a very violent manner at the station, and had as- saulted two or three ladies who came by a Liverpool train. He was fined 5s and costs. A further charge against the prisoner of having travelled without a ticket was with- drawn. SILVER STAR BRIGADE (WIDNES BRANCH) FIRST DIVISION.—The usual monthly entertainment was given on Tuesday by the members. Captain Mason took the chair, and in the course of an address urged his hearers to keep the pledge and fight for the cause of temperance, and to get as many as possible to join the society. The following was the programme of the entertainment, which was creditably executed :—Recitation, "Our Minnie," C. J. Roberts; reci- tation, "Buttercups," S. J. Taylor; reading, "Vat you please," Captain Taylor; song, "Hurrah for sparkling water," Captain Davis; reading, "Homeward bound," Captain Taylor. The customary votes of thanks and the singing of "God save the Queen" brought the proceedings to a close. YOUNG WIDNES THIEVES.—Rose Mullen and Catherine I Heyes, raggedly dressed, and wild-looking girls, 13 years of ' age, were charged with atealin; 621bs of scrap iron, value is., from a railway siding, on the 20th instant, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. The prisoners were seen to steal the iron by Detective Wilkin- son, and were afterwards apprehended by P.C. Skinner. The mothers, who were comfortably dressed and comfortably looking, elected to have their children dealt with sum- marily, and Mr. Gibbon gave the parents a lecture on the benefits their children would receive if sent to school. He said it was disgraceful that while the parents were well clothed the children s'aould be allowed to walk about dirty ' and half naked.—The prisouera were discharged with a , caution.

month. A WIDNES CASE AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.— OR SaturAiy, at the Liverpool Assizes, the case of Ennis and Wife v. Golding, Davies, and (,o. was heard before Mr. Jiistice Watkin Williams: This was a claim for compensation for the loss of a son' of the female plaintiff, a youth named John O'Brien, who was killed at the defendants' works. —Mr. Segar and Mr. Wilkinson were for the plaintiffs. and Mr. Mulholland for the defendants.—The plaintiff, Ennis is a carpenter living near Wexford, lieland, and the de- fendants are chemical manufacturers at Widnes. In August last O'Brien' who had been in the defendants' ser— vice-only a few weeks; was killed whilst engaged in putting a strap on a fly wheel connected with the Hargreaves patent mill process.. He had been in the habit of contri- buting a.weekly sum,to his mother, who now claimed com- pensation for his death.—His Lordship, after the casa had been partly heard, saidithere was no question for the jury, and non-suited the plaintiffs on the ground that the action was not maintainable under Lord Campbell's Act, and that no pecuniary darnage•had been proved. SAD ACCIDENT AT A RUNCORN' FOUNDRY:. —At the
Egerton Arms.--- Bridge-street, Runcorn,oan Thursday after- noon, Mr. J. E. Worsleyrthe deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of .Samuel Cross,

a boy 13 years of age, who resided at 8, Norfolk-street, Run- corn. About a month ago deceased was taken from Dut- ton Workhouse, of which he was an inmate, by his brother John, who succeeded in finding him employment as errand lad at the Bridgewater foundry, where be (John). wag also employed as a dresser. He also found a house for him. It was one of the duties of the deceased tol. break coke into

small pieces for the furnace, and on Thursday morning about nine o'clock, Samuel Britland, carter, took a load through the smithy to the place where the coke is usually "tipped." He stopped the cart about a yard from the back- wall, and then left the horse's head with the intention of "scotching" the wheels. The horse suddenly backed the, cart against the wall, and a scream was heard. Britland ran to the horse and drew out the cart, when he saw the de- ceased fall sideways to the ground. Edward Ponton, a smith, living at 23, Bold-street, who had seen the deceased go behind the cart, raised the poor youth, who after a few gasps, expired. The deceased had evidently intended to pull down the tail-board, as he had taken out one peg. He had, it was stated, been on several occasions warned to keep away from the cart, but his anxiety for work seems to have overcome his discretion. The Coroner, in concluding his summing up, said he was very glad, indeed, that the Rev. Canon Barclay had attended the inquiry as chairman of the Board of Guardians. Every- one must be glad that the Guardians took so much in- terest in the boys under their care that Canon Barclay should have attended that inquest for the purpose of seeing that a full inquiry was made, and to show that the boy, although without his natural guardians, had someone to look after him. (Applause.)—A verdict of I "Accidental death" was returned, and the Rey. Canon Barclay said he was perfectly satisfied with the finding of the jury.—Mr. Arthur Linaker (of Mr. W. H. Linaker's office) was also present on behalf of the Guardians. THE REV. W. PRES'TON, M.A.. ON THE CHURCH Asso- CIATION.—The Rey. W. Preston, M.A., presided over a lec- ture. on "The life and times of Luther," which wa3 delivered' in Holy Trinity Schools, on Friday last week, by Mr. Henry Miller, of London. The lecture was given in connection with the Runcorn branch of the Church Association, and the Chairman, in opening, said much misapprehension ex- isted regarding the Church Association, which had in conse- quence been termed a persecuting society. They might as well call the bench of magistrates such because they put in force the law against evil-doers. It was a loyal society— loyal to the Crown, the Church, and the Prayer Book. Its object was to maintain the law against those who sought to transgress it and to bring into the Church fatal errors, and who told them plainly that they wanted to extirpate Protese tent opinions in the country. Protestantism meant a free and open Bible. religious liberty, and toleration. A Protes- tant was one who witnessed for the truth against errors that overthrew it. Some years ago, when the Homeward move- ment began in the Church the bishops were called upon to check it. They declared their inability to do so owing to the law's uncertainty. Several Church- men then formed a society to strengthen the hands of the bishops' and to determine the legality or illegality of what was being done, It was called "'The Church Association." It had taken into the law courts very many of the proceedings of those called Ritualists and in every case the highest authorities had declared those pro- ceedings illegal. For refusing to obey the law Mr. Green was sent to prison. Why should a cleric who defied the law of the land be more tenderly dealt with than a layman? The Church Association was no persecuting society, but one that every loyal churchman who wished well to his church and country ought to support. It came into being after the Church Union, whose object was to-support Ritualists and law-breakers. How any honest man could uphold the latter association was a phenomenon, and strange contradiction ! those who rejected the secular authorities in matters of ritual were appealing to those authorities to compel the good Bishop of Manchester to do what his con- science told him he dare not do. The fact was, these men wished to make a law to themselves. The lecture was then proceeded with. A WIDNES MILS DEALER'S TROUBLES. At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Mr. James Wright, farmer, Cuerdley Moss, near Widnes. sued Mrs. Ann Board- man, milk dealer, 37, Mersey-road, Widnes, and 66, Widnes- road, Simms Cross, for £l5 138., for milk sold and delivered. There was a counter-claim brought under the Sale of Food and Drugs Act, 1875, 38 and 39 Vic., c. 63, sec. 28, which deals with the recovering of penalties.—Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, appeared for Mr. Wright, and Mr. Taylor, bar- rister, Liverpool, instructed by Moore and Son, solicitors, Warrington, appeared for Mrs. Boardman.—Mr. Riley said that defendant had paid £4 7s. sd. into court, and had set up a counter-claim of £ll lie. 6d. Although that amount did not quite balance the debt and costs of the action, he (Mr. Riley) was told it was intended to do so, and the whole con- troversy would be on the counter-claim for costs incurred by the defendant under a conviction for selling adulterated milk, which milk defendant alleged was part of that for which they were suing.—Mr. Taylor said their counter claim was a somewhat peculiar one. The figures £ll us. 6d. were made up of fines and certain costa which defendant had to pay, through, as they alleged, the fault of the plaintiff. The latter had agreed to supply defendant with a quantity of milk every day which was to be pure and fresh. On the morning of the 4th July plaintiff's man took a tank of milk and first called at 37, Mersey-road, where the defendant resides. He there left eight quarts of milk, and then pro- ceeded with the remainder to the branch shop at 06, Widnes- road, Simm's Cross. Immediately after leaving, an inspector of police entered the premises and bought a sample for analysis, and a few days after defendant was summoned for having sold adulterated milk and fined £2 and costs. He would call evidence to prove that they bought the milk not knowing that it was adulter- ated, and that it was really in the same state when it had been seized by the inspector as when it was brought to them. —Mrs. Boardman was then called, and corroborated this statement. On reaching the point in her evidence about the conviction, it was found that the necessary document to prove that this had been the ease was not in court, and his Honour thereupon said the case could not proceed unless it was produced, and he would, therefore, adjourn the case for a fortnight. It would be very difficult, on the fa-,:e of the conviction, for plaintiff to show that the milk had not been adulterated. Very likely some arrangement would be come to.—The contending parties then' consulted together, and about half an hour later Mr. Riley asked his Honour to re- cord judgment by consent for plaintiff for £lO lfts, includ- ing money paid into court, and for plaintift on the counter- claim with costs, payable in a monit.—His Honour con- sented to this arrangement.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A RUNCORN
div.p: MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A RUNCORN

WOMAN. AN, UNTRUTHFUL WITNESS CENSURED. On Wednesday morning, at the Beard Room Cemetery, Mr. T. Ji Ridgway, coroner, held an incigest on the body of Annie Williamson, better known as Annie Leach, who was found near Parr's Leek on Saturday night, about half .past ten, in what appeared a state of helpless intoxication. P.C's Kelley and Finney removed the woman to the police-station in a wheelbarrow, and placed her in a cell, Dr. McDougall was afterwards called in and discovered that the woman was quite dead.—Superintendent Williamson watched the case for the police.—The first witness called was Thomas Wil- liamson, of 11, Cross-street, who said he was a labourer, The body the jury had viewed was that of his wife, who was about 43'. years of age. He had not lived with her for over two years.—Samuel Shallcross, of IL Union-street, boat- man, siid deceased had worked with him on the boat about two weeks ago, when she took two journeys to Manchester. He saw her about eight o'clock on Saturday night and gave her a glass of beer, and sixpence, for which she asked Lim. This was at Charles Eritishaw's beerhouse in Cooper-street. She wee "sober enough." He had not seen her since.. He knew where the deceased was found, and, he could not tell why she was there, unless she was usable to get a place to sleep in, and was going down to one of his boats for that purpose. She would have to cross over the bridge in order to reach the boat.—Thomas- Hyde, living in Nelson-street, said he was a dagger by trade, but he had been working for Shallcross for some time past. He last saw deceased about nine o'clock on Saturday night. The deceased was working with the boat on Satur- day until four &Clock in the afternoon. When he saw her at night in the Albion public-house, Nelson-street, she ' was " the worse for drink." The deceased slept on board the boat when it was in Runcorn. During the past, ten days. she had slept in the boat. By Foreman. (Mr. Sinnott) : Witness had slept ashore eight days out of the ten he had mentioned. By the Coroner : He knew that the de- ceased had slept on board because he had found her in the cabin with Shallcross at five and six o'clock in the morn- ing when he had gone down to the boat.—Shallcross was then re-called and put through a vigorous cross-examination by the coroner with regard to his statements. He now ad- mitted that the woman was on the flat on Saturday morning,. hut denied that she slept on board on Friday night, or that she lived with him.—Thomas Dutton, labourer,. Weston Point, said he was in the Duke of Wellington, Percival's- lane, about nine o'clock on Saturday night, when the de- ceased entered with two young men, one of whom paid for her a glass of beer. They shortly afterwarle departed, and about half-past nine witness went on his way home. When he was walking along near Parr's lock he heard somebody I moaning, and a voice said, "Will no one help me." Witness went over to the bridge at the foot of which be fluted the deceased lying on her ' face. He raised her up, but she was unable to stand, and' after staying with her ten minutes, three young men passed, and he called them to his aid. Then two captains and a woman came up, and witness went home.—By Superinten- dent Williamson: When in the Wellington the deceased. appeared to have had a great deal of drink.—P.C. Kelly said he was on duty in High-street about half-past teas o'clock on Saturday night. He received information that a woman was lying in an unconscious state at Parr's Lock. He proceeded there at once with P.C. Finney, and found the deceased lying on her back. She was alive. There was nobody else on the spot. He recognised the deceased and said, "Nan, what are you doing here ? " and she opened her eyes and groaned. He procured a wheelbarrow, put her care- fully into it, and conveyed her to the police station.— Dr. :MacDougall deposed that about a quarter to twelve he examined the deceased at the police station. She was dead. He could not discover anything which pointed to violence of any kind. He made a post mortem examination on Mon- day afternoon. There was no cut or bruise on the deceased. The heart was very much diseased.l;eThere was a large clot of blood protruding into the pulmonary artery, preventing the flow of blood to the lungs. The cause of death was heart disease. He thought everything was done that could be done, for nothing could have saved the deceased. He thought that death had been accelerated by drink. —Shalleross was then called into the room and his deposi- tions were amended. The Coroner : Do you know what it is to tell a lie? Sliallcross : I didn't know that I was telling lies, or I should not have done so.. Do you know that for telling lies, which is perjury of which you are guilty, you are liable for seven years' imprisonment? Do you know that? Yes, but I was not just thinking about it —I don't know what course the police may adopt with you, but I advise you for your own sake, whenever you again swear to tell the truth and the whole truth, never to keep anything back. Don't think that you can swear that you will tell the ' whole truth, and then just talk in the same manner as if you had not had the oath administered to you. Did you ever give evidence before? No.—Shallcroee was then ordered from the room.—The Coroner said that Shallcrosit not telling the truth had not male any difference in this case, but if his conduct in regard to this woman had been called in question it would have been a serious matter indeed, but there was nothing in the evidence to make him morally guilty at all. It was a great pity that Shallcross did not tell the whole truth, because his action had put a colour upon the case which it would not otherwise have. The jury would probably conclude from the evidence that death resulted from natural causes.—The jury returned a ver- dict to the effect that death resulted from natural causes. —Shallcross was again called into the room, and the Coroner addressed him as follows :—"The only way in which I can mark my dissitisfaction with the way in which you have given your evidence is to refuse to al- low you anything for coming here to-day to give evi- dence. I shall not allow your expausea,"

HOUSE OF LORDS.

Lord WAvEteßv called attention to the resolutions-passed at a tenant right meeting in Ulster, and moved that resolu- tions 1 and 2 should be embodied in a supplemental Land Act.—The Earl of LEITRIM condemned the system under which the Trinity College lands were let.—Lord CARLING- TON deprecated the debate as irregular, and said the Govern- ment were not disposed to legislate in the sense suggested. —The motion was withdrawn, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

THE RELEASE OF THE IMPRISONED MEMBERS.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE gave notice that on an early day he should move the appointment of a Select Committee to inquire into and report on all the circumstances connected with the release of the three members from Kilmainham in thespring of 1S82; and that such committee should have power to examine witnesses on oath. On Monday he would ask the'' noble lord if he would name a day for the discussion. RETURN OF THE PRIME MINISTER.—Lord HARTINGTON said the Prime Minister would next week be in his place, and he had no reason to believe the second reading of the Affirmation Bill would be taken before that. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS: MR. PARNELL'S REPLY.—The adjourned debate on Mr. Oorst's amendment to the Address was resumed by Mr. PARNELL, who said he did not think that anything he might say would have any effect on public opinion in that House or the country. He had worked for the prosperity of Ireland, and his utmost desire was to make his position clear to the Irish people at home and abroad, He contested the right of Mr. Forster to to question him, because he (Mr. Forster) stood in a posi- tion little better than an informer in reference to the pro- ceedings of the men with whom he had been associated. He strongly repudiated all responsibility as regarded the Irish World; He said he had never seen that paper while in prison, and if it was thought articles incited to crime, why, he asked, was its circulation not suppressed in Ireland ?- MT. FOrster. had the power to do that, but he preferred to take advantage of the prejudices which existed, and make foul charges against him. He ac- cused MT. FOrster of suppressing truth. Dealing with Carey's evidence, be said it had been proved to be unre- liable, and be denied that the Ladies' League Fiend had sent money to any of the prisoners except for sustenance while in prison, and that had, been done to hundreds of families whose head hadheen.placed under arrest. He gave a strong denial that any of- the funds of that organiza- tion had been devoted to the•promotion of crime, He ac- cused Mr. Forster of witholdlng the truth, as while he had mentioned the name of Sheridan' he had kept back the names of the other two- had that had been given. namely, Davin and Boyton. Mr. Forster, he said,. had tried to get a promise from him which would have discredited him with the Irish people, and failing in that he. (Mr. Forster) had lost his,own position. Both he and MT. Forster had fallen into the ditch, but he had not suffered from that so much assthe ex-secretary for Ireland'. He in- sisted that the present officials were quite incompetent to administer the Crimes .Act, and he advised the Government to send Mr. Forster back to Ireland to assist Lord Spencer in setting tip the gallows and distributing blood. money in that unfortunate country. Hs concluded by expressing the belief that Ireland would survive the oppresaion.—Mr. TREVELYAN defended, the action of the Government in Ire- land since May last, and said the only policy that would be successful in that country was to say what you mean, and do it. (Loud. cheers.) He justified extreme action, and in- sisted it was true wisdom to go on punishing crime until the people saw that crime was criminal. He admitted the pre- sent situation in Ireland was grave, but his firm belief was that the ultimate result of the exertions of the Government would be to give peace to Ireland. [LEFT SITTING.]

THE BIRTTE AND DEATH RATE OF WAIRRINGTON.—For week ending February 17th.—The mean temperature was 30-2 Fahrenheit, and therefore slightly higher than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 52 F. was recorded on the 14th inst., and the minimum ternpepature 26 F. on the 16th inst. The rainfall measured .69 inches. The general direction of the wind was south-west. During the week, which was the 7th of the current year, 33 births and 22 deaths were registered. The death rats from all causes was equal to 26 S per 1,000, against 27 the average of toe previous four weeks, and against 26 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 2 irons whooping cough, 1 from rheumao fever, 6 from lung disease, and 2 from pulmonary consumption.-4 cases . of scarlet fever was reported under the requirements of . the Act of Parlia,ment.-,—Jons H. A letter was read from Mr. Brewis, town clerk of St. Helens, asking for a copy of the accounts of the Prescot Union for the last financial year. It appeared that the accounts hid not yet been published, and therefore could not be supplied. The last published accounts had been furnished.—Mr. FIDLER inquired if Mr. Hartley had received a letter from the Corporation of St. Helens, com- plaining of what they read in the papers.—The CLERK replied that he had not received any communication with reference to the vagrant wards.—Mr. FIDLER said the Board might have anticipated a sharp letter from the Cor- poration if they were to believe the reports in the news- papers —The CLERK said he had expected a letter, but none had reached him. THE DYING WOMAN IN PHYTHIAN-STREET, Sr. HELENS.

The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he had been going to ask the St. Helens Guardians if they bad taken any steps to prevent the recurrence of such a sad case as that of the woman in Phythian-street, who was found half petrified on.a doorstep. If the relieving officer had lived in his district the case would have come more readily under his notice, and if the Widnes system bad been in operation he might have billeted the woman on some one. If that were done it would go far to- wards rendering unnecessary the application for casual wards in St.' Helens.—Mr. HALL said the Board bad nothing to do with the Phythian-street case. It was a matter between the police and the relieving officer in St. Helens, and should not be thrown in the Guardians' teeth for the kepf gettins casual wards in St. Helens.
THE LATE MR. PARIS.

Mr. LEATITERBA.RROW said that said that since their last meeting they had lat one of their dear and valued friends, Mr. G. J. Paris, and he moved that a letter of condolence be addressed to the friends and relatives of the deceased gentle- man.—Mr. JACKSON seconded the motion.—Mr. HALL said he bad known Mr. Paris long, and a more amiable man could not have been. He had always paid great attention to the business of the Board, and put in all the attendances he could, and he felt great regreat at his having gone from them.—Mr. FIDLER joined in expressing sorrow for the re- moval of Mr. Paris.—The CHAIRMAN thought Mr. Paris had the respect of every member of the Board. He had acted consistently all the time he had been a member, and they all felt his loss.—The motion was agreed to. The Rev. J. BARNACLE brought under notice the fact that aged and infirm people very often walked long distances to the workhouse for a &mall amount of relief, and asked if the relieving officer had not power to arrange for them without their being put to such trouble. CONTRACT TICKETS ON THE LONDON AND

NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY. Sir,—' was glad to see attention called, in your last week's issue, to the question of third-class contracts between Liver- pool and Runcorn, and to the action of the London and North-Western Railway in connection with the same. See- ing an advertisement in December last in one of the local papers, that after December 31st third-class contracts would be issued by the above line, and also that the rates for second-class contracts would be revised, I wrote the super- intendent at Liverpool (Mr. Shaw) asking the price of second and third-class contracts between Liverpool and Runcorn, and was courteously informed that there would be no alteration in the rate between those two places. Why this should be so, I should be glad to be informed. lam aware that Runcorn is not the most important station on the line, but I'll be bound the company are issuing third-class contracts to very much less important places; and, unless it is that they have an objection to doing anything that has the least appearance of favouring Runcorn, or will do nothing unless compelled by a more enterprising competi- tion, I cannot imagine why this boon has been with held from that portion of the residents (or would-be residents) of Runcorn who are compelled to earn their livelihood in Liverpool.—l am, fic., EX-RUNCORNIAN.

THE RUNCORN POLITICAL PARTIES. Sir,—After a :somewhat lengthy period of almost absolute silence, the political atmosphere of Runcorn is to be dis- turbed. A "storm warning," in the shape of a placard in the well-known party colours, has been received, and thunder, if not lightning, may be confidently looked for on Tuesday next. From the "Napoleon" of Liverpool "Tory Democracy" or "Democratic Toryism" (Mr. Forwood will set us right when he comes), we may expect such a torrent of criticism as may probably take away the breath of the most sturdy Radical among us. Some people are looking forward with great interest to the advent of this notorious "Tory Democrat," and do not despair of some day seeing a block snow drop, if he turns out to be a genuine specimen of the species. Our two bucolic members, who seldom put in an appearance except at a church tea party, have shown great prudence in shrinking from the ordeal of a large public meeting in a radical town like Runcorn until they could get the assistance which the presence of Messrs. Algernon, Egerton, Forwood, and Tobin will afford. There is sure to be a great amount of misrepresentation after the style of Sir Robert Peel's reckless utterances at Warrington and Lord C. J. Hamilton's " inexact " statements at Liverpool. Just as Nemesis in the person of Mr. Duncan has been on the track of the latter, so the Liberal party in the town must not be slow to furnish an antidote to the Tory poison that is sure to be administered on Tuesday next. Never were the Liberals in a more united and hope- ful condition than at the present time, nor were the Tories ever in a more desolate and despondent state; everything is favourable therefore for a demonstration on the part of the Liberals here that will knock the Conservatives into the proverbial "cocked hat." The near approach of an alteration of the county franchise makes it more than ever necessary that the people should be informed on the great political questions that are agitating the public mind, so that they may act at the bsllot-box in harmony with those great principles of progress and liberty which have made England prosperous and great.—Yours, &c., Runcorn, Feb. 22, 1883. RADICAL.

div.head: DR. STEELE AND THE COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: DR. STEELE AND THE COMMISSIONERS.

Sir,—While not disposed in endorse the fulsome flattery with which " An Apostle of Order" plies Dr. Steele in com- mending his determination to put down the wearysome chatter which appears to be the stock-in-trade of some of our local authorities. I agree with him that an " immense amount of resolution and repressive power " is necessary to keep some, at least, of the obstructionists he mentions within the limits of business-like utterance, and if the doctor is possessed of these qualifications and disposed to display them, the time and temper of many of his colleagues will be spared, at no sacrifice whatever to the interests of ! the town. The "Eloquent Obstructionist" aptly (yet severely I submit) compared by the " Apostle " to Messrs. Parnell, Biggar, and Healy, and other Hibernian orators, ' whom the doctor has to restrain and guide, should in all fairness be taken into consHeration,whes we are disposed to pass strictures on the little slips he occasionally makes, otherwise I should have been constrained to write in terms of the strongest possible censure of his action in allowing Mr. Whittaker, as a gas director, to record his vote on the recent important audit question, seeing that by this vote a desirable investigation was deprived of that authority which the Commissioner?, in the interests of the ratepayers, should certainly have invested it. —Yours truly, ANOTHER APOSTLE OF ORDER. February 22nd, 1883.

div.head: PUBLICATIONS.
div.p: PUBLICATIONS.

A copy of May's British and Irish Press Guide" for 1883 is to-hand. It contains a mass of information relating to the newspaper world, and the care which has evidently been bestowed in the compilation makes that information tho- roughly reliable. After each publication particulars are in- serted relating to its day of issue, price, publisher, political and religions pri.tciples, tc., and altogether the volume will be found of much service to those who require to consult such a work.

We have received from Mr. H. Sell, advertising agent, of Fleet-street, London, a copy of his "Philosophy of Adver- tising." This is the second year of publication, and the volume contains several improvements on the first issue. Many excellent practical hints on advertising are given in its pages, and these may be followed with profit by those who require advice on such matters. The volume contains a complete register of the newspapers in the United King- dom, a few opposite remarks on each of the London dailies, a number of interesting apothegms on advertising, and it is accompanied by a very useful map. The work on the whole reflects credit on Mr. Sell.

Messrs. Cassell, Petter, Galpin, and Co. have sent us the usual monthly parcel of their publications the chief being The Family Magazine, The Quiver, and Little Folks. The interest in "Pardoned " and " Down in the world," the two serial tales running in the Family Magazine is still sus- tained, as we are satisfied it will be, considering the reputa- tion of the authors, until the conclusion. In the same magazine the prize essay on "Some thoughts on domestic training for girls," is a contribution of considerable merit, and some excellent hints are thrown out in it, while a kindred article on the "Remunerative employment for gentlewomen," is full of information as to the various rneans by which fancy needlework can be disposed of. The poetical and musical contributions come up to the average standard ; and "The Gatherer" is as attractive as ever.— In The Quiver an excellent account is given of the first London Soup Kitchen, the illustrations rendering it additionally interesting; and a church worker's description of an Ediaburgh working men's "Free and Easy" will, we are sure, be perused with pleasure and profit. The Icrip- ture lessons for school and home are this month exception- ally good, and, indeed, this remark may with justice be applied to the whole of the contributions to the February part. The Quiver lifeboat fund, we may add, now amounts to £lO2 3s. ld.—The February part of Little Folks is full of instructive and amusing contributions for the juveniles, and they are not without interest for adult readers. The items under " The Editor's Pocket-book " are exceed- ingly good.—" Old and New Edinburgh" and " Cassell's Popular Educator" have each reached their 27th part, and their excellence is maintained; and "The World of Wit and Humour," which has only recently been com- menced, will, we doubt not, prove to be one of the hest pub- lications of this enterprising firm.

DEATH IN A ST. HELENS TRAMCAR. On Saturday evening last a woman named Esther Brough died in a very sudden manner in a tramcar, at St. Helens. Toe deceased, it appeared, who lived at 78, Park-road, Parr, about eight o'clock in the evening got into a tramcar along with her husband, and they were being conveyed to Peasley Cross to the house of their son. On passing along Corporation-street Mrs. Broneh complained of being unwell, and at once appeared to fall into a fit. As she did not recover her husband naturally felt alarmed, so that on arriving at the Oxford- street terminus, Dr. Twyford, whose surgery was near at hand, was called to see her, and at once saw that she was dead. The body was then conveyed to the residence of her son at Peasley Cross. Deceased, it seems, had been a sufferer from heart disease and had been attended by a medical gentleman, so that it was considered unnecessary to hold an inquest. RELEASE OF THE REY. M. BRAILSFORD. In the Chancery Division, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Chitty, Mr. Cecil Russell applied for the discharge from Ipswich Jail of the Rev. Mr. Brailsford, who was imprisoned some , manths ago for misappropriating trust funds. Mr. Brans- ford is an old man, and when in prison the doctor certified tbat he required better than prison fare, and special fare was ordered for him. This, however, he refused, and he also re- fused to take exercise on the ground that it was derogatory to is social position to ba seen with the other prisoners. Certificates had now been sent to Mr. Justice Chitty in which medical gentlemen who had seen the prisoner described symptoms which he exhibited, which in a man of his age were very serious, and might lead to a fatal result. His discharge was therefore asked.—Mr. Bramwell Davies appeared on the other side, but made no objection.—Mr. Justice Chitty ordered the immediate discharge of the pri- soner, and directed a telegram to be sent to Ipswich directly to that effect, with a similar telegram from the Home Secre- tary.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 24, 1883. DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 24, 1883. DISTRICT NEWS.
ASHTON.

THE CAVE BROWNE PROTESTANT INSTITUTE LIBRARY. —During the past week the committee of the Cave Browne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, Ashton, have received another handsome gift of books for their library, making a total of 270 books added to the school and library during the present year. There are now upwards of 250 volumes in the library. ACCIDENT AT ASHTON.—On Monday, Isaac Bradburn, farmer, Gladdenhey-brow, North Ashton, met with a pain- ful accident whilst engaged in feeding a bay-chopping machine driven by steam upon his farm. The some inad- vertence his hand was caught in the machinery, and being drawn forward under the revolving knife, was cut off in slices up to the wrist, when by some chance the driving strap came off the wheel, thus enabling him to escape more serious injury. The injured min was cormved home and attended by Dr. Anderlion, of Billinge, who 'found it necessary to amputate the limb just above the wrist. We understand that owing to recent illneqs from the effects of which he is still suffering, Bradburn is only making slow progress towards recovery,
