BAND OF Hors ENTERTAINMENT AT LYAIM.-1 he monthly meeting of the members of the Primitive Metho- dist Band of Hope, Lymm, was held on Monday evening. The chair was taken by the Rev. Samuel Stafford, superin- tendent, and there was a very large attendance. An enjoyable evening was spent in listening' to songs, recita- tions, and dialogues by the members.

BRUNNER MOND, AND COMPANY] LIMITED, WIN NINGTON. The half-yearly meeting of this company (alkali manu- facturers) was held at the Law Association Rooms, Cook- street, Liverpool, on Tuesday, the chair being occupied by Mr. John Crosfield, of Warrington. There were also pre- sent—Messrs. L. Mond, Wilmington • C: M. Holland, f:ackr. ter; E. Solvay and A. Solvay, Itoitsfort, Bei-glum Milner, Warrington; H. Coghill, Liverpool; J. Licerpool ;J. G. T. •W• d P .7'aerUn'ner, - T .tverpool ; W. Blain, Liverpool.; ueorge Jones, Liv , 8"-eool ; N, Greening rrartington ; and T. H. Forgan I,°-ecretary), The following was the "ert of the directors :—The balance sheet and nro f;.` and loss account, certified by the auditor, and prese".ited, show a balance to the credit of ' profit and lost account on the working of the half-year ended V:t the 31st December, 1882, of £47,816 12s 7d, which, witt the amount of £4,611 8s lid brought forward from the previous half-year, makes a total of £52,428 is 6d. The large increase in the gross profits now shown over those of the previous half-year, is mainly due to the fact that the whole of the new works at Winnington, the erection of which was one of the chief objects of the formation of the company, have been at full work since the Ist July last. The directors propose to deal with the above balance as follows :—Dividend on the preference capital £5,788 17s 10d, dividend on the ordinary capital, at 25 per cent, per annum £28,125, amount to be written off patents' account £lO,lOO, amount to be placed to a reserve fund £B,OOO, balance to be carried forward £414 3s 8:1—£52,428 is 64. The directors propose that the name of Mr. Alfred Solvay, of Boitsfort, in Belgium, be added to the present board of directors. The director who retires by rotation, is Mr. John Crostield, who, being eligible, offers himself, and is recom- mended for re-election. The auditor also retires, but is eligible for re-election.

The following was the profit and loss account for the half year ending 31st December, 1882: To office salaries and auditing, £909 9s 11, Directors' salaries and fees, £1,860 Os. OZ., general charges and in- come tax, £1434 16s. 2d., preliminary expenses, one-sixth written off, £194 13s. t4d., interest on mortgage, £l5O Os. Od-, balance, £47,816 12s. 7d.—£52,365 2s. 66.; by gross pro- fits, £52,001 19s. 01, rents, £360 is. Od.' transfer fees, £3 2s. Gd.—£52,365 2s. 6d. •' by balance brought down, being profit this half-year, £47,816 12s. 7d., balance from last half-year, £4,611 8. 11d.—£52,428 is. 6d. The CHAIRMAN said that as each shareholder had re. ceived a copy of the report, it might Le taken as read. He congratulated them on having had such a prosperous half- year. A dividend of 25 per cent was such as must satisfy any man, and they were also increasing the value of the concern by putting to the reserve fund the handsome amount shown in the financial statement. He had gone through the accounts with the auditor, and as far as he could judge they were perfectly accurate, and the dividend was honestly earned. He regretted that Mr. Brunner had been abroad for some months in consequence of ill health, but according to latest reports he was improving, and hoped soon to return. -He might state that the directors had every confidence that the year 1883 would be as prosperous, if Hot more prosperous, than 1882. He ,moved the following resolution " That the direc- tors' report and statement of accounts be adopted, and that a dividend be paid the holders of the pre- ference shares ea the rate of seven per cent, per annum on the amount paid up or credited on such shares, and that a dividend be paid to the holders of the ordinary shares at the rate of 25 per cent. per annum for the half-year, free of income-tax."

Mr. CoGHlLL'seconded the resolution, and it was unani- mously carried. Mr. MOND moved the re-election of Mr. John Crosfield as a director of the company. He had pleasure in testifying to the valuable &I-vices rendered by Mr. Crosfield as chairman of the company and to the great interest which he bad taken in all its affairs. He should be very sorry to see him removed from the directorate.
The resolution, having been seconded by Mr. BLAIN, was adopted.

Mr. C. M. HOLLAND proposed that Mr. Alfred Solvay, of Boitsfort, Belgium, be appointed a director. Mr. Solvay was the brother of the original inventor of the process in opera- tion at their works, and had been his co-adjutor for the past 18 or 20 years. It was thought very advisabje in the interest of the company that he should be directly connected with it, one advantage being that they would be kept in commu- nication with the other side of the Channel. Ho had no doubt that the resolution would commend itself to the share- holders.
Mr. MILNER seconded the motion, which was unanimously passed. On the proposition of Mr. JONES, seconded by Mr. GREEN- ING, Mr. T. W. Reid, accountant, Liverpool, was re-elected auditor.

A cordial vote of thanks was given to Mr. Crosfield and his co-directors for the valuable services they had rendered to the company during the past half year. The motion having been cordially carried, The CHAIRMAN expressed kis obligation, and said that he considered it an honour to be the chairman of such a prosperous company. The directors always worked har- moniously together, like a happy family, and he believed that so long as they continued to do so the company would remain in a flourishing condition. This brought the proceedings to a close.

The subject for debate was as 4,0110w5, viz., "Is the patrenp.;tof the theatre consistent `'Jith true Christianity," troduced by Mr. 8- .4nauel Davies, who, 1.7, an able and , lengthy paper, str4wing a thorough knowledge are. apprecia- tion of the I.egi'..tanate drama, expres.:-,ed himsel7 in favour of the affirmat men took. HOLLAND ON PEaMaNEXT PAST MRS.—The half-yearly meeting of the Cheshire, Shropshire, and North Wales Farmers' Association was held at Crewe, on Tuesday, when Mr. R. Holland, of Frodsharn, read an interesting paper on "Permanent pastures" He pointed out that the breadth of permanent pasture was gradually increasing throughout the United Kingdom, in the past ten years it having increased by nearly two million acres. One would naturally suppose that this great increase would have enabled them to keep a much larger head of cattle; but the number of their farm stock had decreased by over 784,000. In the present condition ,of things it was apparent that a larger amount of live stock could be supported upon arable land than upon pasture. One of the chief reasons why the larger breadth of pasture land was supporting less stock was that a very large portion of the pasture in this country was in a bad condition. Go where they would they would see a most marked deterioration of pasture land during the last few years. This was partly to be accounted for by the long series of wet seasons which they had had. The continuous rains had destroyed many of the finer herbs and grasses,- and rendered those which remained less nu- tritious in their character. The fertility of the land must, however, be maintained. Every gallon of milk that was produced from the grass, and every pound of meat that was sold to the butcher took something away from the land, and unless this something was periodically replaced, it was idle to suppose that permanent pastures, however well laid down in the first instance, would not in time deteriorate. In the course of a discussion Mr. Latham said that no man couli safely lay down land to permanent pasture unless he was guaranteed compensation for unexhausted improve- ments. He hoped that the Government would pass a really good sound act dealing with this subject. Mr. Chaplin's bill would leave the tenant farmer as badly off as he was now. Earl Cairns's Entailed Estates Bill would not have the effect of removing these old abominations of which they complained. It would not abolish settlement. He hoped to see a bill in the spirit of that promoted by the Farmers' Alliance. (Loud applause.)—The usual votes of thanks terminated the proceedings.

div.head: GOLBORNE,
div.p: GOLBORNE,

SERVICE OF SONG AT THE GOLBORNE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—The popular and interesting service of song en- titled " The basket of flowers, or the triumph of truth over falsehood," was given in the Golborne Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, on Tuesday evening last, by the choir, kindly assisted by a few friends from Manchester, Leigh, and Gol- borne. The proceeds were in aid of the new school fund, and also towards pewing the interior of the chapel. The want of school premises apart from the chapel has been a long-felt one, and the Wesleyans of Go!borne will only be gratified and further encouraged in their noble work, whes the movement they at present have on hand is carried to a successful issue. It is a pleasure to know that on Tuesday evening the service of song proved to be a decided success, both in the attendance and the ability displayed by the performers. The latter numbered about 40 voices, and were ably conducted by Mr. William Entwistle, Mr. W. Jones efficiently presiding at the harmonium. Mr. Ball read the connective readings. There was a crowded attendance, and Mr. Howard, of Golborne, presided. Mr. William Mitchell (of Brook Vale), Mr. William Garton, and Mr. D. Mather very kindly lent a pleasing variety of flowers, which were attractively arranged in front of the rostrum, while overhead a basket of flowers was suspended from a chandelier, giving effect to the title of the service. In briefly addressing the meeting at the com- mencement, the chairman observed that the compiler of the service, Mr. E. Billingsley, of Runcorn, had promised to read the connective pieces, but he had since died. He trusted Mrs. Billingsley would derive some benefit from the sale of the books. Be was glad to have upon the platform Mr. Ball, who consented to read in the place of the late Mr. Billingsley. The service was then proceeded with, and from beginning to end was much appreciated by the con- gregation. At the close Mr. J. S. Entwistle, on behalf of the trustees, moved a deserving vote of thanks to the singers and reader, which was heartily accorded. The proceedings shortly afterwards concluded.

div.head: IIAYDOCK.
div.p: IIAYDOCK.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD.—On Wednesday afternoon last Mr. Barker, coroner, held an inquest at the Stork Inn, Billinge Chapel. End, on the body of Walter Turner, infant son of John Turner, farmer, Winstanley, who died suddenly early on Sunday morning last. Since birth the child ap- peared a strong and healthy one. It was taken to bed as usual on Saturdiy night, but when the mother awoke at half-past five on the following morning she found her child had expired. The hands were clenched, and the legs drawn up as if the child had had a fit.—The jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes." 'BLUE RIBBON GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MEETING. - The usual weekly meeting in connection with the Blue Ribbon Army was held on Wednesday evening in the Mission Tent. Mr. W. Houghton occupied the chair. After the usual opening services an excellent programme was gone through, each of the pieces being given in an efficient manner. A very earnest address %vac; given by Mr. Weaver, in which he congratulated the members upon the success of the move- ment, and spoke in eulogistic terms of the week's mission lately held by Mr. T. Rosbottom. He then went on to speak of the social, moral, physical, and ludicrous phases of the drink question. At the close seven new pledges were taken and eight ribbons donned. There was a good attendance at the meeting. Mr. Rosbottom commences another week's mission on next Monday week.

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

HUTTON LITERARY AND SCIENTIFIC A SSOCIATION.—A meeting of this association was held on Thursday in the reading-room of the Huyton Working Men's Club, the pre- sident (Rev. W. T. Southward) in the chair. Mr. S. J. Capper, president of the Liverpool Entomological Society, read an extremely interesting paper on the "Study of In- sects," which beilltrstrated by exhibiting a great variety of specimens. Among other things, he gave an interesting account of the way the specimens had been collected. A short discussion followed. There was a good attendance. It is interesting to notice that the interest in the association continues to increase.

HUYTON TEXPERANCE SOCIETY.—A well attended Meet- ing of this society was held on Tuesday evening, in Huyton Park School, to hear an address by the Rev. R. McAll, of Bristol, one of the leaders of the movement known as the Protestant Evangelical Mission. Mr. S. J. Capper pre- sided, and, in introducing Mr. McAll, adverted to the great strides made in recent years by evangelical work generally. He also referred to the progress of temperance societies, contrasting those of the present day with those of the past. The Rev. R. McAll, in the course of an address of consider- able length, described the foundation of the Protestant Evangelical Mission in Paris by his cousin in 1872, and gave an account of its operations and development. At present the mission had 35 chapels, with accommodation for 6,800 worshippers. It was statei that Mr. McAll was about to alvocate the claims of the mission in America. On the motion of Mr. J. B. Leach, seconded by Mr. E. Capper, a vote of thanks was given to Mr. McAll. A pleasant mis- cellaneous entertainment by members of the Huyton Tem- perance Society followed. DASTARDLY ASSAULT ON A HUYTON CARRIER.—At Pres- cot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Holcroft was sum- moned, but did not answer, for assaulting Thos. Baldwin.— Complainant said he lived at Huyton, and was a carrier be- tween Prescot and Liverpool. Defendant had owed him a grudge fora couple of years, and a few days ago he assaulted him very badly. He (complainant) had stopped his cart in order to leave a bale of cotton at Mr. Morrison's shop in ' Church-street, Prescot, and was in the act of removing the bale from the end of the cart, when defendant came behind him and 'struck him a blow on the head. He turned round to expostulate, and then defendant struck him a heavy blow under the eve, knocking him among his horse's feet. He got up again, and defendaet knocked him down a second time, repeating the process about five times, and varying it with a few kicks. Defendant had threatened him many times. On one occasion he had dragged him from his horse, and on another occasion he had drawn a knife and threatened to "run it through his heart."—Superintendent Brirker said defendant was one of the worst characters in Prescot. He had several times suffered imprisonment for vagrancy, assault, larceny, drunkenness, and disorderly conduct. He did nothing but scamp about the neighbourhood and steal whenever he had an opportunity.—Defendant was sentenced to two months' imprisonment.

div.p: KNUTSFORD.
The Rev. J. T. Evans, B.A. (Trinity College, Dublin), head master of the Knutsford Grammar School, has been licensed by the Bishop of Chester to officiate in the diocese.

div.head: RAINHILL. •
div.p: RAINHILL. •

A DISORDERLY WOMAN AT RA.INHILL.—OR Tuesday, at Prescot Petty Sessions, Jane Kitchen was charged with committing a breach of the peace. It was stated that on Monday, the sth inst., defendant stuck her head out of a bedroom window in Church-place, Rainhill, and shouted and bawled, making a great disturbance, to the annoyance of her neighbours. She was bound over to keep the peace, herself in £lO, and one surety in .£5, for three months.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

• STEAM ON THE WIGAN TliAntwokYs.—Major Hutchinson, lone of the inspectors of the Board of Trade, has held an in- quiry at the offices of the Pemberton Local Board into an application made by the Wigan Tramways Company for a renewal of the license to use steam on the section between Wigan and Pemberton.—The Inspector,after hearing parties interested, said he would report in due course to the Board of Trade, under whose directions the inqairy was held. WIGAN COAL AND IRON COMPANY, LIMITED.—The re- port of the directors of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, Limited, for the half-year ending 31st December last, says : "The output and sales of coal have increased this half- year. The demand for fuel was very dull during the first two months; a brisk demand than sprang up, but it sub- sided, and trade again became depressed, and so remains. There was an advance in prices consequent on the increased demand, but it has not been maintained. An advance of 10 per cent, has been made on the wages paid to colliers." After referring to works in progress, the report continues:— "Seven furnaces have been in blast during the half-year. The work for further application of the Whitwell stoves has been continued. The furnaces have continued to work very satisfactorily. Prices of iron have been somewhat higher. Hale's works, the land for which was held under a lease from the company, were recently offered for public sale, and were subsequently purchased by private contract for the company, with the view of re-letting them as an ironworks to secure the consumption of iron and coal on premises adjoining the company's pits and blast furnaces. We present the balance sheet of the company duly audited. The net result of the company's opera- tions in coal and iron is a profit of £23,978 8s sd. This sum, with £642 2s 6d carried forward from last half- year, makes £24,590 10s lid available for dividend. Your directors recommend a dividend after the rate of £2 lOs per cent, per annum, which will absorb £22,621 us 3d, leaving £1,958 16s 8d to be carried forward. Mr. Samuel Swire and Mr. Alfred Hewlett, directors of the company, retire from the board by rotation; they are eligible for re-election." The auditors in their report state—" There has been deducted for depreciation the sum of £31,064 14s 3d, whilst additions to plant amount to £22,000 6s 6d. All expendi- ture properly chargeable to revenue in our opinion has been so charged. The debenture debt has been reduced by the sum of £2,800 falling due and paid off witliin the half- year. A dividend has been paid during the half-year absorbing £20,359 8s hi, which, deducted from the disposeable balance of the 30th June last, left £612 2s 61 to be carried forward. After providing for interest on deben- tures amounting to £3,595 14s sd, the net profit is £23,978 Eis sd, which, added to the balance brought forward from last half-year, makes a total of £24,590 lOs lid available for dividend.'" The balance-sheet shows that the share capital of the company is £1,809,725, there has been borrowed on debentures £1515,705 2s id, and the reserve fund amounts to £10,500. •

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.
A Ngw SALT WORKS —Another salt works company has begun operations upon land between the 2nd and 3rd Flashes, not far from the Dairy Farm. The new company has found brine and is now sinking a shaft.

THE SALVATION ARMY AT WINSFORD.—The latest move of the Winsford detachment of the Salvation Army is to set up a brass band. The noise created by the drum and tambourines used by the arty was bad enough on the Sabbath, and the townspeople look upon the contempla`el introduction of a brass band with anything but favour. With the Salvationists Sunday list was a field day. At 11 a.m, there was " Saints rejoicing"; 2-45, '. Cloud of witnesses " ; 5-30 p m., "Firing of heavy guns," led by the "Converted Swell," from Manchester. A great praise and thanksgiving meeting was held on Monday evening, when the "real hallelujah men," from Nantwich, took part.

MISSIONARY SERVICES AT WINSFORD. - The annual mission sermons and meetings connected with the United Methodist Free Church, at Weaver and Over, were preached on Sunday. The annual meeting was held on Tuesday night, when addresses were delivered by Mr. J. Buckley (who occupied the chair), the Revs. W. T. Symons and J. Wright (the circuit ministers.) At Over, the meeting was quite as successful as the one last year. The annual mis- sion services of the London Missionary Society were con- ducted in Over Independent Church, on Sunday last, by the Rev. Mr. Ward Price, of Chester, who preached at Over, morning and evening, and at Minshull in the afternoon. The public meeting on Tuesday was presided over by the Mayor (Mr. J. Slater), who was supported by the deputation, the Rev. M. Granger (Middlewich), Rev. F. Carter (Nortkwich), and the Rev. J. T. Maxwell (pastor). The collections were good.

div.head: HEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: HEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

At Chester, on Saturday, the magistrates tined a married woman named Roberts £5, or two months' imprisonment, with hard labour, for hitting a mau named William Sutton such a violent blow over the head with a poker as to render him insensible, and to require his daily attendance at the hospital.

At the Cheer Police Court, on Monday, Ernest Libley, a farm bailiff, was fined twenty shillings and costs for hav- ing been drunk on Saturday. The prisoner was being driven in a hansom cab, when a bullet which was discharged from a revolver in his possession passed through the splash- board of the hansom and lodged in the horse's leg.

VALI:ELF, Ain PRESENT TO CHESTER. Sir Thomas Frost, Mayor of Chester, has presented to the Corporation a series of historic and valuable portraits of the Earls of Chester, originally in the possession of the family of Sir Thomas Stanley, Bart., of Hooton. The eight earls now adorning Chester Town Hall were Kings of the district from 1069 to 1237. The line then became extinct with John the Scot. The succeeding earls were invariably the eldest sons of Kings of England, the present Earl of Chester being the Prince of Wales.

LIE CWSIIME TRAGEDY.—The Inquest on the body of Mary Moran, one of the victims of the double murder at Smallwood, Cheshire, was held on Monday. John Stack and Edward Sarnpley, lodgers, gave evidence as to the con- dition in which they found matters on returning to the house on the day of the tragedy. Dr. Latham described the result of a post-mortem examination. He attributed death to blows with the hammer found in the house. The Coroner characterised the crime as perfectly disgraceful to the human being concerned in it. It behoved everyone in Cheshire to assist in the discovery of the offender. A verdict was returned of wilful murder against some person unknown.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT HIGH LEIGH. On Tuesday Mr. Yates, coroner, held an inquest at High Leigh, touching the death of an old man, named Nathaniel Jeffs, eighty' years of age. On the 15th instant, the deceased attended a sale at Mr. Wright's, at High Leigh. He was leaning against the shaft of a trap, when a cow that came out of the shippon to be sold became frightened at the sight of the people, and darted past the deceased. The horse and trap moved back a little, and deceased fell under the horse, which put one of its fore feet on his chest. He was at once taken into the house, and Dr. Wright was sent for. He did not then consider the accident a serious one, but deceased became worse, and died on Saturday. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

CHESHIRE, SHROPSHIRE, AND NORTH WALES FARMERS ASSOCIATION.—The half-yearly meeting of this association' was held at the Royal Hotel, Crewe, on Tuesday, Mr. G. W. Latham, of Bradwall Hall, presiding. There was a good attendance of directors and shareholders. The balance-sheet for the half-year ending 31st December showed the total receipts £9,656 and payments £9,447, leaving a balance of £209. The working expenses had been £247, and the gross profits from trade account £385 18s 2d. The sales amounted to £8,289. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, said that during the past half-year they had done considerably more business than in the corresponding period last year. fie wished to condole with tenant farmers who had borne the burden and trouble of the last few months. They had had terrible weather lately, and at present he could not see, either physically or metaphorically, a gleam of sunshine. Although they hated it, yet a good dry east wind for the next six weeks would benefit the farming in- terests immensely, and enable farmers to carry on their work satisfactorily. (Hear, hear.)—The report and statement of accounts were adopted. Some alterations were made in the rules of the association.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DEATH AT RUNCORN.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DEATH AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday last, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner, held an inquest at the Sessions-room, Town Hall, on the body of James Briscoe, aged 15 years, step-son of Thomas Lydiate, grocer, Devonshire-square, whose death was reported in our last issue. Mr. Wm. Handley was the foreman of the in- quiry. The circumstances of the case are fully detailed in the following evidence :—Thomas Lydiate, grocer, 48, Devonshire-place, Runcorn, said the body the jury had seen was that of James Briscoe, his step-son, who was 15 years of age. The deceased was learning the trade of a carpenter. On the 2nd December, the deceased was assaulted in War- rington. He stated that he was struck on the neck by a man as he was on his way home, but he never complained of any pain arising therefrom, and until a fortnight ago was in his usual health. On that day he was playing football, and about eleven o'clock the same night, when he returned, he remarked•that he had a black eye. He said he was not aware of the fact until told by a companion, and he did not know how he got it. The Wednesday morning following, he complained of having the head ache, to which it appeared he was subject, and he remained in bed all day. Next day he was rather better, and on the Friday he got up and had a walk. On Saturday his head was again worse, and Dr. Carruthers was sent for, and attended him up to the time of his death which took place on the 15th inst.—Walter Heyes, who lives in Stone-street, Halton, said he was a blacksmith. Ile knew the deceased well, and was playing football with him on Saturday the 3-d inst. After the game was finished and the players were in the dressing-room, witness said to deceased " You have got a black eye." He replied " Yes I know I have, but whether I got it when we were mauling or when we were playing, I don't know." lie (witness) saw no unfair play, nor did he hear any complaints. Deceased did not say that he had been kicked or treated badly.—Wm. Cox, of 8, Irwelt-lane, ship's carpenter, said the deceased worked with him at the same place. On the sth instant, while they were repairing the bottom of a ship, the deceased and some of the other apprentices commenced to discuss football topics, when the deceased said " I got kicked, and the first time we drop in with them they will have to look out." He did not say when or by whom he was kicked.—Dr. Carruthers, of Halton, stated that he was called in to attend the deceased on the 10th instant. He was suffering from general feverish symptoms and headache, and complained of pain at the inner side of his right thigh, which was swollen and tender to the touch. On the follow- ing day he noticed the bruise round on the left eye, and attributed the acute head symptoms to a blow which had been received on that part. The symptoms of inflammation of the brain rapidly increased, and he ultimately died of that disease. He had made a post mortem examination of the body. The only external mark of violence was a slight discoloration and smelling on the upper part of the right eye. On opening the head he found the skull thinner than usual. The brain itself, and the membranes, were intensely inflamed and congested. There was slight congestion of the lower and back part of the lungs' and there was commencing disease in the left kidney. The other organs of the body were perfectly healthy. From the symptoms and the evidence he had heard, he concluded that whilst the deceased was playing football, he received a blow or a fall which caused concus- sion of the brain, leading on to inflammation. He did not think the assault upon the deceased had had anything to do with his death, because he would have complained of some symptoms much earlier than he did. He (witness) I refused to give a certificate, and his reason for doing so was because he thought his death was due to violence, and was a matter for the coroner to decide.—P.C. Cheeney, of the Warrington borough force; and Robert Gill, of 32, Orford- street, Warrington, having been examined with regal(' to the assault upon the deceased, on the 22nd December, by a man named John Rigby, who was sentenced to a month's imprisonment, the jury considered their verdict.—The Foreman remarked that this case ought to lead them to ex- press their abhorrence of the game of football.—The Coroner said if the game was to be played at all he could not see how it was to be done without a certain amount of rouglineas.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died of inflammation of the brain, caused in all probability by a blow or a fall received during a football match, in which the deceased was a player.— The Coroner said perhaps the jury might feel that Dr. Car- ruthers—be believed a second doctor was called in—having attended the deceased during his illness ought to have given a certificate. In his opinion Dr. Carruthers had acted most preperly in refusing to give a certificate until the coroner was ecquainted, seeing that he thought that the inflamma- tion had arisen from a blow or violence. That opinion he ( the Coroner) thought had been borne out by the evidence that day. Had Dr. Carruthers given a certificate, and the case had been reported to him as being a case where vio- lence was the primary cause, or a cause leading up to death, he should have held an inquest all the same.

ENGLAND AND ManaGascatt.—The Foreign Office issued on Wednesday night thc test of the declaration between the Governments of Great Britain and Madagascar amend- ing Article V. of the Treaty of June, 1865. It is provided that British subjects shall enjoy rights equally with the subjects of the most favoured nation to rent or lease land, houses or other property in .the domini(ms of the Queen of Madmeasear. The absolute sale of land is, nevertheless, prohibited.
LECTURE AT T_IIE EARLESTOWN THE RFTBk.'IST CHAPEL. 01. QUEENS ELIZABETH AND
VICTORIA CONTRASTED.

!tante entitled "The reigns of Queen Elizabeth and queen Victoria reviewed and contrasted," was given by Mr. Alexander Pitt, of Liverpool, in the Baptist Chapel, Market- street, Earlestown, on Monday evening last. There was a pretty good attendance, and the lecturer was supported by the Rev. W. C. Taylor, of St. Helens, pastor, Charles Pit- kington, Esq., J.P., and Mr. G. F. Aveline. After the meeting had been opened with singing bud prayer, the Rev. W. C. Taylor announced that Mr. Pilkington, J.P., had very kindly consented to preside over the proceedings. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN observed that that was the first time he had been inside that building and it was a little pretty place. There was only one thing about it which he did, not like, and he supposed they liked it still less than he did. That was the debt existing upon it. They came together with two objects, and he would first mention the secondary one. He believed they had a debt of 450 on the chapel, and the sooner it was paid off the better it would be. He hoped they would be doing a little towards it that evening. But the main object was to hear a lecture on the reigns of Queens Elizabeth and Vic- toria. They were the reigns of two of the greatest Queens of England, and it was a review of two of the most pros- perous periods of English history. The reigns were very different indeed, however. At present we were in the midst of Queen Victoria's reign, and on that account we were unable to take a proper review of the reign or what its effects would be, but he hoped Mr. Pitt would be able to review the two reigns and place them in their true light, showing the bearings they had on the history of this country. With regard to Queen Elizabeth's reign, three centuries had thrown a sort of mist over it, and most of them had not penetrated that mist as they ought to have done. But he hoped instead of hindering Mr. Pitt it would assist him in some ways, and blot out some of the has important events and bring into prominence those that had an influence on our history. He had the greatest pleasure in calling upon Mr. Pitt to give his lecture. (Applause.) Mr. Parr commenced by remarking that Queen Elizabeth came to the throne on the 17th November, 1558, and died on the 24th March, 1603, Queen Victoria being crowned on Saturday, June 20th, 1837. The former reign was 44 years and four months, the latter exceeding that period by about a year, and it was the hope and prayer of all that her reign might be indefinitely prolonged. (Hear, hear.) Both reigns being about the same duration and fall of events, it had occurred to him that they might beneficially review and contrast them. With the reign of Queen Eliza- beth a new era in England was commenced. Romanism was superseded, and in all probability no more to become a power in this country, and Protestantism was triumphant. He would contrast the reigns under four heads —the social and commercial life, literature, politics, and Nligion. In referring to any reign they must consider the personal character and position of the Sovereign. "Good Queen Bess" sounded very interesting, but he was afraid history would scarcely accord the name Elizabeth bore. In contrast with Queen Mary she was good, veal, good; but still she was unsympathetic, scheming, proud, and untrust- worthy, and, to say nothing else, was a dissembler and at times perverter of the truth. Representative Government was almost unkown, while the consent of Parliament was very rarely asked for. The Government was almost an autocracy, and such a rule was bound to be hurtful to all parties including rulers. Now, however, our Queen did not act without the consent of her Parliament, though she was not simply a constitutional dummy, as her Ministers did not act without her knowledge and consent. The Queen's position and England's position at the time of Elizabeth might be summed up in a very few words. The Queen was poor, and the Exchequer poor, good soldiers and sailors were wanted, the people were out of order, justice not executed, war with France, steadfast enemies, but no steadfast friends; and religious differences existirg everywhere, while Scot- land was a great anxiety as Ireland was at present. Queen Elizabeth had her hands full, and had a great difficulty in freeing herself from a variety of conflicting interests. Queen Victoria at no time had any such difficulties to cope with, neither would she personally have been expected to cope with them had she had them. The lecturer then referred to various events in the reign of Queen Elizabeth, alluding to the establishment of theatres, and remarking that one of the most obnoxious cus- toms was that of wearing swords, which were frequently drawn with but slight occasion, the extreme degree of un- certainty that attended human life being uncomfortable, to say the least of it. 'The means of travelling were touched upon, after which he observed that the reign of Queen Eliza- beth was distinguished for the rise—he could not say crea- tion—of the great middle-class. That middle-class became the backbone of the English people, and its influence had been gradually strengthening. In times of danger those men were the stabili.y and the mainstay of the State in its poli- tical and religious character, and three centuries had only increased their numbers and power. Slowly, doggedly, consistently, and wisely they had sustained and strengthened their position, and to-day Queen Victoria sat secure and camfortable on a Throne elevated aboveany other throne in the world through the steady painstaking people of this country, who felt it was to their interest that good government in the shape of security for life and property should be enjoyed by all classes of society. (Applause.) Of commerce .in Elizabeth's reign little need be said, but a great impetus was given to foreign trade and most of the London companies, celebrated for their good din- ners were instituted. Several years after Elizabeth began her reign the first cargo of African slaves was sold with the knowledge and consent of the British authorities, and during Elizabeth's reign that trade largely increased. One read with sickening sorrow that Sir John Hawkins returned from a second voyage having captured 300 slaves and sold them, leaving a profit to the proprie:ors of whom Elizabeth was one—of 60 per cent. That was a dark blot that obscured Elizabeth's reign, and its removal brightened Queen Victoria's. The "100 too and utterly utter " school found its origin in Elizabeth's reign, and the thing was utterly detestable. "Life is real ; life is earnrrst, ' and he hoped he might be excused for fancying that if all parties had to do a honest day's work to get a day's bread, the" Greenery yell ery, Grosvenor gallery "business would soon be the last heard of. In alluding to the lecture and literary writers of the period, the lecturer said that no poet had a chance of succeeding unless he could secure the patronage of some wealthy person. It was the fashion to say that Queen Victoria's reign was far behind Elizabeth's in literary production and power, but with all respect to those gentlemen who held that opinion, he was presumptions enough to express one of the contrary, and in his judgment the literature of to-day was ahead of that of the past. Of literary statesmen certainly Elizabeth's reign and times did not surpass and did not equal our Gladstone and Lord Bea- consfield and others whom he might name. But Elizabeth's reign was a wonderful period, adorned by illustrious writers. Spencer's Facrze Queens and Shakespeare's dramas had not been equalled in this age, much less surpassed, but the general average of literary work, in quantity and quality in our time was, in his opinion, ahead of Eliz ibeth's. It was a matter for intelligent discussion, and would amply repay the most careful study. Proceeding to refer to the politics of Elia ibeth'4 reign, Mr. Pitt observed that it was not easy to contrast them with our times, as Whig, Tory, Conserva- tive and Liberal were n imes not then in existence. The chief differences between the English people were upon religion and the nation was divided accordingly. There was no Cabinet then as there is now, and there were no newspapers to criticise policies and persons. Elizabeth was the loser and the , country was the loser in that she did not oftener take the Parliament in her confidence, and she bad to scheme, lie, and deceive in order to keep up a show of right-doing. Elizabeth was blamed for everything, but personal respon- sibility was an uncomfortable burden. They might object Ito a thing on principle, but they had no ground of com- plaint when the elected representatives passed anything into law. No ruler in the world was so free of anxiety and care las Queen Victoria, and no persons had so free a Republic in which to live as we. With Elizabeth religion was a matter of policy and suitability to the times—at one time she encouraged the one, and ,at another time encouraged the other. Her policy was an opposite one to that parsued by Queen Mary, but her determination to please both parties was evidenced in her prayer book. But Protestant principles and practices became more in the ascendant, and of a population of 6,000,000 two-thirds or three-fourths were Protestants, and ' the rest Catholics. He asked the question "How stands religion in our time? " and proceeded to refer to it by alluding to the differences existing in the Church of England, pointing out the essential characteristics of the Ritualists, Evangelicalism, and the Broad Church, observing that to his mind worship was a recognition of the worth of the Almighty, which lead him to offer and entitled Him to his most humble and reverent adoration and praise. He was taught that God, through faith in His Son, was his father, so that he might approach him in the dual position of son and subject, with that boldness which should be without presumption I and that humility which should be without fear. Both sections of the Church—conformists and nonconform- ists—bad to encounter an amount of indifference and sceptic- ism that Elizabeth's reign knew nothing of. As to the scep- ticism due to scientific inquiry and deduction,the divines of Elizabeth had nothing to do with, but during the last 300 years men were finding out that God had a revelation in His works, and one was said to contradict another. Science was every day bringing light and fresh ktiowledge, and yet at every fresh discovery some eager enthusiast rushed into print to show that that discovery was in harmony with the Bible. He believed science was daily telling them in wondrous nature how He worked, and that it only mani- fested the wondrous power and diversities of operation of which God was :capable, and which He put forth in the exercise of His sovereign will. He believed vital Chris- tianity was stronger to-day in England than ever. Under- neath all there was much living work being done, and he believed it would go on and prosper until all peoples and nations should be blessed with the same liberty we had, and be brought to a knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ. (Ap- plause.)

, Mr. AVELINE, in moving a cordial vote of thanks to the lecturer, said the lecture had been an instructive one, and was good for the thought of all. Lectures of that kind were much needed. They had had some really substantial intel- lectual food, and he had very great pleasure in proposing a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Pitt. (Applause.) Mr. COOPER cordially seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation.

The LECTURER responded, and moved a similar compli- ment to the chairman, which was seconded by the Rev. W. C. TAYLOR, and carried.—The CHAIRMAN acknowledged the compliment, and the proceedings concluded with the sing- ing a hymn.

LIVELY MEETING OF RATEPAYERS. In compliaece with a requisition, Mr. F. H. Gossage, chairman of the Local Board, called a meeting of owners and ratepayers of the townships of Widnes, for the purpose, if t thought desirable, of approying and giving orment to op- posing by the Board of the following Bills in Parliament for conferring further powers upon the L. and N.W. Railway Company (additional powers) in connection with their own dertaking, and upon that -COMB iny and the Lancashire un and Yorkshire Railway Company in respect to their union railway, and upon the Lancashire Unions Raid.way in respect of their undertaking, and for other purposes. Secondly, a Bill to authorise the construction of a ship canal to Man- •chester, and for other purposes. The meeting was held in the Board-room, Alforde Chambers, on Wednesday morning, under the presidency of Mr. F. H. Gossage. There were a large number of workmen present, the room being well filled. Amongst those present were Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. S. Sadler, T. Handley, F. H. Pankhurst, E. Carey, J. Midwood, 'W. Martley, Johnson, W.ll. Kershaw, Robert Davies (of Warrington, solicitor to the Board in this matter), Allen (clerk), J. Beech, W. Sadler, J. Potter, T. Robinson, and Cooke (of Widnes Ironfaundry), Samuel Robinson, J. Robinson, B. Brown H. Johnson, .1. Taylor, J. Burroughs, J. Mooney, F. Neil, and Mr. and Mrs. Jamieson. The Clerk having read the requisition, the CHAIRMAN moved a formal resolution approving and consenting to the -opposition by the Local Board of the Bills which had been referred to e and that the district rate .or other funds or rates should he applied to the payment of the costs attend- ing such opposition. He should like to say that in this matter they were bound to take some action—they must decide either to oppose or not to oppose. Any opposition 'that they might offer would not commit them to any particular plan. What the Board required was that they ehould be able to pay from the rates the expenses of the opposition, which it was necessary should be taken.—Mr. Thews seconded the motion.—Mr. B. BROWN asked if the Bills could not be separated.—The CHAIRMAN : Mr. Davies -is here as our legal adviser, and I think we should take his opittion.—Mr. Deems was under- stood .to -say that they would be obliged to call another meeting with regard to the Ship Canal Bill --Mr. ROBINSON, senior, said he felt bound to oppose the. wishes of the Board in the matter of the street crossing. He thought they must use their best efforts to get the plan proposed by the railway company carried out. He under- 'stood that the Board had COllB reed that, if the railway com- pany would carry the road to Victoria-street, they would be satisfied. If that were done there would be two very sharp angles, which would render it impracticable for the Widnes Foundry Company to convey their heavy traffic of boilers, ekc., to the work. He begged to remind the Board that the Widnes Foundry Company were very large ratepayers, as well as the shopkeepers in Anne-street, and if the road was carried into Lugsdale-road they had no opposition to make. —A RATEPAYER : You don't care, I suppose, if you shut up all the shops in Anne-st—Mr. ROBINSON deprecated-such an insinuation.—Mr. Wm. SADLER : If your plan was carried out it would mean that the shops in Anne-street would all be ruined. I think the shopkeepers in Anne-street are as great ratepayers as the Widnes Foundry.—Mr. Robinson made a reply which was inaudible at the reporters' table.— At this point a number of workmen, evidently just coming from their labour, crow& I into the room.—Mr. SADLER : Have you any more men to send for Mr. Robinson ?—The CHAIRMAN: Order. order. He could not allow such ob- -serrations as that to be made. If Mr. Robinson had said all he had to say they could proceeed with the business.—Mr. Branonons : I understand that this is a meeting of rate- payers.—The CHAIRMAN :It is.—Mr. BURROUGHS : There is a very large number here who are not ratepayers at all. —The CHAIRMAN: Well, only those who are owners or ratepayers can vote. Mr. T. Coos (Widnes Foundry) : I should like to ask what are the grounds upon which the Board wishes to oppose the :Bill.—The Csmnares : I understand it is because they • don't approve of the London and North-Western 'Railway Company's scheme of crossings. We don't think it would be to the interest of the district if it were carried out —Mr. RosiNsox: But could sot an addition be made to the scheme which would meet both parties.—The CHAIRMAN: I don't know. You will have to oppose now or not oppose.—Mr. Theirersoet said the new road would be almost like a snake in its winding course, and it would make a great difference to the company which be represented.—The CHAIRMAN said the Board bad not committed themselves to anything. The London and-North-Westera Company had accepted nothing that was submitted to them, and the Board, if the resolution proposed werepassed, would be in a position to make a new ,proposition.—Mr. Rontersoer remarked that he did not think the Board would be justified in carrying their opposition into 'Parliament. Mr. CAREY observed that the •Board only desired te do the best they could for the general public. (Hear, hear.) With that object in view they had already put several schemes before Mr. Worthington, who repre- sented the company, and endeavoured to come to scone satisfactory conclusion. Mr. Worthington said it was per- fectly impossible to spend the money which would be needed to carry out a scheme which would satisfy the Anne- street people and the Foundry Company. It might he that no defined scheme was practicable, and that it would be better that they shot:aft-leave Anne-street in it present state. The Board wished to oppose the scheme in order that they ceukl get ptoper terms.—Mr. ROBINSON said it was perfectly easy to use the words, "best interests of the public," and he daresay the Widnes Foundry Company would join in with this Board in the use of those words But he contended that the road proposed by the railway company was the best for the public. When he considered the action of the Board towards the Foundry Company he wee really alarmed.—Mr. COOKE : You hear that the Board have not pledged themselves to any definite scheme, Mr. Robinsem—Mr. Roottesoer said the Board was taking an action which his firm would imperatively require to watch. —The CHAIRMAN: We contredicted the statement that we have decided upon any definite scheme.—Mr. CAREY said if it had not been for the interests of the Foundry Company and the people on the other side of Anne-street, the Board would have been perfectly satisfied with the first scheme. They had asked the railway company to continue the road in order to meet the views of the Foundry Company. He maintained that there was plenty of room allowed for taking the boilers and other heavy things round the corners mentioned by Mr. Robinson.— Mr. ROBINSON held an opposite opinion.—Mr. CAREY: There is plenty of opportunity to extend the road into Lugsda'e-road.—Mr. ROBINSON: When I am dead there will be plenty of opportunity. (Laughter.)—At the call of the • Chairman, Mr. DAvIES explained that the position of affairs that day was very simple. They had not to discuss what road would ultimately taken, but to get authority to oppose .the particular scheme of the London and North- Western Railway Company in Parliament, more with a view .of making terms than of carrying out the opposition. He thought he might say, from the instructions he had received, that there was no member sitting at the Board • ; who was in favour of any particular conceived' plan at all. He had advised the chairman within the last two minutes that the proper way in which this thing should be brought • before the. Board, was to let Mr. Robinson move an amendment • on that occasion that power be not granted, and then some gentlemen who was capable of setting before them the op- posite views, speak on Mr. Robinson's proposition. Let the • Board really know what the township of Widnes really wished, and he was sure that to the best of their abilities 7 , the members would carry out the wishes of the general body of ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) What they wanted that day was merely power to oppose the Bills now in Parliament. There would have to be another meeting, because the Canal Bill was not really in Parliament. —Mr. ROBINSON said he - should hesitate about adopting the suggestion of Mr. Davies to move an amendment. —The Cnetnereet : What we wish to know is whether the ratepayers will lend us the public funds to carry on the opposition, which we say is absolutely •necessasy.—Mr. Deer Les : If the ratepayers are decided in favour of the London and North-Western---- - The CHAIRMAN (interposing): Then they would outvote the Board.—Mr. Coos said there seemed to him reasons why • the Board should have the power to oppose the Bill indepen- dently of which way the road should go. It was no doubt • .quite right that the Board should hav, locus stencil iu the committee of the House of Commons.—The CHAIRMAN . observed that Mr. Robinson seemed to forget that this was 'no new matter: This matter had • been discussed for years. —Mr. Coos : Quite so.—The CHAIRMAN: The whole thing -has been discussed over and over again. So far as the mem- • doers are concerned, they would be quite willing to meet any -deputation which Mr. Robinson might wish to bring before them.—Mr. Coos said the raatter had been discussed but in • an indefinite manner. It has now become a definite pro- . ,posal. and we find it will be detrimental to our interests.— , The CHAIRMAN: We must do something, and if the ‘ratepayers say that we shall not apply the rates to the .opposition, we have done our duy, and the ratepevers will' 'have to suffer.—fr. ROBINSON: I should hesitate about preventing the Board getting locus stand!: in the matter, but 'it is of such vital importance to us that that road .shouldbe carried forward that we (Foundry Company) are asompelled in self-defence to oppose the Board.—Mr. BOWL- soar, as a ratepayer independent of the foundry, thought it • would be unwise to spend the ratepayers' money in on- posing this scheme, considering the stee of the town and .44 the towa's excheciner..-,Mr. D. HURST said the only desire of the owners in Anne-street was to have a bridge from Anne-street end for the convenience of traffic from Cross-street and other streets.—Mr.Coecturrr. said it was his opinion that Anne-street should not be changed. Mr. B. DUTTON said the Board was simply there to att.& for power. te spend the rate- payers' money je protecting the interests of the public. Now they had entire confidence in the Board, and, therefore, why shoeld they not em- power them to protect the ratepavera' in- terests? There were tell large vested interests involved in the matter that the Board oneht to be repre- sented in Parliament with regard to the Bill. —Mr JOHN ROBINSON: Might I ask Mr. Davies if he will give us an idea of the cost of opposing this seheme •in Parliament? There are some persons who cannot afford to pay the Board rates. We are weighed down with rates. The ratepayers ought to know how many millions it would came to.—Mr. B. Duetrow: You may rely that the Board will not spend your money foolishly.—The CHAIRMAN: I think you may rely with confidence upon Mr. Davies to give his opinion upon that matter. I think the Board are quite prepared to protect the interests of the rate- payers, but if we have no powers granted to us we shall tso stultified, and we may be ridden rough shod over by Anyone who chooses to cut up the town.—Mr. DAVIES remarlsed that if a petition was presented it would be the W 4,1,4 a bringing the Board into cemmunicetic.4l with a

the railway company, and they might not have to appear in the committee rooms of the House of Commons at all. Of course, if the Board got before the committee he could hardly tell the expenses, but it would not be thousands nothing of the sort. [h. ratepayer Millions was the word. (Laughter).-1 The opposition might cost hundreds, but he did not think. it was the wish of the Board that it should do ?O. If people brought schemes into Widnes' whether it was expensive or not, they would have to fight them by the only constitutional means—that was by petitioning against the Bills. He thought that very large questions would come be- fore the ratepayers if the Ship Canal Bill got into Parliament, because it tvould be a serious matter BO far as the fiver was concerned. But it was not necessary to go int 3 that to-day. What he said was let the Board have their con- fidence and present this petition, which will coat only. a few pounds. so as to put themselves into communication with the railway company Then it would be quite foolish to throw any money away.—Mr. T. HANDLEY remarked that the Board had received a petition in favour of the Board's scheme from the property owners in Anne-street.— Mr. Coos and Mr. ROBINSON said they would withdraw their opposition, on the understanding that they should have time to present a petition to the House of Commons on the matter.—The CniialiN: Anne-street ratepayers said they were quite content with what the Board proposed.—The motion was then put, and declared carried by a fair majority.—The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN.
div.p: BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual cangregatioual tea party and meeting was held in the school-room, on Tuesday evening. A large number of members sat down to tea, and at the subsequent proceedings there was a still greater attendance. The Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor, occupied the chair, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. Walker, 8.A., of Huyton ; Rev, Geo. Hack (Wesleyan), Runcorn; Mr. and Mrs. W. Hand- ley, Mrs. Thomas, Mr. and Mrs. 'I hos. Handley, Mr. and Mrs. F. Fairhurst, Mr. and Mrs. F. Beck, Mr. and Mrs. W. Brookes, Mrs. Chadwick, Mr. and Mrs. Littler, Miss Littler, Mr. and Mrs. W. U. Chadwick, &c. Daring the evening the following programme was gone through in a praiseworthy manner, Mr. J. Ravenscroft presiding at the harmonium : Anthem," I will love Thee, 0 Lord!" choir; song, "The pilot of the State," Mr. W. Gowanloch (encored); quartet, "In heavenly love abiding," by the Misses Handley, Mr. W. Handley, and A. Stanway ; song, "Life is a river." Mr. Littler (encored) ; quartet, "Soft as fades," Mr. Geo. Lacey, Miss Littler, J. teaunders, and F. Fairhurst; song," Angel ot hope," Miss Handler; recitation," How Harry Conquest's wife rang the bell," Mr. E. Rhodes (encored) ; anthem, "0 worship the Lord'!" choir; quartet, "Saviour, breathe," Mies Ainsworth, Miss.E. Handley, Mr. F. Fairhurst, and J. Towers. The CHMRMAN said it was with great pleasure that he was standing before them that night after another twelve months toil. He was glad to think that they were in cir- cumstances equally as happy and equally as prosperous as they were at the anniversary twelve months ago. He was also glad to be able to say that in all the labours in which they had been engaged during the past year he had been supported freely by a large number of the members of the church and congregation. First of all he must mention his deacons. He deemed that he owed to them a debt of gratitude for the kindness that they invariably manifested towards him, and he RAS happy to feel that he could say the. same in tegard to the whole of the church and congregation. From no one belonging to 'Bethesda Chapel had he received anything exceprkindness during his pastorate—(applause) —and he had, he thought, a pretty fair trial of Bethesda Chapel by this time. He had been there something like four years, and his experience during that time was such that he wished to remain there four years longer. (ap- plause.) He must not forget to mention the singers. Those who are strangers to the congregation had had a specimen of what they were able to do, hut that was nothing compared with what they could do—(applause)—and they had only to come to the Sunday morning or Sunday evening service in order to discover what they were really capable of performing. He was sure that their singing bad been a great help to him in the conduct of the service. The Sabbath school teachers also deserved a word. They had worked hard and labouriously during the year which had gone. Perhaps all bad not worked equally hard, but he hoped, however, that those who had been negligent and bad failed in their duties would at once reform. Don't delay the reformation, for in that, as in everything else that was good, delay was always dangerous. The officers, the superintendents, and secretary's both at St. Luke's and Bethesda had given a great deal of time and labour to their work, and he hoped the days to come would prove that their labours had not been in vain. During the past year they had lost a considerable number of members from the congregation. They had gone to other towns to reside, and he believed that some of them were doing a good work in their present positions. They were now about to lose one more from their midst, one who had for the past four years been an exceedingly faithful teacher. He re- ferred tether friend Mr. Tait. They all knew him. (Applause.) They all respected him very highly, and he was sure they would all wish that the town to which he was going to reside the blessings of God would follow him. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas concluded by remarking that the Rev. S. J. Baker, who was announced to be present, was unable ' through another engagement to fulfil his promise. The Rev. J. W. 'WALKER, after observing that it gave him great pleasure to be present because he cherished the warmest regard for their faithful pastor, delivered an address, mainly .directed to the young folks, and it was listened to with attention. Mr. F. FAIRHURST, at the call of the Chairman, said be should not have troubled the audience with any remarks but for the fact that a telegram had been received. which referred to a subject which was of great interest to the members of the Church They all knew that durine the last year there had been a house erected for the minister, upon which was a mortgage for £3OO, and a balance of £2O 63. 4d. due to the bank. The house, with various pieces ef furniture and fittings, had cost a little over £7OO. It was freehold, and therefore they had nothing to pay in the shape of ground rent, and that was a good thing. (Applause.) The telegram to which he had referred was from their old friend, Mr. James Handley (applause) who, in it, offered to give £5 towards clearing off the back balance if they would ty the other £l5. He thought that was a very good offer —(applause)—and although those present might not be thinking about the debt, they would see that someone else was. He was not going to beg —be could not beg if he tried—(laughter)—but ho wished to point out that only 36 persons had contributed to the fun( for the erection of the manse, and he was satisfied that a much larger number was able to give a sum however small for that purpose. The subscription list contained sums varying from £25, the handsome gift of Mr. Hudson. to 2s, and as treasurer of the ; fund, he did not feel too proud to receive the widow's mite. There was no reason why each member of the church, and each child in the Sunday Echoot, should not contribute the cost of a "brick " or two in that house, and he hoped that the generous offer which Mr. Handley now made, in addi- tion to his previous donation of £lO, would not have to be rejecte.d because they had not cleared off the remaining £l5. He should be glad to receive any subscription, or accept any premise that might be made that night or at any future time. (Applause.) The Rev. GEORGE HACK remarked that he was very glad to be amongst them, for if his Christianity were not stronger than his Methodism it would not be of much worth. He had lived long enough in the world, and travelled about sufficient to 'find that other folks were as good as himself, and in some respects perhaps a little better. He was very glad to have been honoured by an invitation to address a few words to them that night, (Ap- plause.) He felt very much at home ;—he felt in a kind of Methodist spirit, especially after Mr. Fairhurst's speech. Methodists were always :at home when they were after money. (Laughter.) Mr. iFairhurst's talk about money took away from him any tender feeling that he might have had, any fear that he was net in accord with the meeting ; and as a Methodisthe• felt that he was in complete accord with the Independents because they were after money. (Ap- plause.) When became to the town Mr. Thomas was the only minister that gave him a brotherly call, and he had of course respected -that :honour. (Applause.) As far as he was concerned it had created within him a feeling of special affection for him. He believed that there was a friendship between them which did not exist between him and the other ministers in the town for that reason. He did not know why they had changed ther name from Independents •to Congregationalists. The very word Independents reminded them of the ancient times when they had so much ecclesiastical intolerance and political feeling, and were it not for the Independents they in -all probability would not have had today •the intellectual freedom, 'the spiritual piety, and national prosperity which they had. (Hear, hear.) As a nation we owed a greatdealrnot to the Congregationalists, •but to the Independents. (Applause.) Although some people alleged that Independentasvere political dissenters, he ventured to say that it was the•religious interests of the cause which drove them to take hold of what he might call political resources and political forms, and that caused them to come into existence with a little bit of a .political touch--it was their necessity and not their forte. There were thousands of sturdy Nonconformists of the past who were .called not Congregationalists but Independents. (Ap- plause.) Referring to the literary aspect of Congregation- alism, Mr. Hack said they had to thank them for the kind of literature which came forth from their abler men. He read sometimes the literature which belonged to other denominations because it gave so much freshness to any Methodist sermon. He wished Bethesda Chapel God speed in its work-ding the next year. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. flecK, seconded by Mr. T. HAND- LEY, a vote of thanks was pissed to the chairmaa, to the gentlemen who had delivered addresses, to tbe chair, and to the ladies who had contributed in giving them so much enjoyment that evening. The CHAIRMILIS, In reply, observed that that was the first occasion since he had been in Runcorn that a minister from another denomination in the town had given his presence at :heir annual meeting. (Applause.) It was no t the firs, trifle one bad been asked, they had been asked many times ; but this was the first time one had attended. (Applause.)

div.head: EXNINEIL SATURDAY, FEBRUARY t 4, 1883
div.p: THE EXNINEIL SATURDAY, FEBRUARY t 4, 1883

LIFE OF JOHN BRIGHT, LECTURE AT RUNCORN. Mr. F. J. Norman read a paper on John Bright before the members of Brunswick Mutual Improvement Society, on Wednesday evening. Mr. T. Simister, the president, occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance.—The LECTORER said while the middle cusses of the country would ever point to their hero as a most noble example of the healthful influence of an honourable business training, while Saxon oratory would pin her faith to live down the ages on serne of his eloquent outbursts, and while Noncon- formity boasted of him as her sturdiest son, and Quakerdom proudly allotted to him the chief place in the crowded gallery of heaven-created nobility l-ed within the pale, the , world at large would know him best and honour him most in his political character. Descended from a noble line of sturdy Nonconformists, who in their day and generation did not shrink ft om avowing their principles at the expense of their liberty, he was given as a second son in a family of eleven to Jacob and Martha Bright, the former being then the struggling proprietor of a Rochdale woollen mill. This worthy couple, beetewing on their family the priceless heritage of a Christian training, had exemplified the truth of the Biblical injunction "train up a child in the way he I should go," fir all the members of their large family bad turned out blessings to themselves aed their country. At the age of 15 he completed his school term, and became an assistant in his father's mill. His leisure he devoted to study, reading with avidity the poets of his native tongue. About this time his strong political opinions were formed, probably being imbibed from Nichol is Nuttall. an intelligent Radical, in his father's employ. Catholic Emancipation was the stirring question of the day, and they found young John on the side of perfect religious equality. In 1833 he travelled on the Continent, and on his return engaged in the discussions of the Rochdale Literary Society, speaking against Republicanism in favour of a limited Monarchy, opposing capital punishment, and demanding the severance of Church and State. In 1836 he visited Italy, Egypt, and the Holy Land, and on his return lectured in his native town on the ancient cities he bad , visited. In that year he established an in- timacy with Richard Cobden, which had not inaptly been compared to the loving friendship of David and Jonathan. After referring to Mr. Bright's marriage with Miss Priest- man in 1839 and her death in 1841, Mr. Norman spoke of his connection with the Anti-Corn Law League. In 1843 he entered Parliament as the representative of Durham, which place he forsook for a seat at Manchester in 1847, in which year he married Miss Margaret Elizabeth Leathern. He then dealt with Mr. Bright's efforts in 1853 to counteract the war spirit then rampant, his sympathy with the North in the American war of separation, his speeches on the Reform Bill of 1866, and his acceptance of a seat in the Cabinet of Mr. Gladstone's Government in 1868, and con- cluded by remarking that crowded into the events of the past forty years bad been many of the most mighty revolue tions that history vet recorded. In the world of science, discoveries of an importance which it was impossible to exaggerated had rewarded the patient investigation of the restless, self-denying searchers after truth. In the world of politics the men of the Manchester school, discarding tl:e w•rn-out foibles of their ancestors, had laid on the sure foundations of truth and righteousness a policy which received its inspirations from the teachings of Divine Writ, and casting to the winds the sel- fish principles of a narrow patriotism, aimed at the universal brotherhood of mankind; while in the religious world had arisen noble souls of broad charity and far-reaching sym- pathy to call within the folds of Christian influence those whom sanctimonious phariseeism had relegated to the con- fines of the lost. Unfortunately these mighty forces, step- ping aside from the clearly defined path of duty, often wasted their spendthrift powers on futile and unseemly wrangles with each other. Science, through the misapplication of her devotees, appeared arrayed against religion, while both were often found despising, in tones of supercilious contempt, the manly efforts of the politician. Casting their eye down the vista .of a few more years, if they read aright the signs of the times, they saw these blunders rectified, and when happY humanity, reaping in fell the boundless blessings which these mighty forces yielded, should look with gratitude back to the stirring times in which they 'ived for the cause which brought about the lasting good, and, freed from the preju- dices which warped their minds, should read the story of their hero's life, and note his manly struggles to carry into the turmoil of political affairs the business-like qualities of trade, and the stern, unflinching principles of the moral code, they should write his name high in the list of those whom a grateful England ehould delight to honour. (Applause )—An interesting discussion, in which Messrs. Craig, J. D. Jones, 0. Leak, W. Stanway took place, followed.—On the motion of Mr. J. D. JONES, seconded by Mr. B. KNIVETON, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Norman for his eloquent lecture.
