HEAVY PENALTIES AT WIDNES. John Fletcher, farmer, Farnwortb, Joseph Grice, farm bailiff, Bold, William Halsall,. auctioneer, Prescot, Mrs. Warburton, farmer. Bold, were each charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with committing a breach of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act.—Mr.MacKenzle, of Prescot, defended.—Superintendent Barker said the order under which the proceedings were taken was enacted on the 14th of November, 1882, but the County of ' Lancashire was not included in the schedule until the 24th of January, 1883. On Tuesday evening, the 6fh met, Mr. Halsall called at his office at Prescot, and asked for instructions with regard to a sale of cattle he was to hold at Mr. Fletcher's farm on the B.h inst. He (Mr. Barker) explained to Mr. Halsall that if the cattle which were to be sold had been upon the farm where the sale was to take place 14 days, no license would be required. Mr. Halsall then remarked tkat there was a cow coming from Mrs. Warburton's farm at Bold, which it was wished to put in the sale. He (Mr. Barker) told Mr. Halsall that it could not be done," and that be rendered himself liable to a penalty for selling without a license under such eireura- eauc;;. Ia order that there might be no misunderstanding on Mr. Halsall's part, he took the trouble to read to him the section of the order bearing on the matter, and thoroughly explained the legal aspects of the case. Mr. Halsall then promised that the Caw he had mentioned should net be brought to the farm and sold, adding that even if it were brought he would see that it was not offered for sale, but should be taken whence it had come at once. On Thursday, the Bth February, he (Mr. Barker) was engaged at the Widnes Police Court all day, and while in the office during the afternoon, a person handed Inspector Barnett a letter, which was to the effect that Mr. tialsall had soh.l the cow and wished to know what license was required for its re- moval. He told Mr. Barnett to make inquiries, and he did sa.—Richard Baxter, butcher, Albert-road, Widnes, stated that he knew the defendants. He attended a sale at School Brow Farm, Farn worth, the residence of Mr. Fletcher, on the Bth inst. He purchased a fat cow there. At that time ha did not know that the cow sold to him had belonged to Mrs. Warburton, but he learnt that fact during the evening. He gave £l9 lOs for the animal, and he was asked to advance £2 108 as a deposit. He did as. In consequence of what was said to him he did not remove, nor had he seen the cow since, and the money he deposited had not been returned to him. Inspector Barnett said on Thursday, the Bth February, Mr. Halsall's son went to the police office and asked some questions in regard to the license for removing a cow. Inspector Barnett told him that under the circumstances the cow could not be removed, when Mr. Halsall's son said that his father had arranged the matter with Superintendent Barker. The Inspector re- plied "If it's right for Mr. Barker it's right for me, but I don't know anything about it." The same evening the In- , spector went to Mr. Fletcher's farm and saw the cow, wh:ch ' had been sold in the shippon. Mrs. Warburton acknow- ledged in his presence that the cow wag hers, and that she had sent it to the farm that morning. She said Mr. Halsall at first told her that he could not sell the cow, but afterwards he did sell it.— Superintendent Barker having repeated his opening state- ment under oath, Mr. MacKenzie addressed the Bench at great length in behalf of the defendants. His chief con- tention was that Mr. Halsall on the morning of the sale found that the cow had arrived at Fletcher's farm before him, but he refused to sell it. In the course of a conversa- tion which ensued, it was mentioned that although notices of the orders of Privy Council had been served in some cases, in others they had not, and also that the servant of Mrs. Warburton, who had inquired at St. Helens Police Station, had baen told that there was nothing to prevent the cow being removed. Thinking there might be something in these statements, Mr. Halsall took a proper course and sent his son with a letter tolnspector Barnett, at Widnes, to ascertain the truth of the statements. Inspector Barnett informed the son that the cow could be removed providing; his father made a declaration as to the purchaser. There- upon the cow was sold.—Evidence in support of this state- ment was given by Mr. Halsall, Mr. Joseph Grice, and Mr. Frederick Halsall. Mr. Grice stated a constable told him that he did not know that there were any orders on the sub- ject of removing cattle.—After the Magistrates had consulted for about 10 minutes, Mr. Gibbons said the Bench felt it to I ,be their duty to fine Halsall £lO and costs. They regretted to do this very much, but he ought to have refused to have anything to do with the cow after the instruc(ions which were circulated in the district by order of the Privy Council. Halsall was just the man that he (Mr. Gibbons) should have thought would have led people out of trouble of this kind instead of bringing them into it. In the opinion of the bench Mrs. Warburton had nothing to do with the active management of the farm, and they shonld fine her 20s and costs. As regarded Grice, he must have known that foot and mouth diseasa was exce tingly rampant in all directions, but in spite of all this he acted upon the statement made by a man who simply said he knew nothing about the matter. He would be fined £5. Fletcher made a very accomodating neighbour, and he would be fined 40a and costs.
MiiNCHESTER, LIVERPOOL. AND
NORTH LANCASHIRE AGRICULTURAL
SOCIETY.

On Thurs Jay, the adjourned annual meeting of the Royal Manchester, Liverpeol, and North Lancashire Agrictiltura: Society was held at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, Mr. L. Rawstorne (Preston), vice-president, occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance. The SECRETARY (Mr. T. Rigby) stated that the Mayor aud Corporation of Liverpool had consented to grant the free use of a portion of Newsham Park for the purposes of the society's next show. The site adjoined a field in pos- session of Mr. Millington, a member of the society, and was most suitable and compact. They were to have the use of this part of the park free on condition that they restored any damage which might be done to the rails or surface of the land, and they would have to pay Mr. Millington for the use of his field, which covered some 15 or 16 acres. Lord Derby had signified his assent to his selection as President for the year, and had expressed his intention to attend the show if his public duties would permit. The list of prizes suggested for the show to be held on the sth, 6th, and 7th September next was then submitted by the secretary. It proposed the division of a sum of £3,146 as follows :—£.lBo for farms and crops; £7BO for cattle; £1,025 for horses; £lOB for sheep; £lB6 for pigs ; £137 for farm produce, cheese, and butter; £146 for dogs; £324 for poultry ; £l5O for implements; and £lO for servants. In addition to these it was suggested as desirable to bold a parade of Liverpool cart horses, similar to that which took place on the occasion of the Royal Agricultural Show, and £lOO were set apart for this purpose, making the total prize money £3,146. The society had decided to contribute £2,000 towards this sum, and it was anticipated that the local committee of Liverpool would provide at least £l,OOO, the secretary remarking that on the last occasion that the show was held in Liverpool the local committee gave £1,500. The details of the prize list were then considered, and it was adopted as drawn up by the metting. "GRASSES OF OUR PASTURES."

Mr. ROBERT 'HOLLAND, botanist to the society, read a paper on the "Grasses of our pastures." He said a good deal had been heard lately of the desirability of laying down land to permanent pasture. There were not a few who urged the conversion of arable land into pasture, as a panacea for all the misfortunes which had so persistently assailed the British farmer for the last few years. There I might be considerable advantage in increasing the breadth f. of their permanent pastures, provided it was done judiciously and not indiscriminately: but he was afraid that a good deal of land had been laid down that would have paid better if it had remained arable, and he was sure that there was a good deal of arable land in the country which would be more profitably utilized for grass. He believed that when land had become too poor to grow corn or turnips to advantage, it bad been their custom to say " lay it down to grass to give it a rest," and the result had been complete disappointment. He held that if land was not in sufficient heart to grow a good crop of corn or turnips, it was simply absurd to expect it to be in a fit state to grow a good crop of grass. Upon referring to the Board of Trade returns he found that in 1872 there were 12,576,606 acres in permanent grass in Great Britain, that for the last ten years the quantity had been steadily increasing, and that in 1881 it had risen to 14,643,379 acres, being an in- crease of 2,067,791 acres, or something like 17 per cent. Grass land was chiefly utilized for the maintenance of cattle and sheep, and it would be fair to expect that cattle and sheep taken together had increased in number concurrently with the increase of the grass land that they occupied, if not to the extent of 17 per cent., still to a very considerable extent. The facts, however, did not bear out this expecta- tion. For simplicity's sake it would be best to convert cattle and sheep into one denomination, as the mathema- ticians would say, by considering so many sheep to be equal to one cow. Taking five sheep as equivalent to one cow, and reckoning accordingly, he found that in 1872 we had of horned stock 5,624,994, and of sheep 27,921,507, equal to 5,584,301 of horned stock, making a total of 11,209,295. In 1881 we had of : horned stock 5,911,642, and of sheep 24,551053, equal to horned stock 4,916,211, making a total of 10,827,211. So that although during the 10 years there had been a &Wit increase in horned stock, there had h?en in cattle and sheep together a marked decrease equal to 481,442, or almost 5 per cent. of all their flocks and herds. Therefore, either arable land was capable of supporting more stock than pastureland or the latter was not in as efficient a state as it should be, and was not carrying anything like the stock that it ought to do. He was convinced that the latter was the true explanation. Many of them must have observed a marked deterioration in the pastures of their own county. It might be partly owing, as he thought it was, to the many continuous wet summers which had, SO to speak, drowned out a number of the most nutritious but at the same time less hardy kind of grasses and other herbs, whose place bad been taken by poorer kinds that could withstand the wet. It might also be owing partly. as was no (.I,,ubt the case, to the fact that for several years the farmers had been working under difficulties, and had not had much money to lay out upon the land, which was going back for want of timely help. The fact had been veiy , generally noticed that a great deal of their pastureland was ' getting very poor. Agriculturists appeared to be of opinion that the increase in the extent of pasture at the expense of arable land was likely t? cantinue. If that was so, land must be laid down with judgment and intelligence. That ' which would pay best to plough must still be ploughed. div.head: CHEATING CHESHIRE FARMERS,
div.p: CHEATING CHESHIRE FARMERS,

A RUNCORN FRAUD CASE. Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Captain C. W. Hazlele-urst, Henry Dixon, a young man, of 42, Queen- street, Warrington, was charged. on remand, with having, on the 6th February, at Clifton, fraudulently obtained from Joseph Stokes, the sum of 2s 6d4from William Baker, 2s 63, and from Hervey Talbot 10s, by means of false pretences. —.Mr. F. A. Lake appeared for the prisoner.—Mr. Joseph Stokes., farmer, Clifton, and a member of Runcorn Board of , Guardians, said on Tuesday, the 6th instant, about eleven o'clock in the morning the prisoner called at his house, andi presented the following petition, saying, "This will explain all " :—" I hereby certify that the widow of the late James Platt has bad a severe misfortune by the death of her only two cows through inflammation, and therefore knowing her to be quite destitute and a woman of good character, I beg to reeommend her case to the notice of a few kind and benevolent friends, so as to enable her to purchase two more for to support her large and helpless family in respects which she bath hitherto done :—Dated this day of Feb- ruary.lBB3. William Whitlow, £1; subscription eubscribed by neighbours, &c, £5 103 6 1 ; James Weir, 10s; S. A., So; William Lowe, 103; Rev. E. Marsden, 10-3; Thomas Prieet- man, £1; Henry Reynolds, £1; J. Baguley, ss; J. Stokes, ss; W. Baker, 103; H. Talbot, 10s." Witness glanced at the petition and at the signatures which it bore. The prisoner said he was a poor man with a large family, and waseonly receiving 13s. per week. He remarked that he thought witness would perhaps know the gentleman who bad written him the petition, Mr. Whitlow. Mr. Stokes replied that he did very well, and as he was in a hurry he gave the prisoner half-a-crown. At the request of the prisoner he signed his name to the peti- tion, and recorded the amount he had contributed. The amount had since been altered on the petition to 53. He should not have given the prisoner anything had it not been for the petition. He did not know anyone of the name of Platt.—Mr. Wm. Baker, farmer, Ciifton, deposed that OA the morning of the 6th instant the prisoner went to his house. At that time witness was very busy, and the prisener said "I see, Mr. Barker, you are very busy. I will go down and see Mr. Stokes." In half an hour he returned, and saki "I suppose you don't know me." Witness assented, and prisoner informed him that he was the son of ' a widow at Preston Brook. He produced the petition, which witness read, and from the names which were appended he thought it was a genuine document, although it occurred to him that it was strange that the prisoner's mother should lose two cows. He gave the prisoner 35., signed the petition, and placed the amount upon it. The amount had since been altered to 10a.—Col. Henry Talbot said he was a justice of the peace for the county, and resided at Aston Grange. One day during the present month the prisoner presented the petition which had been read in court. He stated that he lived upon Sir Richard Brooke's estate, and that it was his mother who had lost the cows. In consequence of what the prisoner said, and reading the petition, he gave the prisoner 103. He noticed the name of the clergyman of the parish, Mr. Mars- den upon the petition, but he had since ascertained that he had not given him anything.—Mr. Wm. Whitlow, publican and farmer, Preston Brook, a member of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, said he did not know the prisoner, nor did he know a widow of the name of Platt at Preston Brook. He did not sign the petition (produced) nor con- tribute the subscription of £1 which was marked upon it.—Mr. Charles Lee Evans, agent for Sir Richard Brooke at Norton, deposed that on Friday last the prisoner went to his office and presented the petition. In consequence of what he had heard he sent his servant for P.S. Loundes, who arrived soon afterwards, and teok the prisoner into cus- tody.--P.S. Loundes, Halton, deposed to apprehending the prisoner and receiving the petition from Mr. Evans. The prisoner said, "I think you are mistaken," but whilst being conveyed to Runcorn he said, "I may as well plead guilty. It is all my own handwriting with the exception of Mr. Baker's, Mr. Stokes', and the bottom one." At the police station the prisoner was formally charged, but he made no reply. The same day the Sergeant went to Warrirgton and ascertained prisoner's address, and that he was a hawker. He also discovered that the prisoner's mother, whose name was Elizabeth Kearns, lodged at 2, Ship-yard, Warrington, and had no cows, nor ever had had any. There was no widow earned Platt at Preston Brook.— The prisoner, who was charged and cautioned in the usual way, said it was poverty that had caused him to do this. He had a wife and five little children. He had kept nothing back ftom the police.—The prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Knuteford sessions.—Mr. F. A. Lake, who appeared for the prisoner, applied for bail, bat Super- intendent Williamson objected, remarking that this was not the first time the prisoner had been in trouble.—Bail was refused.—lt is stated the prisoner has been carrying on the fraud for a long period, and about three months ago he pre- sented a similar petition to Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, who, however, was not to be cajoled by the prisoner's pre- ences, and declined to subscribe.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Offices, Victoria- road, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided. and there were also present the Revs. Father Finegan, Clarke, Messrs. R. Bradshaw, John Brock, H. Brunner, R. H. Davies, Robert Shaw, and G. 11. Danby (clerk). , PROPOSED MEMORIAL : INTERESTING DISCUSSION ON TIM

EDUCATION acr. The District Education Committee reported that during the month of January the number of cases summoned before the committee was—application for payment of fees 123, tor con- travention of Education Act 255. total 378. Fees were recom- mended to be paid in 108 cases. Twenty pers ,ns wereconvicted before the magistrates. The followleg recommendation was on the minutes of the committee :—That the Board do express concurrence in the object of the Ipswich School Board, and that the seal of the Board be affixed to the petition suggested by the said Board, and that the petition be then forwarded to the Education Department, for presentation, viz., To the Bight Honourable the Lords of the Committee of the Privy Council on Education. The memorial of the Widnes Sch rot Bard humbly sheweth ti-at your memorialists are of opinion that it would be for the Interest of the children themselves, of their parents, and of the country generally, to apply, more firmly than has hitherto been done, the provision made by recent legislation for securing to the rising generation the benefits of educetion, the oppor- tunity for which is now afforded by the existence of an adequate supply of efficient schools and competent teachers; and they believe that if the habit of early and regular school attendance were once secured for a few years, its further en- forcement would cease to be generally necessary. Your memorialists are of opinion that it is only by a thorough and judicious alteration of the Education Acts that these results can be attained, and beg to offer the following suggestions : .1. That the Elementary Education Acts should be codified; that the r resent system of bye-laws should be abolished ; and that compulsory education should be enforced by Act of Parlia- ment. 2. That the present doubtful state of the law liaising , front the want of agreement between the Elementary Educe- ' tion Acts and the Factory and Workshops' Acts seould be remedied: 3. That the lowest penalty in first offences for neg- lecting to cause a child to be efficiently instructed sh /uld be .five shillings, and that In second and subsequent offences the , penalty should increase with each conviction according to a fixed scale. 4. That the Summary Jurisdiction Act, 1879. so far as it relates to the administration of the Education Acts, should be repealed, as the present system of distre s warrants renders the working of the Acts very slow and expensive; and that the present excessive cost of summonses should be re- duced. 5. That a limit should be placed upon the discreti nary powers of the magistrates; and that simpler and less expen- sive means should be provided for access to the Court of Appeal. 6. That no private adventure school charging a fee under a shilling per week should be recognised, unless licensed by the School Board, subject in all cases of dispute to an appeal to the Education Department, whose decision thereon Labatt be final, Your memorialists therefore pray that your Lordships will take such steps as are necessary to bring the subject before the Houses of. Parliament. Ordered to be seslea i, with the seal of the Widnes School Board, this 22nd day of -February, 1883.—T. BUTTON TIMMIS, Chairman of the Hard. G. R. DANIsIr, Clerk of the Board." The Itev. Father CLARKE, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said there were some of the clauses in the memorial with which he did not agree, but there were some which had his entire approval. The Board had already . power over the schools mentioned in clause 6, which he did not think should be included in the memorial.—The Crratnttert : You think it might be harshly administered? —Father CLARKE : I think so. If the school is not efficient we have a remedy.—The CLERK said if the Board dis- covered that private adventure schools were not efficiently conducted it was the duty of the Board to prosecute the parents, upon whom would rest the onus of proving that their children were receiving efficient education.—Mr. BROCK wished to know whether it had been found in the experience of the Board that these alterations were re- .quirad.—The CLERK replied in the affirmative.— r. BROCK moved that the matter be referred back to the committee.—Father FINEGAN seconded the motion.— Mr. BROCK, referring to clause three, said it was rather hard upon those people who could not get their children to school. Take the case of widows who had to eafit their own living. It they had to take their children to school they had to ne- glect their work, and thus sustain a loss. But the magis- tratbs bad no power; they were bound to inflict a penalty: and be did not know whether it was wise to increase the penalties.—Mr. BRUNNER took objection to that part of -clause one, which read that the present system of bye-laws should be abolished. He thought it would be extremely difficult to get an Act of Parliament which would apply to fidas<arholacauntry, because what might suit a working popu- lation like-that in Widnes would not do for a purely agricul- tural population, nor for the children in a fishing village. Some years ago he was in favour of compulsory education by Act of Parliament, but in consequence of the working of the Education Act, he was less inclined to that view.—The Rev. .Father FttitsGaN said one great flaw -in the 1341ucation Act was what was known in the schools aa passing. He found by experience that there was a great difficulty in get- ting children to work when they left school. He thought the memorial had brought before them many things which might be useful, butte submitted that the matter he had mentioned was a question of great importance to them. When a child had passed a certain standard he ought to 1.e.-! allowed to leare school, so thet he could commence work. At present the laws of the Factory Act and the Edecation Act were not alike in this matter, and he thought they should be assimilated.—The CHAIRMAN suggested that the Rev. Father Finegan should draw up a draft of what he desired, and have it inserted in the memorial.—Mr. Srraw said if a child was sent to school early he could leave earlier than a boy who was sent later or attended school irregularlay.—The memorial was referred back to the cow.mittee.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority met on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. There were present :—The Revs. Canon Barclay (chairman), John Lockwood, and J. W. N. Tanner ; Messrs. John Ashton (vice-chairman), John Mclntwe, .T. Darbysblre, J. Mid wood, C. Rigby, J. Knowles, _Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). FRODSHAM AND SUTTON WATER SUPPLY..

A meeting of the Sutton Water Supply Committee warn held in the Clerk's office, Frodsham, on Friday, the 16th February. Present :—Mr. John Ashton (chairman), Rev: J. Lockwood, Messrs. E. A. Wallington, T. Andrews, H. Linaker (clerk to the Authority), H. Bancroft (engineer); J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances).—Mr. Bavcnorr read the following scheme and estimate of supplying Frodsham and part of Sutton with water :—"ln compliance with your verbal instructioas, I beg to inform you that I have gone carefully into the question of supplying Frodsham and part of Sutton with water. The springs at Five Crosses appear to me the most desirable, if not the only source, from which a good supply of pure water can be ob- tained within a reasonable distance of the town. The water has been analysed by the late Professor Calvert and Dr. Cart, r Bell, county analyst. Professor Calvert reported that both free and albuminoid ammonia were absent from

the sample sent to him; and that the water was rather hard, but that its hardness is not sufficient to render it objec- tionable for detergent purposes; and concludes by stating that the witer is entirely free from pollution by decompos- ing animal matter, which fact, he says, is very remarkable. Dr. Carter Bell's analysis indicates only a very slight trace of ammonia, viz: of free .02, and of albuminoid .02 parts in one million. The amount of albuminoid ammonia almost always bears an exact proportion to the amount of organic matter in ths: r•er. Dr. Carter Bell concludes his report as follows :—" This is a very good water, and one that I can recommend for supply." The springs were carefully gauged by Mr. Farrington from early on in March to marly the end of September' 1879, and gave an average yield of 35.430 gallons in 24 hours: the mini- mum yield being 27,500 gallons, but this did not last for any considerable time, whilst the maximum reached 05,200 gallons. The rcort stated that since the last meeting of the I Authority gaugings bad again been taken, and the average I supply was 95,056 gallons in 24 hours. The number of I houses within the district that could be supplied was MI,

and estimating thepopulation at .3,100 and the quantity re- quired for works, there would be a total consumption of 37,000. The average yield of the springs, in Mr. Bancroft's opinion, throughout the year might be taken at 55,000 gal- lons per day, which would allow for an increase of the .population along the line of mains of at least 50 per cent., and the only future expense would be in providing more -storage room. At the springs he proposed forming a tank. or small reservoir, six feet deep, and taking two lines of pipes out of it. The lower one would be to supply the property down the road from Five Crosses to and from the village of Overton, and the upper one would convey the water direct from the service reservoir. By this arrangement there would be a constant supply to the higher part of the district. There would be no expense in turning the water on and off moening and evening at the reservoir, and the whole of the water could be utilized if necessary. The springs should be walled in ; and to prevent the possibility of any pollution of the water, Mr. Bancroft considered it advisable for the Authority to purchase the strip of garden land abutting upon the road. The site of the proposed reservoir was on Mr. Aston's land. in Tewnsfield-lane ; but if a plot of land could be procured at a lower level it would save a little expense in service piping, as the pressure would be rather considerable at the lower parts of the. town. In tkis estimate, Mr. Bancroft stated that he had allowed for piping down Red-lane and Church-street, Fluin-lane and Chapel-street. By doing as the water could be passed in either direction to the main street in case of an accident. The piping would ex- tend to the railway bridge, opposite Mr. Wright's house, Booth-street, Ship-street, Cobden-street, Newtown, the glue woks along the river side, and to the houses in Sutton, near Frodsham Bridge. The total estimated colt was £4,075. The total income he estimated at £473 8s 4d. This estimate was based upon all cottages at and under £lO per annum be- ing charged 2d per week, and houses above that rental is in the pound on the rack rent. In addition to this source of income there would be the sale of water to various works, which he estimated at £55 per year. The scheme, he estimated, would pay 11t per cent., and, with the exception of the cost of collection of water rents *ere would be no annual expenses incurred, except sundry repairs."—The committee, after careful con- sideration and discussion, resolved that they were of opinion a public water supply was very desirable for Frodsham and that part of Sutton which was immediately adjacent to Frodebam Bridge, and that the scheme as prepared by Mr. Bancroft was the most feasible, and would be sufficient to supply the requirements of the district, and they recom- mended that it be carried out.—Mr. ASHTON moved that the report be adopted, and that the necessary proceedings be taken far carrying the plans into execution.—Mr. Mnewoon said he was quite satisfied that the scheme would be ye 7 beneficial, and he had pleasure in seconding the adoption o' the report.—The motion was carried unanimously. 1 grass, needed proper preparation, draining, cultivating, en- riching, and when this was accomplished the selection of seeds was by no means the least important part of the busi- ness. Opinions differed as to whether it was better to sow a few strictly pereanial kinds which produced a large amout of herbage, or a considerable number of SpedieS filmy of which might not be of a large size. He favoured the sowing of not too much of one sort, but a considerable number of sorts, provided they were of known excellence, and were suitable to the soil. Many individual members of one speices, grown on a given space, say a square-yard, were all trying to ob,ain the same food from, the soil and elbowed each other out, the stranger plants getting the mastery, and the weaker ones drying and leaving bare spaces. But a great number of different speices were able to exist together upon a given space for they each required, and were en- deavouring to obtain different kinds of food which ,they sought at varying depths in the soil.

- DEATH OF LORD EGERTON OF TATToN. Lord Egerton of Tattoo, lord-lieutenant of the county of Cheshire, died on Wednesday night, at his seat at Tatton Park, Knutsford. His lordship, who was in his 77th year, has been in bad health_for some time, but latterly had ap-
peared muck better. When seized with bronchitis, medical aid was summoned, but without avail. His lordship was taken worse about five o'clock on Wednesday morning, and
kept gradually sinking to the time of his death, at ten minutes to -eight. His successor is his son, the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, one of the representatives_ for Mid-
Cheshire, where his elevation to the Upper House will
cause a vacancy:
The deceased _peer, William. Tatton _Egerton, was of

ancient lineage, being descended from Robert Tatton, of Wythenshawe, who had for ancestors Nicholas Tatton, baron of the Exchequer of Chester in 1451, and Robert de Tattoo, of Northenden, 1297. His father, Wilbraham Egerton., his grandfather William, and his great uncle Samuel were members of Parliament for Chester, whilst he himself spent nearly thirty years of his life in the House of Commons. lii political life his character was one of _ _ _ _ .
acknowledged weight and influence, and in both Houses he served as Chairman of Private Bill Committees, though for some time he had ceased to take an active part in

Parliamentary duties. He was a justice oi the peace and deputy-lieutenant, and in the various offices which he filled he won the confidence of those with whom he was associated. The father of Loid Egerton married Elizabeth, daughter of Sir Christopher 1 Sykes, of which union there were several sons and daugh- ters, the eldest son being William 'Patton, who was born on the 30th of December, 1808. Educated at Eton, Lord Egerton afterwards proceeded to Christ Church, Oxford, and it was in the year 1830 that he was returned to the House of Commons for Lymington. After the passing of the first Reform Bill he was elected member for Cheshire,

and he represented his own county for more than a guarter of a century. It was in 1859, under the Premiership of the late Earl of Derby, that he was raised to the Upper House under the title of Lord Egerton of Tatton. He married the Lady Charlotte Elizabeth Loftus, eldest daughter of the Marquis of Ely, who died in 1878, having had several sons and daughters. In public and private life, the late Lord Egerton was highly esteemed. A firm friend, a candid counsellor, and generous interpreter of every duty belong- . . .

ing to his high station, he was valued by all who came in contact with him. He was thoroughly Conservative in politics, as every phase of his public career abundantly atL tests. His duties as a county gentleman were habitually and conscientiously attended to as far as health and manifold en- gagements would permit. As lord-lieutenant of his county and chairman of quarter sessions he was assiduous, painstaking, and considerate. When he sat upon the bench prisoners were always sure that their cases would be inves- tigated carefully,dispassionately,but shrewdly. As a landlord Lord Egerton took the most serious views of his responsibi- lities, and was accustomed to act with promptitude, rapidity, and straightforwardness. His charities were numerous, and were spread over a wide area. He gave of his substance in small sums as well as in large—in the shape of donations to struggling men and of benefactions to public institutions. All that he did in this way cannot, of course, be known but the public has long bad before it evidence to repletion of his generous tendencies and the ungrudging character of the support which he gave to any cause which appeared to him to be deserving. His charities were at the same time al- ways discriminatingly dispensed, and in this respect he was a pattern worthy of imitation by those who have to spare of the good things of this life. He was a Churchman to the backbone, and manifested the solidity of his principles and the sincerety of his sentiments in the most conclusive way. The Church, therefore, naturally benefited largely by his liberality. His early connection with Christ Church, Oxford, no doubt gave a tone to his mind which never wore off. His sympathies were with what is known a‘the Oxford school of theology; but his sympathies were by no means of sectional narrowness. With the Bishop of London's Fund the name of Lord Egerton will be closely identified, and none have more reason to be grateful to him than the London clergy. He was an active member of the committee of the Lancashire Cotton Relief Fund, which sat in Manchester in 1862-5, and during that time he employed hundreds of poor operatives in his own county. Lord Egerton had the patron- age of several church livings, and it was always judiciauslv exercised. The remains of the deceased nobleman will be interred at Rostherne Church, on Tuesday. At the adjourned annual meeting of the Royal Man- chester, Liverpool, sad North Lancashire Agricultural So- ciety (of which the deceased nobleman was for many years a president), held on Thursday at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, the news of his death was communi- cated to the members by Mr. Hough (Mere), who said that for many years his Lordship had been highly respected in the county as a good landlord and former representative in Parliament; he was a constant friend to the :society, and his death would be felt as a severe loss to many in Cheshire. (Hear, hear).—The Chairman (Mr. L. Rawstorne) said he was sure all the members of the society shared the feel- ing of regret which had been expressed. Lord Egerton had always taken the greatest interest in everything connected with agriculture, and had often presided at their meetings. In his opinion, however, it would be premature to make any formal expression of opinion at that meeting.—(Hear, hear).—Mr. R. Lansdale (Boothstown) concurred in the gen( ral sentiment of regret, and said that during a fifty years' acquaintance with Lord Egerton be bad never failed to observe the keen interest which his Lordship took in matters connected with the welfare of Cheshire farmers and the agricultural cemmunity generally. The vacancy in the representation of Mid-Cheshire will probably lead to an exciting and interesting contest. For a tong time Lord Egerton bad been in failing health, and, in view of the fact that a vacancy might occur at any time, the Liberals have kept their machinery in a forward state of preparation, and have given close attention to the register. There is a robust Liberal feeling in the constitu- ency, and the party is anxious to make another effort to obtain a share of the representation. They made a deter- mined effort in 1868 to wrest the two seats from the Tories, but the Egerton interest was too strong for them, although they had the active influence of Lord de Tabley (whose son was one of the candidates) with them. In 1874 there was no contest, nor was the re- turn of Mr. P. E. Warburton in place of Colonel Egerton Leigh challenged when the latter died; but at the last general election another effort was made to change the colour of the representation. On this occasion Mr. G. W. Latham and Mr. 'V Armitage opposed Mr. Egerton and Mr. Warburton. They were not successful, but the result was highly encouraging. The numbers were: Egerton, 3,868; Warburton, 3,700; Latham. 3,374; Armitage,' 3,247. No steps will be taken, as a matter of course, by either party until after the funeral of Lord Egerton ; but it may perhaps be assumed that Mr. G. W. Latham will again do battle for the Liberals. Who the Tory candiaate will be it is not so easy to say; but in any case the Conservatives lose their strongest candidate in the elevation of the retiring member. The Egerton influence will no doubt, as heretofore, be given to the Conservative candidate, but this will not be so strongly felt as in the case of the eldest son of the family. On the other hand, if the Liberals choose Mr. Latham as their representative, they will have a candidate whose public work, and especially the interest he has displayed on behalf of the farmers, has increased his influence' apd they have certainly not numerically decreased. There is a strong Liberal feeling in Sale, Altrincham, and Bowdon, where many Manchester men live; and Northwich and Lymm, two of the other larger centres of the division, will alto give solid support to the party. Our Runcorn representative writes: The elevation of the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, of Rostherne MaLor, to the peerage creates a vacancy in the representation of Mid- Cheshire. It was rumoured yesterday that the Hon. A. Egerton, the younger brother, will be the Conservative can- didate,and there is little doubt that Mr, G.W.Latham,of Brad- well Hall, will contest the seat in the Liberaleinterest. Mr. Latham was the Liberal candidate at the general election in 1874, and again in 1880, but he was unsuccessful on each occasion. There is. every reason to believe, however, that Liberal principles have won net a few from the Tory in- terest during the past few years. Mr. Latham has lost no opportunity of addressing the electors, who are chiefly agriculturists, and his intimate knowledge of all that per- tains to land, which he has freely used in advocating the interests of farmers, has gained him much popularity. Run- corn is one of the largest towns in the division, and the Liberals there may be expected to give a good account of themselves. Their organisation is in good working order, the members of the association are enthusiastic in the cause, and everything that can be done will be done to return a Liberal member. At the last revision the Liberals made a net gain of about 40 votes over their Conservative opponents, mainly through the keen foresight of Mr. 0. Leak, the secretary. That gentleman sent in claims for about 32 householders, who, though not rated at £l2, yet paid that amount, or over, in rent, and in every c ise he was successful. The Conservatives adver- tiaed a meeting for Tuesday next, but in consequence of the death of Lord Egerton it has been indefinitely postponed.

The hay is of excellent quality, well got and stacked, and the while is highly deserving the notice of the public. Continued search has been made for gold at Llanelltyd, near Bartnouth, North Wales, where a few days ago several pieces of the precious metal were found near an old copper mine by a lad who was digging for copper. Farther nug- gets have been found. and it is thought not improbable that a rediscovery have been made of a gold mine where in 1860 a quantity of gold was found to the value of £36,000, and for a few years the mine was worked so successfully as to yield a profit cf £20,000. A- mine was also worked with much success for some years at Bala by a company; under the chairmanship of Mr. John Btight, M.P., but was ulti- mately abandoned.
